# Contributing to Zoomies

Thank you for helping Zoomies give self-hosted GitHub Actions runners a better
run. Contributions of code, tests, documentation, bug reports, design feedback,
and real-world deployment experience are all welcome.

By participating, you agree to follow our [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

## Before you start

- Search the [issues](https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies/issues) before opening a
  new one.
- Small, focused fixes can go straight to a pull request.
- For a substantial feature, architectural change, new dependency, or breaking
  configuration change, open an issue first so the approach can be agreed
  before a lot of work is done.
- Report vulnerabilities privately as described in
  [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). Do not open a public issue for a security problem.

Zoomies is early-beta software that creates runners on other people's machines.
Changes to authentication, authorisation, secrets, runner isolation, container
backends, networking, upgrades, or deletion paths deserve an explicit threat
and failure-mode review.

## Development requirements

The core binary is written in Go. The web UI is built with Svelte and embedded
in that binary.

- Go 1.27.1 or later (the floor in `go.mod`; CI builds and releases with 1.27.2)
- A C compiler (`gcc` or `clang`), because `make test` runs under the race
  detector and Go refuses `-race` without cgo
- Node.js 22 or later and npm, when changing or rebuilding the UI. `make lint`
  also runs `npm ci` in `web/`, so it needs them too
- Python 3.12 (`python3`), only for building the documentation site
- Git
- Docker or Podman for backend and image work
- A GitHub App only for tests or development flows that actually talk to GitHub

Start by forking the repository, then clone your fork:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/zoomies.git
cd zoomies
git remote add -t main upstream https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies.git
```

`-t main` keeps `git fetch upstream` to the one branch you need. The repository
also carries a generated `zoomies-ai-context` branch whose history is large, and
a plain fetch would download all of it.

Create a branch from the latest `main`:

```sh
git fetch upstream
git switch -c fix/short-description upstream/main
```

Use a short, descriptive branch name such as `fix/agent-reconnect`,
`feat/pool-draining`, or `docs/runner-security`.

## Build and run

Run `make help` for the maintained list of targets.

A fresh checkout does not compile on its own. `internal/api` embeds the built
UI, which is a build product that is not committed, so a plain `go vet` or
`go test` fails with `pattern all:webdist: no matching files found` until it
exists. Run this once first:

```sh
make build-nogui    # Go-only build; writes a placeholder UI, needs no Node
```

`make build` does the same with the real UI (it needs Node), and either is
enough for every Go command afterwards.

```sh
make build          # build the Go binary with the web UI embedded
make build-nogui    # fast Go-only inner loop
make dev            # local controller with debug logging and auth disabled
make ui-dev         # Vite UI against a controller on localhost:8080
```

`make ui-dev` needs the UI's dependencies, so run `npm ci` in `web/` first.

The development mode disables authentication and is for a local workstation
only. Do not expose it to a network.

## Make a focused change

- Keep pull requests small enough to review and explain the reason for the
  change, not only the implementation.
- Follow the surrounding code and UI patterns. Go code must be formatted with
  `gofmt`; web code is formatted with Prettier. `make fmt` does both.
- Read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) before changing anything structural. Written for
  coding agents, it is also the contributor's map: which package owns what, the
  boundaries between packages that review is meant to catch, and the house
  voice (British spelling, comments that explain why, no em dashes). The
  reasoning behind the shape is in [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md).
- A new documentation page goes under `docs/` and into the `nav` in
  `mkdocs.yml`; a page that is in neither is easy to miss and is checked by
  `mkdocs build --strict`.
- Add or update tests for changed behaviour.
- Update user documentation, configuration examples, API definitions, and
  screenshots when the public behaviour changes.
- Preserve safe defaults. If a change weakens isolation or exposes a new
  capability, make the trade-off explicit in both the UI and documentation.
- Never commit credentials, GitHub App keys, tokens, local databases, generated
  logs, or build output.

Generated files have a single source of truth:

- After changing `api/openapi.yaml`, run `make openapi` and commit both files it
  writes: the Go copy the API serves (`internal/api/openapi_spec.go`) and the
  TypeScript client (`web/src/lib/api/schema.d.ts`). A test fails on either one
  when it is stale.
- After changing the runner image catalogue in `internal/naming`, run
  `make generate` and commit everything it updates. Do not hand-edit generated
  catalogue sections.

## Test your change

Run the narrowest relevant tests while developing, then the standard checks
before opening a pull request:

```sh
make test-short     # the quick Go tests, a few minutes
make fmt            # gofmt and Prettier; make lint fails on what this would change
make lint           # vet, gofmt, staticcheck and the UI lint
make test           # every Go test with the race detector
```

`make test` can take an hour with few CPUs (CI splits it across six runners), so
`make test-short` is the loop to work in. `make lint` runs staticcheck only if it is installed and says
so when it is not; CI always runs it, so installing it
(`go install honnef.co/go/tools/cmd/staticcheck@latest`) saves a round trip.

A change made for speed is held to a number. Run the benchmarks of the package
it touches before the change and after it, and put the comparison in the commit
message:

```sh
make bench BENCH_PKGS=./internal/scheduler | tee before.txt
# make the change, then
make bench BENCH_PKGS=./internal/scheduler | tee after.txt
benchstat before.txt after.txt     # go install golang.org/x/perf/cmd/benchstat@latest
```

`make bench` runs every benchmark six times, so that `benchstat` can say how
far apart the runs were; `BENCH=Decide/quiet` narrows it by name. Leave the
machine alone while it runs, because benchmarks that share the CPU contaminate
each other, and compare only runs made on the same machine.

For documentation changes, install the pinned dependencies and run the same
strict build as the site workflow:

```sh
python3 -m pip install --require-hashes -r docs/requirements.txt
mkdocs build --strict
```

The build must produce `site/sitemap.xml`, `site/llms.txt` and `site/badge.svg`,
and the header must name the latest release, `hooks/source.py` asks the GitHub
API for it at build time, so set `GITHUB_TOKEN` if the anonymous rate limit is
in the way. These checks catch broken links and missing published assets before
a PR is merged.

For web UI changes, also run:

```sh
cd web
npm ci --no-audit --no-fund
npm run check
npm run test:unit
npx playwright install chromium   # once, for make test-ui
cd ..
make test-ui
```

Some suites intentionally require more setup:

- `make test-drill` runs a real controller and agent against fake GitHub.
- `make test-e2e` exercises Docker-backed end-to-end behaviour and skips when
  required GitHub credentials are absent.
- `make screenshots` captures documentation screenshots from the real UI.
- `make vet-tags` vets the suites behind the `e2e`, `drill` and `load` build
  tags. A plain `go vet` never compiles them; `make lint` and CI both run this
  target, and it is the quick check after editing a file under one of those tags.

You do not need to run an unrelated privileged or credential-dependent suite.
State exactly what you ran and what you could not run in the pull request.

CI runs what a change's files can affect, decided by the `changes` job at the
top of `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, on a pull request and on `main` alike:

| A change to | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| Markdown, `docs/`, the site, the workflows | the `internal/docs` and `internal/naming` checks, which hold the prose to the code, about a minute |
| `install.sh` | the `install.sh` checks and the upgrade test; no binaries or images |
| `web/` | the UI and Playwright jobs, and the docs checks |
| `deploy/` | the image builds and the tests that read those files |
| Go, or anything not listed | the whole set |
| `ci.yml`, the `Makefile`, `go.mod` | everything |

The Go suite is split by package across six runners (the controller and API
packages are two shards each, the store is one, and everything else shares the
last); `make test TEST_PKGS=./internal/store/` runs one the way CI does. Coverage is
measured on `main`, when the whole Go suite ran. `main` publishes the dev
channel's binaries and images only from a commit that changes what ships (Go,
the UI or `deploy/`) so a documentation merge leaves `--version dev` where it
was. A manual dispatch runs everything. CodeQL, govulncheck, the fuzz targets
and Scorecard run only when their own inputs change, and weekly regardless.

A pull request's checks stop when the pull request does. Pushing to it replaces
the run in flight, and closing or merging it starts a run that takes over the
pull request's concurrency group, cancels the one still going and skips every
job, so a merged pull request does not keep its fleet slots while the commit
on `main` queues behind them. Only a pull request is ever cancelled: runs on
`main` queue instead, because they publish the dev channel. A new workflow that
runs on `pull_request` needs the same three parts, and `internal/docs` fails
without them: the `closed` type, the shared group, and a
`github.event.action != 'closed'` guard leading every job's condition.

## Commit and open a pull request

Use clear, imperative commit subjects:

```sh
git add path/to/changed-file
git commit -m "Add runner reconnect backoff"
git push -u origin fix/agent-reconnect
```

Open a pull request against `eyupio/zoomies:main`. Include:

- the problem and why it matters;
- the chosen approach and important trade-offs;
- the tests and manual checks performed;
- screenshots or a short recording for visible UI changes;
- documentation, configuration, migration, or compatibility impact; and
- any follow-up work deliberately left out.

Keep the branch current with `main`, respond to review comments, and avoid
mixing unrelated cleanup into the same pull request. Maintainers may edit,
squash, or reword commits when merging.

## Coding and design principles

- Prefer straightforward code and explicit failure modes over cleverness.
- Errors should tell an operator what is true, why it matters, and what to do
  next.
- Keep the controller usable as one Go binary with SQLite; do not introduce a
  required external database or orchestration platform without prior agreement.
- The CLI and web UI are clients of the same API. Keep their behaviour and
  terminology aligned.
- Preserve accessibility, responsive layouts, keyboard operation, light and
  dark themes, and the guidance in
  [docs/ui-guidelines.md](docs/ui-guidelines.md).
- Treat logs, metrics, audit records, and documentation as part of the feature,
  not an afterthought.

## Releases

Maintainers cut releases. The shape a tag must have, the signing key and what to
do when a release build fails are in [RELEASING.md](RELEASING.md).

# Zoomies

A self-hosted GitHub Actions runner fleet controller. This glossary fixes the words an operator sees in the web UI, so that one word means one thing wherever it appears.

## Language

### People

**Operator**:
The person who runs a Zoomies fleet and watches it, often all day. Setup flows and the public status page serve other audiences with their own rules.
_Avoid_: Admin, user (when meaning the person watching the fleet)

### Capacity

**Machine**:
A virtual machine that a provider rented or created. It exists before any agent has joined it.
_Avoid_: VM, node, instance

**Host**:
Anything running a Zoomies agent that the controller can place runners on, rented or your own. A machine becomes a host when its agent joins.
_Avoid_: Agent (as a thing an operator manages), node, server

**Agent**:
The software on a host that runs runners. It is never the thing an operator manages; the host is.
_Avoid_: "the agent on this host" as a stand-in for the host

**GitHub-hosted**:
Work that ran on GitHub's own runners rather than on this fleet.
_Avoid_: Hosted elsewhere, elsewhere, other runners

### Stopping and holding

**Drain**:
Finish what you have, take nothing new, then go. Applies to a runner or a machine.
_Avoid_: Cordon, disable (for a runner or machine)

**Pause**:
Hold, reversibly, with nothing lost. Applies to a pool, a provider, a host or a queued job's demand.
_Avoid_: Cordon, disable, hold (for a pool, provider, host or queued job)

**Disable**:
Switch an account off so it can no longer sign in. Used for accounts only.
_Avoid_: Turn off (for an account); disable (for a pool, provider or host)

**Remove**:
Take something out of the fleet or the queue for good. The action and the resulting state use the same word.
_Avoid_: Delete (for the action, where the state is Removed), deleted

### Work

**Run**:
One execution of a workflow, made up of jobs.
_Avoid_: Workflow (when meaning a run), build

**Job**:
One unit of work inside a run, placed on a single runner.
_Avoid_: Task, build step

**Queue**:
The jobs waiting for a runner, and what the fleet will do to start one for each. Where the demand itself is meant, say "queued demand".
_Avoid_: Provisioning (for the queue), backlog

**Provisioning**:
The state of a runner that is being set up. It describes runners only, never the queue.
_Avoid_: Provisioning demand, provisioning (for queued jobs)

### Things that are wrong

**Problem**:
Something that is currently wrong with the fleet, shown with a severity of Info, Warning or Error.
_Avoid_: Issue, risk, "to fix", warning (as a noun for a live fault)

**Finding**:
A result in the Kennel Club report about one repository. A report about a repository, not a live fault.
_Avoid_: Problem (for a Kennel Club result), warning

**Fixable, Advice, Optional**:
The three words a flagged row in a host's check tables carries beside its Warning or Suggestion badge: Fixable when the report offers the row to `zoomies tune`, Advice when it does not, Optional for a trade-off. Words about one row, never a state of the host. Warning stays reserved for the badge on a counted check.
_Avoid_: Warning (for what a person can do about a row), Safe (for Fixable, which is also a tier name)

**Accepted**:
A counted warning on one host that an operator has decided is deliberate, with a reason and an end date. It keeps its row and leaves the counts, the problems and the pill, and counts again when its value changes or its date passes. Neither a state of the host nor a fourth kind of check result: the badge is the accent tone, never a status colour.
_Avoid_: Ignored, muted, silenced, suppressed, dismissed (which is a problem's word)

### Kennel Club

**Kennel Club**:
The part of Zoomies that checks how a repository measures up against what affects CI and the fleet. It is the only meaning of "Kennel" in the interface's structure.
_Avoid_: Kennel (alone), AI Context (which is separate)

**AI Context**:
Repository context that Zoomies generates for AI tools to read. A top-level area of its own, not part of the Kennel Club.
_Avoid_: Kennel Club (as its parent), operational context

### Updating

**Update helper**:
The root-owned pair of systemd units that runs `zoomies upgrade` on a host for a release the service asks for. Only the host's owner installs it, and a host without it is never updated from the web UI. Not the agent, and never installed by it.
_Avoid_: Updater, update agent, update service, helper (alone, where another helper could be meant)

**Soak**:
How long a release must have been public before `auto` takes it, counted from when GitHub published it. A newer release restarts it. Applies to `auto` only: a person pressing Update has decided.
_Avoid_: Delay, grace period, cool-down, bake time

**Rollout**:
Taking the hosts behind the controller to the release it runs, one host at a time. It is running, halted (held after a failure until a person resumes or cancels it), done or cancelled. Never the controller's own update.
_Avoid_: Deployment, wave, batch

### Theme words

**Dog-park vocabulary**:
The optional playful state names, such as "Walkies!" and "Back in the kennel", that stand in for the plain state names when an operator switches them on. A theme, not a set of domain terms: every one has a plain equivalent that carries the meaning.
_Avoid_: Kennel vocabulary, quirky status

# Give your GitHub Actions runners the Zoomies. **Free and open source.** Install in minutes, manage every runner from a live web UI, and move off static runners without rebuilding your CI. Zoomies gives each job a fresh runner, scales across the hosts and runner operating systems you already use, and makes the fleet easy to see and operate, without Kubernetes and without a database server. Single Go binary. SQLite. AGPL-3.0. *The [support matrix](https://zoomies.sh/#what-is-qualified) separates what a test has actually run on from what merely builds. Read it before you put anything precious on this.* [![Licence: AGPL-3.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/licence-AGPL--3.0-2F80ED?labelColor=080808)](LICENSE) [![Latest release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/eyupio/zoomies?display_name=tag&include_prereleases&color=2F80ED&labelColor=080808)](https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies/releases) [![CI](https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/eyupio/zoomies/branch/main/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/eyupio/zoomies) [![OpenSSF Scorecard](https://api.scorecard.dev/projects/github.com/eyupio/zoomies/badge)](https://scorecard.dev/viewer/?uri=github.com/eyupio/zoomies) [![OpenSSF Best Practices](https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/14604/badge)](https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/14604) [![Website](https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies/actions/workflows/docs.yml/badge.svg)](https://zoomies.sh) [![CI has the Zoomies](https://zoomies.sh/badge.svg)](https://zoomies.sh) ```sh curl -fsSL https://zoomies.sh/install.sh | sh ``` Just looking? To run a local demo, add `-s -- --demo` after `sh` and nothing is installed: a controller with a fleet already in it runs on your machine only, and goes when you press Ctrl-C. **[zoomies.sh](https://zoomies.sh)** · [Quick start](https://zoomies.sh/quickstart/) · [See the web UI](https://zoomies.sh/ui/) · [Architecture](https://zoomies.sh/architecture/) · [Configuration](https://zoomies.sh/configuration/) · [Migrating](https://zoomies.sh/migration/) · [Security](https://zoomies.sh/security/) · [API](https://zoomies.sh/api-surface/) · [FAQ](https://zoomies.sh/faq/)
--- ## Your home lab. Your runner fleet. **Bring private machines into the pack with built-in Tailcat connections.** Use the hardware you already own for GitHub Actions: no public host IP, no port forwarding, no Tailscale account and no separate tunnel installation. Choose **Private connection · Tailcat** in Add a host, run one command, and manage private and cloud hosts together in the live web UI. Free and open source. Your hardware, your network, one pack. [Connect a private host](docs/private-hosts.md). ## What it does You point Zoomies at a GitHub organisation, or at a repository on a personal account. It watches for queued jobs, starts a fresh runner for each one, and destroys the runner when the job finishes. ```mermaid flowchart LR q["a job is queued
on GitHub"] w["workflow_job
webhook"] d["the scheduler decides,
and says why"] s["an agent starts
a runner container"] a["GitHub hands
the job to it"] e["the job finishes,
the container is destroyed"] q --> w --> d --> s --> a --> e ``` * **A live web UI.** Fourteen pages, one job each, all updating in place from the controller's event stream; you never have to press refresh, though there is a button where you want to be sure. Light and dark, a command palette, and a log viewer built for a hundred thousand lines. [See every page](https://zoomies.sh/ui/). * **Elastic CPU zoomies.** Every runner keeps its guaranteed share of its host, and a busy one is lent the CPU nobody else is using; the next queued job's room held back, the host's reserve untouched. New pools measure it by default and move nothing until you say so. [How it works](https://zoomies.sh/elastic-cpu/). * **Elastic memory.** A job about to be killed for its memory limit is given more, out of memory no other runner on its host was promised, raised, never lowered, with swap as the last resort. [How it works](https://zoomies.sh/elastic-memory/). * **Ephemeral by default.** One job per runner. Nothing leaks from one workflow run to the next. * **No pasted tokens.** Zoomies authenticates as a GitHub App and mints single-use JIT registrations itself. * **Event-driven.** `workflow_job` webhooks, with polling only as a fallback so a misconfigured webhook does not silently stop your fleet. * **Multi-host, multi-OS.** One controller, any number of agents. Agents connect outbound only, so a host behind NAT needs no inbound rule. Runner images for Ubuntu 24.04, Ubuntu 26.04, Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, Debian 13, Fedora 42 and Rocky Linux 9, each for amd64 and arm64, and a pool is only ever placed on a host that matches the one it asked for. * **Actually observable.** SQLite for state, Prometheus metrics, structured logs, live log streaming, job history with queue waits, and an audit row for every mutating action. * **Backed up by itself, and off the machine.** A consistent copy of the database nightly, kept to a ceiling, and every copy sent on to as many S3-compatible destinations as you name, added and tested from the Backups tab without editing a file or restarting anything, sealed with that destination's passphrase before it leaves the host, and caught up automatically after a bucket that was unreachable comes back. The same tab takes one now, verifies it, downloads it plain or sealed, brings one back out of a bucket, uploads one from elsewhere, and stages a restore the next restart applies. The configuration alone exports as a `zoomies.yaml` and imports with a preview. [Backup and restore](https://zoomies.sh/backup-and-restore/). * **Safe defaults.** Loopback bind, auth on, no Docker socket in your jobs, no root, and every deviation named at startup and in the UI. A self-hosted runner still runs your repositories' code, [what that does and does not protect](https://zoomies.sh/security/). ## Quick start Five minutes on a fresh Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora or Alpine host. ```sh curl -fsSL https://zoomies.sh/install.sh | sh ``` The script checks what it needs before it downloads anything (the platform it is fetching for, whether the install prefix can be written and with what, whether there is a terminal to run setup on) shows you what it is about to do, and asks once. Then it hands off to `zoomies init`. **How setup finishes depends on how you choose to run Zoomies**, and that is the one fork worth knowing about before you start. Compose is the default whenever you have a `compose` command: #### Native: finishes in the terminal 1. **Install mode**: single VM with an embedded agent, controller only, or agent only. 2. **Service user and directories**: a dedicated unprivileged `zoomies` user. 3. **Backend**: rootless Docker if it finds one, otherwise Docker, Podman or bare process, with the trade-off on every option. 4. **Bind address and TLS**: loopback, a certificate you provide, a self-signed one, or reverse-proxy mode. 5. **Review**: the whole plan and the exact files it will write, before anything is written. Install, change an answer, or stop. 6. **GitHub App**: opens your browser at a pre-filled App manifest with exactly the permissions Zoomies needs and the webhook URL already set. It asks first whether you also want migration pull requests, which is the one thing that needs write access to code, and the answer is no unless you say otherwise. Create it, and the credentials come back to the installer automatically. 7. **First admin account**, and a **first pool** sized for the host. 8. **Service**: a hardened systemd unit (or launchd), started and health-checked. It finishes with the URL, your login, and the `runs-on:` line to put in a workflow. #### Compose or Docker: finishes in the browser The same questions up to the review, then it writes the deployment (`docker-compose.yml` and a fully populated `.env`, or one container and an env file) and brings it up. The database lives in a volume this installer cannot open, so the last three steps happen in the browser instead: create the first administrator, connect GitHub, create a pool. The closing summary prints all three with their exact addresses, and the Overview repeats them as a checklist that ticks itself off. Prefer to read it first? That is the intended way, and [the quick start](docs/quickstart.md#1-install) has the three lines that download it, page through it and then run it. Automating it instead? Every prompt has a flag and the rest has an answer file: [unattended installs](docs/quickstart.md#unattended-installs). ### Docker Compose instead ```sh git clone https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies && cd zoomies cp .env.example .env $EDITOR .env # ZOOMIES_EXTERNAL_URL, ZOOMIES_ENCRYPTION_KEY, DOCKER_GID mkdir -p data && sudo chown 65532:65532 data # the container runs as 65532 sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/zoomies/shared && sudo chown 65532:65532 /var/lib/zoomies/shared docker compose up -d docker compose logs zoomies | grep 'setup token' ``` Then open the controller, paste that token, and create the first administrator. The token is what proves the instance is yours: the origin is reachable the moment the container starts, and an empty database is a thing a stranger can find too. It changes on every restart and stops being printed once an account exists. (The installer above creates the administrator on the console, so it never needs one.) Three values are required, and compose will not start without them: * `ZOOMIES_EXTERNAL_URL`: the https address you and GitHub reach the controller at. Webhooks are delivered there, and creating the GitHub App sends your browser back there. * `ZOOMIES_ENCRYPTION_KEY`: `openssl rand -base64 32`. Back it up; without it the stored App key cannot be read. * `DOCKER_GID`: the gid that owns `/var/run/docker.sock`, which `stat -c '%g' /var/run/docker.sock` prints. It is not always the group called `docker`. The container is put in that group so it can create runner containers; with the wrong number it comes up healthy and can start nothing. If that happens, the Hosts page says which group the container holds and which line to change, and `docker compose up -d` recreates it. If `stat` prints `0`, the socket belongs to root's group: give it a group of its own (`sudo groupadd docker`, then restart the daemon) or use a rootless daemon rather than putting the container in group 0. The database lives in `./data` beside the compose file, so a backup is a copy of a directory. It has to be owned by uid 65532: a bind mount keeps the host directory's ownership, and the container is not root, so the `chown` needs `sudo`. Open the https address, not `http://`: the session cookie is marked Secure because the external URL is https, and a browser on a plain-http page throws it away. Zoomies refuses to sign you in from such a page and says why. This path has no `zoomies init`, so nothing creates a pool for you. Once GitHub is connected, make the first one on the **Pools** page; nothing runs until a pool exists. The compose file is set up for running behind Cloudflare: the origin serves plain HTTP on port 80 and Cloudflare terminates TLS, with `ZOOMIES_EXTERNAL_URL` set to the https address so cookies, webhook URLs and links are all correct, and Cloudflare's ranges in `ZOOMIES_TRUSTED_PROXIES` so the audit log records real client addresses rather than Cloudflare's. Firewall the origin to Cloudflare, or use a Tunnel and publish no port at all. See [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md#behind-cloudflare-or-any-reverse-proxy). ### On a PaaS, with Nixpacks There is a `nixpacks.toml` in the repository root, so a platform that builds with [Nixpacks](https://nixpacks.com), Coolify, Dokploy, Railway, Zeabur, Easypanel, can deploy Zoomies from the source: point it at this repository, set `ZOOMIES_EXTERNAL_URL`, `ZOOMIES_ENCRYPTION_KEY` and `ZOOMIES_TRUSTED_PROXIES`, and mount a volume at `/data`. What you get is a **controller**, not a fleet. A PaaS gives a container no Docker socket, so the embedded agent is off and nothing on that host can start a runner: join agents from machines that do have a container runtime, exactly as below. See [docs/paas.md](docs/paas.md). ### From a provider's marketplace `deploy/marketplace/` renders a cloud-config that boots an instance into a running controller: pinned images, HTTPS however you want it in front (a Cloudflare Tunnel with no inbound rule at all, Cloudflare in front of a published origin, a certificate from Let's Encrypt, one of your own, or your load balancer) and no credential in the instance metadata. The first administrator is created in the browser with the setup token the controller prints, and GitHub is connected there too. It deploys a **controller**. Zoomies stays self-hosted and bring-your-own-infrastructure: you own the runner capacity, whether that is the same instance, your own machines, or a hypervisor. See [docs/marketplace.md](docs/marketplace.md), including what it has not yet been tested on. ### Add another host **Hosts → Add a host** comes filled in from what the controller already knows and hands you one line to paste on the new machine; leave the page open and it says the moment the host has joined. The token is single-use, and the agent dials out rather than being dialled, so nothing has to be opened on either firewall. The [quick start](docs/quickstart.md#adding-another-host) has the line itself. A host that would rather not have a binary on it can run `ghcr.io/eyupio/zoomies-agent` instead, ideally on the same tag as the controller. `latest` is the newest release and `dev` is the tip of `main`, for the controller and the agent alike; the runner images are the exception and still track `main`. [Which image tag to run](docs/upgrading.md#which-image-tag-to-run) is the table, and [an agent in a container](docs/hosts-and-pools.md#an-agent-in-a-container) is what it needs. ## Your first pool A pool says what labels your runners answer to and how many may exist. On a single-host install, setup creates one for you once GitHub is connected, derived from what the host actually is: named after the platform, capped at the machine's capacity, nothing kept idle when nothing is queued, ephemeral, and Docker with no socket reachable from the job. The [quick start](docs/quickstart.md#4-your-first-pool) has the settings it lands on. A workflow that builds images needs one more thing from its pool, *Docker in jobs* set to `dind`, and that is the whole change: the pool is switched to a runner image with a Docker client as it is saved. Then in a workflow: ```yaml jobs: build: runs-on: zoomies-linux-x64 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: make test ``` Push it. Zoomies sees the `workflow_job` webhook, starts a runner, and you watch the whole thing happen on the Overview page without refreshing. One label is enough, and it is branded on purpose: a reviewer can tell at a glance that the job has left GitHub's runners. [The labels to give a pool](docs/configuration.md#the-labels-to-give-a-pool) has the rest, including the `zoomies` label every pool answers to. ## Moving your repositories over You do not have to edit every workflow by hand. **Migrate** in the UI reads the workflows in the repositories your App can see, rewrites their `runs-on` lines, shows you the exact diff, and opens one pull request per repository. It changes `runs-on` and nothing else (comments, indentation and quoting all survive byte for byte) and it refuses to guess: a job on `${{ matrix.os }}`, a job already on a self-hosted runner, or a label you chose not to map is listed as left alone, with the reason, both in the review screen and in the pull request body. It needs three App permissions the rest of Zoomies deliberately does not ask for (Contents, Pull requests, Workflows), connecting GitHub asks whether you want them, and the default is no, and it tells you which are missing before it tries anything. **Already running your own static runners?** Then the wizard is not the tool; it deliberately leaves those jobs where they are, because somebody made that decision on purpose. Give a Zoomies pool the label your existing runners already advertise and not a line of any workflow changes: the same `runs-on` reaches the new fleet, and you retire the old machines as the work moves across. See [docs/migration.md](docs/migration.md). ## The UI Fourteen pages, one job each: **Overview** (fleet health, queue depth, scaling decisions in plain words, and a problems panel that is quiet when nothing is wrong), **Pools**, **Runners**, **Queue**, **Workflows** (one row per workflow run, opening to the jobs inside it), **Usage**, **Hosts**, **Providers**, **Installations**, **Eli repairs**, **Migrate**, **Kennel Club** (the repositories this fleet serves, checked against what affects CI, with **AI Context** inside it), **Audit**, **Settings**. It is the primary way to configure and run a fleet, and the docs describe each task from there first; the CLI, Compose and the API are [the other ways in](https://zoomies.sh/#run-it-from-the-browser-reach-it-from-anywhere).

The problems drawer: what is true, why it matters, what to change.

A job that went wrong, and where.

Hosts, their room left, and the backends their agents found.

Migrate: the exact diff before a pull request is opened.
Light and dark, keyboard-driven, a `⌘K` command palette, live everywhere, and a log viewer that handles a hundred thousand lines. Every page is shown at [zoomies.sh/ui](https://zoomies.sh/ui/). The screenshots are taken from the real binary against its demo fleet by `make screenshots`, so they cannot show a page the product does not have. Design system in [docs/ui-guidelines.md](docs/ui-guidelines.md), identity in [docs/brand.md](docs/brand.md). ## The CLI Fleet commands and the UI share the same REST API. Local host OS checks and tuning use the installed native binary: health is visible in the UI, while changes require explicit consent in the CLI. ```sh zoomies status # the Overview, in a terminal zoomies pools list zoomies pools create --name zoomies-linux-x64 --labels zoomies-linux-x64 --installation ins_k3f9qz2m --max 8 zoomies pools edit pool_k3f9qz2m --cpu-burst automatic # lend busy runners the host's spare CPU zoomies runners list --state busy zoomies runners drain run_k3f9qz2m zoomies runners logs run_k3f9qz2m --follow zoomies jobs list --repo acme/widgets --since 24h zoomies hosts join-token create --ttl 15m zoomies doctor # readable OS health summary sudo zoomies doctor --interactive # review and approve individual fixes sudo zoomies tune --dry-run # exact proposed changes sudo zoomies tune --revert # restore recorded host settings zoomies audit tail ``` ```sh export ZOOMIES_URL=https://zoomies.example.com export ZOOMIES_TOKEN=zoo_... ``` Host health is collected by the native agent, or by a read-only native health service for container deployments, and updates the host badges automatically. Upgrades never apply tuning. See [Host health and tuning](docs/host-health.md). A coding agent gets the same fleet over the Model Context Protocol, either straight from the controller at `/mcp` with a token or through `zoomies mcp` on its own machine. It reads failed jobs, their timelines and runner logs, and can act only as far as its token's role allows, see [the CLI reference](docs/cli.md#zoomies-mcp). ```sh claude mcp add --transport http zoomies https://zoomies.example.com/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer zoo_..." ``` An agent that drives the `zoomies` command instead can be taught it with the `zoomies` skill, [`skills/zoomies`](skills/zoomies/SKILL.md). It reads the fleet freely, asks before it changes anything and leaves the commands that reshape a host to you. Install the three skills below into a project with ```sh npx skills add eyupio/zoomies --skill zoomies --skill zoomies-kennel --skill zoomies-optimise ``` which writes them to `.agents/skills/` and links them into `.claude/skills/` for Claude Code. Name the skills with `--skill`: the repository also carries two skills for working on Zoomies itself, which your agent should not pick up. Or copy a folder by hand into the agent's skills directory (`.claude/skills/` in a project, or `~/.claude/skills/` for every project, for Claude Code). See [the CLI reference](docs/cli.md#the-zoomies-skill). A second skill, [`skills/zoomies-kennel`](skills/zoomies-kennel/SKILL.md), runs `zoomies kennel check` over a checkout's workflow files with nothing sent anywhere, summarises the findings with security first, and fixes only the ones you choose; see [the zoomies-kennel skill](docs/cli.md#the-zoomies-kennel-skill). A third, [`skills/zoomies-optimise`](skills/zoomies-optimise/SKILL.md), reads the fleet's evidence for one slow job or pull request and says which of the four workflow changes Zoomies can preview fits it, or that none does. # Releasing Zoomies

This is for the people who cut releases. Everything here is what
`.github/workflows/release.yml` and `internal/updates` already do; the page
exists so that none of it has to be rediscovered during a release that has gone
wrong.

## What a release is

A release is a GitHub release. Publishing one starts `release.yml`, which
builds the binaries for five platforms and the controller, agent and runner
images, signs `checksums.txt`, and attaches the binaries, the checksums, the
signature and the provenance to the release. A run can also be started by hand
with the `workflow_dispatch` input `tag`, for a tag that has no release yet, a
draft or a pre-release; a published full release is refused (see "When the build
fails" below).

`install.sh` resolves `latest` through GitHub's `/releases/latest` redirect, so
it can name a release whose files are not attached yet, and it waits a few
minutes for them. `zoomies upgrade` and the Updates page read the releases list
and skip any release that lacks `checksums.txt` or the binary for the machine
asking.

## The shape of a tag

| Kind | Tag | Where it is offered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Full release | `v` and exactly three numbers: `v1.3.7` | `install.sh`, `zoomies upgrade`, the Updates page |
| Pre-release | `v`, numbers, a hyphen and a suffix: `v1.3.7-rc1`, `v0.1-alpha` | Nowhere by default. GitHub keeps it out of `/releases/latest` and the updater skips it |
| The `dev` channel | `dev` | Maintained by CI from `main`; publishing or editing it is skipped by the release workflow |

A full release has exactly three numbers because that is the only shape the
updater accepts. `updates.ValidTag` is `^v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$`; the tag goes
into a download address and into a request a privileged helper reads, so the
check is strict on purpose. The version package orders three numbers and cannot
place a fourth, so a build stamped `1.3.6.1` compares as "differs" from every
other build.

The `setup` job in `release.yml` refuses a full-release tag of any other shape
before it builds anything, and a test in `internal/docs` keeps its pattern equal
to `updates.ValidTag`. GitHub will still let someone publish a release with any
tag, because the workflow runs after publication: the refusal shows as a red
run, not as a release that was never created. Nothing is offered from it, since
no files are attached.

## Before you publish

1. The tag is `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` with three numbers, on a commit whose CI is
   green on `main`.
2. The repository secret `RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY` is set. A release cut without it
   fails rather than publishing unsigned, and so does one cut before the public
   half is committed. See [Signing releases](docs/upgrading.md#signing-releases)
   for how the key is made and rotated.
3. For something that should not reach anyone yet, use a pre-release tag with a
   hyphen, not a full release.

## Check what you published

When the run finishes, list the assets. An updater offers a release only if it
carries `checksums.txt` and the binary for the machine asking, so a release
that lacks them is invisible to every controller:

```sh
gh release view v1.3.7 --json assets --jq '.assets[].name'
gh run list --workflow=release.yml --limit 3
```

## When the build fails

Do the cheapest thing that fits the cause.

1. **A transient failure** (a runner vendor outage, a network error while
   pulling a base image). Re-run the failed jobs of the same run in the Actions
   tab. The run keeps its original `release` event, which the workflow allows to
   attach files to the release that triggered it. This path has not been
   exercised in this repository's history; if it does not work, go to step 3.
   A failure at the step "Sign the release" is the likeliest cause of all:
   `RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY` is missing, or is not the private half of the public
   key the binary trusts (`internal/releasekey`). Correct the secret and re-run
   the failed jobs; the tag stays as it is, and a run that fails there attaches
   nothing, so nothing unsigned was published. `v1.3.6` failed this way.
2. **A draft or a pre-release.** Start the workflow by hand from the Actions
   tab, giving the tag. Rebuilding replaces the files behind it, which is fine
   for something nobody is meant to have yet.
3. **A published full release whose cause is in the tree.** The workflow
   refuses to rebuild it by hand: "A released tag is a promise; cut a new tag
   rather than replacing what people have already downloaded." Fix the cause on
   `main` and publish the next patch version (`v1.3.8` after a failed `v1.3.7`).
   The failed release stays, with no files, and no updater offers it. Say in its
   notes which release replaces it.

Do not repair a failed release by publishing the same version with a fourth
number. It builds, and it is then the release GitHub calls "Latest" while no
controller can be updated to it. That is what the shape check above now stops.

# Security policy

## Reporting a vulnerability

Open a [private security advisory][advisory] on this repository rather than a
public issue. GitHub keeps the report between you and the maintainers until
there is a fix.

Please include:

* the version, from `zoomies version`;
* the configuration with secrets removed, which `zoomies config print` produces
  already blanked;
* what an attacker gains, and what they need in order to get it.

Reports are acknowledged within a few days. If a fix is warranted it ships in a
release, and the advisory is published with credit unless you would rather it
were not.

## What counts

Zoomies runs other people's workflow code on your machines, so the interesting
boundary is between a job and everything else: escaping a runner container,
reading another job's secrets, reaching the controller's API without a
credential, or making the controller act as an administrator.

Some things are dangerous **by configuration** rather than by defect, and each
one is documented, warned about at startup and shown in the UI's problems
drawer. `pool.docker_mode: host-socket` hands the host's Docker socket to
every job in the pool, which is root on the host by design; `security.disable_auth`
treats every request as an administrator. Those are not vulnerabilities, they
are settings with a cost, and [docs/security.md](docs/security.md) says what
each one costs. A report that they can be abused once enabled tells us what the
warning already says.

What *is* worth reporting: a way to reach one of those states without setting
it, a warning that does not fire when it should, or a default that is less safe
than it is documented to be.

## Supported versions

Fixes go to the latest release; there are no maintained release branches. Upgrading is stop, replace the binary, start,
see [Upgrading](docs/upgrading.md).

[advisory]: https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies/security/advisories/new

# Support

Zoomies is free and open-source software, published under AGPL-3.0 by people
who are not on call for it. There is no support contract, no guaranteed
response time, and no paid tier that would buy one. That is the whole boundary,
and it is stated plainly so that nobody discovers it during an incident.

What there is: documentation written to be acted on, error messages that name
the setting to change, and maintainers who read what comes in.

## Where a question goes

| You want to | Go to |
| --- | --- |
| Work out why something is not doing what you expected | [Troubleshooting](https://zoomies.sh/troubleshooting/), and the problems panel in your own UI; it names the setting rather than the symptom |
| Ask how to do something | [Issues](https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies/issues), labelled `question`. Discussions are not enabled on this repository |
| Report a bug | [Issues](https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies/issues) |
| Report a vulnerability | A [private advisory](https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies/security/advisories/new). Not an issue, not a discussion, see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) |
| Propose a change | [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) |

## What makes a report answerable

Most of what a maintainer needs, Zoomies will print for you:

* `zoomies version`: the build, on both the controller and the agent if they
  differ;
* `zoomies config print`: the configuration, already blanked of secrets;
* the problem code from the UI or the log, such as `bind.public_no_tls`. Every
  code has [a row explaining it](https://zoomies.sh/problem-codes/), and naming
  it skips a round of questions;
* what you expected, and what happened instead.

Logs help. Please read them before pasting: a job's output is yours, and a
controller's log can name repositories.

## If you deployed from a provider's marketplace

Your provider supports their platform; the instance, its network, its volume,
its billing. They do not maintain Zoomies and cannot fix it.

So: anything about the machine goes to them, and anything about the software
comes here, on the same terms as every other installation. Nothing about a
one-click install creates a support relationship with this project, and no
provider can offer one on its behalf.

## What is qualified

Not everything that builds has been run. The [support
matrix](https://zoomies.sh/#what-is-qualified) separates the two, and it is
worth reading before putting anything precious on this; a report about a
combination nobody has qualified is still welcome, but it is a different
conversation from one about a combination that is supposed to work.

#!/bin/sh
# Zoomies Proxmox connector, the short form of the setup command the provider
# wizard generates.
#
#   curl -fsSL https://zoomies.sh/connect-proxmox.sh | sudo sh -s -- \
#       --version <tag> --key <key> --controller <url> --setup-id <id> --token <token>
#
# The wizard prints the whole line with the values filled in. Reading this file
# first is safe, and recommended: it downloads one release binary, checks the
# release's checksums.txt against the release signing key and the binary's SHA-256
# against those checksums, keeps a private copy under /var/lib/zoomies-proxmox and
# runs `zoomies providers connect-proxmox` with the values it was given. It never
# touches an installed runner host: no /usr/local/bin, no zoomies-agent unit, no
# join token.
#
# This is the same work the wizard's "Show the full command" text does, in a
# file that is checked in CI instead of pasted from a browser.
#
# POSIX sh, checked with dash in CI.

set -eu
umask 077

die() { printf 'zoomies: %s\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
say() { printf 'zoomies: %s\n' "$*" >&2; }
warn() { printf 'zoomies: warning: %s\n' "$*" >&2; }

# --- release signature check: identical in connect-proxmox.sh and
# --- deploy/instapods/fetch.sh, and a test in internal/docs holds the copies equal.
# The release signing key, base64: the line `zoomies release keygen` writes to
# release.pub. A test keeps it equal to the key compiled into the binary and to
# the one in install.sh, and keeps the two functions below identical in every
# script that carries them.
RELEASE_KEY="6dK2/jDPHR8wAjsIayrxGxL8ednKVKdEMHdRcmNU67U="

# signature_required says whether a release has to carry a signature. The first
# signed release was v1.3.6.1: everything before it has none, so there is
# nothing to check and refusing them would refuse every version published before
# signing began, and the moving dev prerelease is never signed. From v1.3.6 up a
# release that is not signed is refused, because otherwise whoever could replace
# the binary could also delete its signature, and a script that only warns would
# run what is left.
#
# A name this cannot read as three short numbers is held to a signature as well.
# Whoever publishes a release picks its name, so a name nobody can place must
# never be the way out of the check. A number is compared only when it is short
# enough to compare: the shell's [ answers one that overflows with an error
# status, which a caller would read as "not required".
signature_required() {
    [ "$1" != dev ] || return 1
    case "$1" in v[0-9]*.[0-9]*.[0-9]*) ;; *) return 0 ;; esac
    _rest=${1#v}
    _major=${_rest%%.*}
    _rest=${_rest#*.}
    _minor=${_rest%%.*}
    _rest=${_rest#*.}
    _patch=${_rest%%[!0-9]*}
    for _n in "$_major" "$_minor" "$_patch"; do
        case $_n in [0-9] | [0-9][0-9] | [0-9][0-9][0-9] | [0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]) ;; *) return 0 ;; esac
    done
    [ "$_major" -gt 1 ] || { [ "$_major" -eq 1 ] && { [ "$_minor" -gt 3 ] || { [ "$_minor" -eq 3 ] && [ "$_patch" -gt 5 ]; }; }; }
}

# verify_signature <tag> <checksums.txt> <checksums.txt.ed25519> <scratch dir>
# holds a release's checksums to the release key, before the checksums are
# believed. A signature that does not match always refuses. A signature that
# cannot be checked (no openssl that does Ed25519, no signature, one that cannot
# be read) refuses a release that must be signed and is a warning for one that
# cannot be, which is every release before v1.3.6.
verify_signature() {
    _tag=$1 _sums=$2 _sigfile=$3 _dir=$4
    [ -n "$RELEASE_KEY" ] || return 0
    if ! command -v openssl >/dev/null 2>&1 || ! openssl pkeyutl -help 2>&1 | grep -q rawin; then
        if signature_required "$_tag"; then
            die "$_tag is signed, and this host has no openssl (3.0 or later) to check the signature with, so the download cannot be trusted. Install openssl and run this again."
        fi
        warn "there is no openssl here that can check a signature; this download is checked by its checksum alone."
        return 0
    fi
    if [ ! -s "$_sigfile" ]; then
        if signature_required "$_tag"; then
            die "$_tag carries no checksums.txt.ed25519, and a release this new must be signed. Do not run this download."
        fi
        warn "$_tag carries no checksums.txt.ed25519, so the release key cannot check it; this download is checked by its checksum alone."
        return 0
    fi
    # The envelope is the key id, then the base64 signature.
    _sig=$(sed -n '2p' "$_sigfile")
    if ! printf '%s' "$_sig" | openssl base64 -d -A > "$_dir/sig.raw" 2>/dev/null || [ ! -s "$_dir/sig.raw" ]; then
        if signature_required "$_tag"; then
            die "the signature on $_tag could not be read. Do not run this download."
        fi
        warn "the release signature could not be read; this download is checked by its checksum alone."
        return 0
    fi
    # openssl wants the DER public key: the fixed Ed25519 SubjectPublicKeyInfo
    # prefix, then the key's 32 bytes. While a key is rotated RELEASE_KEY holds
    # more than one, one per line, exactly as the binary's key set does, and the
    # signature has to verify under one of them.
    printf '\060\052\060\005\006\003\053\145\160\003\041\000' > "$_dir/key.prefix"
    printf '%s\n' "$RELEASE_KEY" > "$_dir/keys.txt"
    _keys=0 _matched=0
    while IFS= read -r _key; do
        _key=$(printf '%s' "$_key" | tr -d '[:space:]')
        [ -n "$_key" ] || continue
        _keys=$((_keys + 1))
        if ! printf '%s' "$_key" | openssl base64 -d -A > "$_dir/key.raw" 2>/dev/null || [ ! -s "$_dir/key.raw" ]; then
            die "the release key built into this script cannot be read; copy the script again from https://zoomies.sh."
        fi
        cat "$_dir/key.prefix" "$_dir/key.raw" > "$_dir/release.der"
        if openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -keyform DER -inkey "$_dir/release.der" \
            -rawin -in "$_sums" -sigfile "$_dir/sig.raw" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            _matched=1
            break
        fi
    done < "$_dir/keys.txt"
    [ "$_keys" -gt 0 ] || die "the release key built into this script cannot be read; copy the script again from https://zoomies.sh."
    if [ "$_matched" -eq 1 ]; then
        say "the release signature matches the release key"
    else
        die "the release signature on $_tag does not match the release key. Do not run this download."
    fi
}
# --- end of the release signature check.

# Everything runs inside main, called on the last line, so a transfer cut short
# is a syntax error rather than half a setup.
main() {
    version="" key="" controller="" setup_id="" token=""
    while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
        [ $# -ge 2 ] || die "$1 needs a value; copy the complete command from the provider wizard."
        case "$1" in
            --version)    version=$2 ;;
            --key)        key=$2 ;;
            --controller) controller=$2 ;;
            --setup-id)   setup_id=$2 ;;
            --token)      token=$2 ;;
            *)            die "unknown option $1; copy the complete command from the provider wizard." ;;
        esac
        shift 2
    done
    if [ -z "$version" ] || [ -z "$key" ] || [ -z "$controller" ] || [ -z "$setup_id" ] || [ -z "$token" ]; then
        die "a value is missing; copy the complete command from the provider wizard."
    fi

    # The values name a directory and a download, so they are held to the
    # characters a tag and a key are made of before they are used for either.
    case "$version$key" in
        *[!A-Za-z0-9._-]*) die "the version or key contains a character that is not allowed; copy the complete command from the provider wizard." ;;
    esac

    [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ] || die "run this as root, for example: curl -fsSL https://zoomies.sh/connect-proxmox.sh | sudo sh -s -- ..."
    [ "$(uname -s)" = Linux ] || die "run this on the Proxmox host, which is Linux."

    dir="/var/lib/zoomies-proxmox/$key"
    mkdir -p "$dir"

    # A setup that already completed on this host reuses its binary, which may
    # have been upgraded since, instead of downloading another.
    receipt=$(printf '%s%s' "$setup_id" "$token" | sha256sum | cut -c1-12)
    if [ -f "$dir/completed-$receipt" ] && [ -x "$dir/zoomies" ]; then
        exec "$dir/zoomies" providers connect-proxmox --controller "$controller" --setup-id "$setup_id" --token "$token"
    fi

    case $(uname -m) in
        x86_64) arch=amd64 ;;
        aarch64|arm64) arch=arm64 ;;
        *) die "unsupported host architecture $(uname -m); Zoomies ships amd64 and arm64." ;;
    esac
    asset="zoomies_linux_$arch"
    base="https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies/releases/download/$version"

    tmp=$(mktemp -d "$dir/download.XXXXXX")
    trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT
    curl --proto '=https' --proto-redir '=https' -fsSL "$base/$asset" -o "$tmp/$asset"
    curl --proto '=https' --proto-redir '=https' -fsSL "$base/checksums.txt" -o "$tmp/checksums.txt"
    # A release before v1.3.6 has no signature; the file is simply absent then.
    curl --proto '=https' --proto-redir '=https' -fsSL "$base/checksums.txt.ed25519" -o "$tmp/checksums.txt.ed25519" 2>/dev/null ||
        rm -f "$tmp/checksums.txt.ed25519"
    # Before the checksums are believed: a checksum from the same place as the
    # binary says only that the download was not corrupted on the way.
    verify_signature "$version" "$tmp/checksums.txt" "$tmp/checksums.txt.ed25519" "$tmp"
    (
        cd "$tmp"
        awk -v asset="$asset" '$2 == asset || $2 == "*" asset { print; found=1 } END { if (!found) exit 1 }' checksums.txt > selected ||
            die "checksums.txt has no entry for $asset."
        sha256sum -c selected
    )
    chmod 700 "$tmp/$asset"
    # Not exec: the trap has to remove the download once the connector is done.
    "$tmp/$asset" providers connect-proxmox --controller "$controller" --setup-id "$setup_id" --token "$token"
}

main "$@"

# Zoomies controller and agent.
#
# One binary, two subcommands. Built static (CGO_ENABLED=0 -- the SQLite driver
# is pure Go) so the runtime image can be distroless.

# ---- UI ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# UI assets are architecture-independent; build them once on the builder's CPU.
#
# Node 22, the major CI tests the UI on and the release workflow builds the
# binaries' UI with (NODE_VERSION in ci.yml and release.yml, and .nvmrc; a test in
# internal/docs holds them equal). This line was once moved to 26 by an automatic
# base-image bump that nothing else moved with it, so the image shipped a build
# on a Node that no check ran. Changing the major is a deliberate change of all
# of them together, which is why dependabot.yml leaves node's majors alone.
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM node:22-alpine@sha256:fe4f6d74e20370acb04ad889077d14d0f64a9c8ea6a42bc60cddf1e844699914 AS ui
WORKDIR /src/web
COPY web/package.json web/package-lock.json* ./
# No `|| npm install` fallback: that turns a lockfile CI would reject into an
# image built from whatever npm resolved today.
RUN npm ci --no-audit --no-fund
COPY web/ ./
RUN npm run build

# ---- Go ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Go cross-compiles on the builder's CPU instead of running the compiler in QEMU.
#
# The minor release go.mod names. The digest is what pins the patch release, and
# it should be the one CI and the release binaries are built with (the version in
# .github/actions/setup-go): it was left on 1.27.1 while they moved to 1.27.2, so
# the images were built with a different compiler from the binaries.
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.27-alpine@sha256:b8c9b82affbbb82a020bbcf998dad2ba9516944ac7e883524642a481a9505e9c AS build
WORKDIR /src
RUN apk add --no-cache git ca-certificates
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
# Only the Go trees, not the whole context: a change to web/ or deploy/ is
# already represented by the ui stage above, and copying either here would
# invalidate the compile layer for a change it cannot affect.
COPY cmd ./cmd
COPY internal ./internal
# The UI build output is embedded by internal/api; it must be present before the
# Go build so that //go:embed finds it.
COPY --from=ui /src/internal/api/webdist ./internal/api/webdist
# VERSION is the release without its leading v, the same string `make dist`
# stamps into the binaries: one release must not report two versions depending
# on how it was installed. DATE is passed because -trimpath and a build context
# with no .git leave Go nothing to infer one from.
ARG VERSION=dev
ARG COMMIT=""
ARG DATE=""
# Runner tags are separate from VERSION (main-sha-* is not a runner tag).
# Keep this a binary default, not ENV ZOOMIES_RUNNER_IMAGE: a baked environment
# override would incorrectly take precedence over the operator's YAML setting.
ARG RUNNER_IMAGE_TAG=dev
# Redeclare BuildKit's automatic target arguments without overriding their values.
ARG TARGETOS
ARG TARGETARCH
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH \
    go build -trimpath \
      -ldflags "-s -w \
        -X github.com/eyupio/zoomies/internal/version.Version=${VERSION} \
        -X github.com/eyupio/zoomies/internal/version.Commit=${COMMIT} \
        -X github.com/eyupio/zoomies/internal/version.Date=${DATE} \
        -X github.com/eyupio/zoomies/internal/naming.RunnerImageTag=${RUNNER_IMAGE_TAG}" \
      -o /out/zoomies ./cmd/zoomies

# An empty state directory to copy into the runtime stages. distroless has no
# shell, so this is the only way to get /var/lib/zoomies into the image owned by
# the user that runs there.
RUN install -d -m 0750 /out/state

# ---- Runtime ----------------------------------------------------------------
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot@sha256:afa5c872c891853ca7fcf1f12c3edb23f7eeef36189728842dd51042ff57f7ab AS controller
# Re-declared after FROM: the ones set above are out of scope here, and a label
# written from an ARG that is not in scope is silently empty.
ARG VERSION=dev
ARG COMMIT=""
ARG DATE=""
# The image had no labels at all, so a registry listing said nothing about what
# it was or where it came from, and `docker inspect` could not answer which
# release a running container was. The binary inside has always known; this is
# the same fact where a person can reach it without starting anything.
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.title="zoomies" \
      org.opencontainers.image.description="Self-hosted GitHub Actions runner fleet controller" \
      org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies" \
      org.opencontainers.image.url="https://zoomies.sh" \
      org.opencontainers.image.documentation="https://zoomies.sh/quickstart/" \
      org.opencontainers.image.vendor="EyUp.io" \
      org.opencontainers.image.licenses="AGPL-3.0-only" \
      org.opencontainers.image.version="${VERSION}" \
      org.opencontainers.image.revision="${COMMIT}" \
      org.opencontainers.image.created="${DATE}"
COPY --from=build /out/zoomies /usr/local/bin/zoomies
# The state directory must exist in the image, owned by the user that runs. A
# VOLUME on a path the image does not have gets created by the container runtime
# as root, and then uid 65532 cannot create the database in it -- SQLite reports
# only "unable to open database file (14)". Docker seeds a fresh named volume
# from the image, so baking the ownership in here is what makes that volume
# writable.
COPY --from=build --chown=65532:65532 /out/state /var/lib/zoomies
# 65532 is distroless' "nonroot" user. The controller never needs root.
USER 65532:65532
VOLUME ["/var/lib/zoomies"]
EXPOSE 8080
ENV ZOOMIES_STATE_DIR=/var/lib/zoomies \
    ZOOMIES_CONFIG_DIR=/etc/zoomies \
    ZOOMIES_DB_PATH=/var/lib/zoomies/zoomies.db
# The check the compose files already spell out, declared here so that a plain
# `docker run` gets it too -- an unhealthy controller that still has a running
# container is exactly the state an operator finds out about by accident.
#
# Exec form: distroless has no shell, so the string form docker would otherwise
# wrap in /bin/sh could never run. The port is the one EXPOSE names and the
# installer's ContainerPort constant uses; a controller told to listen
# elsewhere overrides this with its own --health-cmd.
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
    CMD ["/usr/local/bin/zoomies", "healthcheck", "--url", "http://127.0.0.1:8080"]
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/zoomies"]
CMD ["controller"]

# The agent needs a shell only when it uses the process backend; for the
# container backends distroless is enough. It talks to the Docker or Podman
# socket, which is bind-mounted in.
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot@sha256:afa5c872c891853ca7fcf1f12c3edb23f7eeef36189728842dd51042ff57f7ab AS agent
# Re-declared after FROM for the same reason the controller's are: the ARGs set
# in the build stage are out of scope here, and a label written from one that is
# not in scope is silently empty.
ARG VERSION=dev
ARG COMMIT=""
ARG DATE=""
# This target went unpublished for as long as it has existed, so nothing ever
# noticed it had no labels. Now that it is published it makes the same promise
# every other image here makes -- say what you are without being started.
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.title="zoomies-agent" \
      org.opencontainers.image.description="Zoomies agent: runs a runner fleet on one host for a controller" \
      org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies" \
      org.opencontainers.image.url="https://zoomies.sh" \
      org.opencontainers.image.documentation="https://zoomies.sh/hosts/" \
      org.opencontainers.image.vendor="EyUp.io" \
      org.opencontainers.image.licenses="AGPL-3.0-only" \
      org.opencontainers.image.version="${VERSION}" \
      org.opencontainers.image.revision="${COMMIT}" \
      org.opencontainers.image.created="${DATE}"
COPY --from=build /out/zoomies /usr/local/bin/zoomies
COPY --from=build --chown=65532:65532 /out/state /var/lib/zoomies
USER 65532:65532
ENV ZOOMIES_STATE_DIR=/var/lib/zoomies
VOLUME ["/var/lib/zoomies"]
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/zoomies"]
CMD ["agent"]

# The Zoomies runner image.
#
# It carries the actions/runner release and its .NET dependencies, and an
# entrypoint that understands the environment contract Zoomies' backends use.
# Built for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.
#
# One file builds every variant in internal/naming's catalogue -- Ubuntu 24.04
# and 22.04, Debian 12, Fedora and Rocky Linux -- published as
# ghcr.io/eyupio/zoomies-runner:<os>-<version>. That <os>-<version> is the same
# string a Zoomies pool name carries, so an operator can read a pool name and
# know which image its runners boot. The variant is chosen with build
# arguments:
#
#   docker build -f deploy/Dockerfile.runner \
#     --build-arg BASE=debian:12-slim --build-arg OS_FAMILY=apt \
#     --build-arg OS_ID=debian --build-arg OS_VERSION=12 \
#     -t ghcr.io/eyupio/zoomies-runner:debian-12 .
#
# `make image-runner` passes each variant's base pinned by digest, from the
# catalogue in internal/naming/images.go; the example names the tag only, so
# that it does not go stale when the weekly refresh moves the pins.
#
# Everything a distribution names differently lives in deploy/runner-*.sh, one
# script per concern, each branching on the package family. That is deliberate:
# the alternative is a chain of shell conditionals inside a RUN, where nobody
# can read one distribution's list without reading all of them.
#
# Alpine is absent on purpose. actions/runner ships glibc binaries and .NET
# dependencies that musl does not satisfy, so an Alpine image would build and
# then fail at the first job.
#
# It also carries the toolchain a build typically reaches for -- a compiler, the
# headers native extensions link against, python3 and node. That is a reversal:
# this file used to argue that a runner should stay small because a smaller
# image means a faster cold start, and that what a job needs beyond the runner
# belongs in its own setup steps.
#
# The argument was sound while an image was pulled in front of the job that
# needed it. It is not any more. A pool's image is prewarmed on every host that
# can run the pool, and images.refresh_interval re-runs that prewarm, so the
# pull happens on a timer in the background and the job finds the image already
# there. What is left of "large image" is disk on the host, not queue wait.
#
# Against that, a runner missing cc is a workflow that fails in the middle, on
# somebody else's afternoon, with an error about a missing compiler rather than
# about this image. Parity with what actions/runner-images ships is the less
# surprising default, and a pool that wants something leaner can name its own.
#
# Three targets come out of this file:
#
#   runner         the image above, published as ghcr.io/eyupio/zoomies-runner
#   runner-docker  that plus the Docker CLI, published as
#                  ghcr.io/eyupio/zoomies-runner-docker
#   runner-full    runner-docker plus the language toolchains, published as
#                  ghcr.io/eyupio/zoomies-runner-full for the Ubuntu variants
#
# The second exists because a pool's docker_mode gives a job a *daemon* and
# nothing else. Without a client on PATH, `docker/setup-qemu-action` and every
# other step that shells out to docker dies with "Unable to locate executable
# file: docker", which says nothing about the daemon being right there. The
# split keeps that cost off the pools that never build an image.
#
# `runner` is the last stage on purpose, so that a plain `docker build -f
# deploy/Dockerfile.runner .` still produces the plain runner; the variant is
# built with --target runner-docker.

ARG RUNNER_VERSION=2.338.0
# The SHA-256 GitHub publishes for each release archive, from the release
# notes; internal/backend/runner_digests.go carries the same values for the
# process backend, and the runner-version workflow moves all of them together.
ARG RUNNER_SHA256_X64=af4b794c1bc41d73d40535e3fe092a39f9679cd8d965954c2aca25a05ca41d32
ARG RUNNER_SHA256_ARM64=628b4a7258487b80c1d3c221095a7ded349f5ae0175fd3dfab708d07428f041b
# What a plain build of this file uses is the catalogue's default variant, on the
# base the weekly refresh last pinned. The line between the markers is written by
# internal/naming/gen_catalogue.go, so it moves with the table; a test compares
# it, and the OS arguments below, with the catalogue's default row.
# zoomies:catalogue-begin
ARG BASE=ubuntu:24.04@sha256:224a1869083a311ef3f13648a154ba79832fbef6364d31493642ca03082da254
# zoomies:catalogue-end

FROM ${BASE} AS runner-base
# Re-declared after FROM: an ARG from before it is out of scope in the build
# stage, and the labels below would otherwise record empty strings.
ARG BASE
ARG RUNNER_VERSION
ARG RUNNER_SHA256_X64
ARG RUNNER_SHA256_ARM64
ARG TARGETARCH

# OS_FAMILY selects the package manager: "apt" for Ubuntu and Debian, "dnf" for
# Fedora and Rocky. It is a build argument rather than something detected at
# build time so that a typo fails the build rather than quietly producing an
# image missing half its dependencies.
ARG OS_FAMILY=apt
# OS_ID and OS_VERSION are what this variant claims to be. They become image
# labels and environment, which is what `docker inspect` and the entrypoint's
# first log line read to confirm a running container is the platform its pool
# asked for.
ARG OS_ID=ubuntu
ARG OS_VERSION=24.04
# Only stable metadata belongs on the shared base. Release arguments are
# declared on the final targets, after every package installation, because
# all RUN instructions implicitly consume the arguments already in scope.
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.title="zoomies-runner" \
      org.opencontainers.image.description="GitHub Actions runner image for Zoomies" \
      org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies" \
      org.opencontainers.image.url="https://zoomies.sh" \
      org.opencontainers.image.documentation="https://zoomies.sh/hosts-and-pools/" \
      org.opencontainers.image.vendor="EyUp.io" \
      org.opencontainers.image.licenses="AGPL-3.0-only" \
      org.opencontainers.image.base.name="${BASE}" \
      io.zoomies.runner-version="${RUNNER_VERSION}" \
      io.zoomies.os="${OS_ID}" \
      io.zoomies.os-version="${OS_VERSION}" \
      io.zoomies.os-family="${OS_FAMILY}"

ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive \
    RUNNER_MANUALLY_TRAP_SIG=1 \
    ACTIONS_RUNNER_PRINT_LOG_TO_STDOUT=1

# git, curl, ca-certificates and jq are what essentially every workflow assumes
# exists. actions/runner's own .NET dependencies are installed further down by
# the tarball's installdependencies.sh, which knows each distribution's names
# for them -- naming them here is what made this file Ubuntu-24.04-only.
#
# The apt and dnf helpers accompany every script that installs packages,
# here and below: they recover from stale indexes and repository metadata
# skew. Each step removes its helpers after installation.
COPY --chmod=0755 deploy/runner-dnf.sh /tmp/
COPY --chmod=0755 deploy/runner-apt.sh deploy/runner-packages.sh /tmp/
RUN /tmp/runner-packages.sh "${OS_FAMILY}" && rm /tmp/runner-packages.sh /tmp/runner-apt.sh /tmp/runner-dnf.sh
ENV LANG=en_US.UTF-8

# The runner must not be root. It gets passwordless sudo because a great many
# real workflows expect it; a pool that does not want that can override the
# entrypoint's user.
#
# uid 1001 rather than 1000: Fedora and Rocky leave 1000 free but Ubuntu's
# cloud images take it, and a fixed uid is what lets a host bind-mount a work
# directory the runner can actually write to.
#
# sudo resets the environment by default, and the proxy variables the agent
# hands every runner on a host behind a proxy went with it: `curl` in a step
# reached the internet and `sudo apt-get install` in the next one timed out,
# which reads as a broken mirror rather than a dropped proxy. env_keep carries
# exactly the six names internal/backend/proxy.go passes on, and a test there
# holds the two lists together. visudo checks the file, because sudo refuses
# to run at all over a sudoers.d entry it cannot parse.
#
# RPM bases ship shadow with mode 0000. PAM's setuid helper cannot read it on
# every container runtime; give its root owner read access without exposing
# it to the runner or bypassing PAM's account checks.
RUN set -eux; \
    groupadd -g 1001 runner 2>/dev/null || true; \
    useradd -m -s /bin/bash -u 1001 -g 1001 runner; \
    if [ "${OS_FAMILY}" = dnf ]; then chmod 0400 /etc/shadow; fi; \
    mkdir -p /etc/sudoers.d; \
    { \
      echo 'Defaults:runner env_keep += "HTTP_PROXY HTTPS_PROXY NO_PROXY http_proxy https_proxy no_proxy"'; \
      echo "runner ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL"; \
    } > /etc/sudoers.d/runner; \
    chmod 0440 /etc/sudoers.d/runner; \
    if ! grep -Eq '^[[:space:]]*(@|#)includedir[[:space:]]+/etc/sudoers.d([[:space:]]|$)' /etc/sudoers; then \
      printf '\n#includedir /etc/sudoers.d\n' >> /etc/sudoers; \
    fi; \
    visudo -c; \
    su -s /bin/sh runner -c 'sudo -n true'; \
    su -s /bin/sh runner -c 'HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.invalid:3128 no_proxy=.invalid sudo -n env' > /tmp/runner-sudo-env; \
    grep -qx 'HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.invalid:3128' /tmp/runner-sudo-env; \
    grep -qx 'no_proxy=.invalid' /tmp/runner-sudo-env; \
    rm /tmp/runner-sudo-env

# Two directories the runner must own before anything is mounted over them.
#
# /opt/hostedtoolcache is the tool cache: where setup-python, setup-node,
# setup-go and the rest unpack what they download, named for the path GitHub's
# own runners use. Left to its default, the runner puts it under _work/_tool,
# which an ephemeral runner throws away with every job; here it is a fixed
# place that an image built FROM this one can fill ahead of time, so those
# steps find the version already there rather than downloading it again.
#
# /opt/zoomies-cache is where a pool's cache is mounted. A fresh named volume
# takes its ownership from the directory it is mounted over, and with no such
# directory in the image it came up owned by root: the pool cache existed, and
# the runner could not write a byte to it without sudo. Owned by the runner
# here, a new volume is the runner's too.
RUN set -eux; \
    install -d -o runner -g runner -m 0755 /opt/hostedtoolcache /opt/zoomies-cache
ENV AGENT_TOOLSDIRECTORY=/opt/hostedtoolcache

# The archive is checked against the digest GitHub published before it is
# unpacked: this image runs whatever is inside it, on every job, and a mirror
# or a proxy between the build and github.com is a place to substitute it.
# The dependency script is allowed to fail the build, too. It used to be
# silenced, which shipped an image that was missing a library the runner dies
# without on the first job rather than failing here, where the log says why.
#
# It is GitHub's script and installs the runner's .NET dependencies with the
# distribution's package manager, so it is exposed to the same archive mirror
# that is briefly out of step with its own index as everything
# deploy/runner-apt.sh covers. It cannot use that helper -- it is not ours to
# edit -- so the attempts are here instead, and the last one still fails the
# build.
WORKDIR /home/runner
RUN set -eux; \
    case "${TARGETARCH}" in \
      amd64) RUNNER_ARCH=x64; RUNNER_SHA256="${RUNNER_SHA256_X64}" ;; \
      arm64) RUNNER_ARCH=arm64; RUNNER_SHA256="${RUNNER_SHA256_ARM64}" ;; \
      *) echo "unsupported architecture: ${TARGETARCH}" >&2; exit 1 ;; \
    esac; \
    curl -fsSL -o runner.tar.gz \
      "https://github.com/actions/runner/releases/download/v${RUNNER_VERSION}/actions-runner-linux-${RUNNER_ARCH}-${RUNNER_VERSION}.tar.gz"; \
    echo "${RUNNER_SHA256}  runner.tar.gz" | sha256sum -c -; \
    tar xzf runner.tar.gz; \
    rm runner.tar.gz; \
    for attempt in 1 2 3; do \
      if ./bin/installdependencies.sh; then break; fi; \
      [ "$attempt" -lt 3 ] || exit 1; \
      echo "installdependencies.sh failed; trying again in $((attempt * 10))s" >&2; \
      sleep $((attempt * 10)); \
    done; \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*; \
    mkdir -p /home/runner/_work; \
    chown -R runner:runner /home/runner

# The build toolchain, after the runner download on purpose: this list is the
# part of the image most likely to be edited, and putting it last means editing
# it does not re-fetch the ~200 MB archive above. What is in it, and what is
# deliberately not, is in deploy/runner-toolchain.sh.
COPY --chmod=0755 deploy/runner-dnf.sh /tmp/
COPY --chmod=0755 deploy/runner-apt.sh deploy/runner-toolchain.sh /tmp/
RUN /tmp/runner-toolchain.sh "${OS_FAMILY}" && rm /tmp/runner-toolchain.sh /tmp/runner-apt.sh /tmp/runner-dnf.sh

# The GitHub CLI, from GitHub's own repository because no distribution here
# carries it.
COPY --chmod=0755 deploy/runner-dnf.sh /tmp/
COPY --chmod=0755 deploy/runner-apt.sh deploy/runner-gh.sh /tmp/
RUN /tmp/runner-gh.sh "${OS_FAMILY}" && rm /tmp/runner-gh.sh /tmp/runner-apt.sh /tmp/runner-dnf.sh

# ShellCheck, which GitHub's hosted runners carry and shell-linting workflows
# assume; deploy/runner-shellcheck.sh says why it is a pinned download.
COPY --chmod=0755 deploy/runner-shellcheck.sh /tmp/
RUN /tmp/runner-shellcheck.sh "${TARGETARCH}" && rm /tmp/runner-shellcheck.sh

# Prove the toolchain is actually reachable, for the same reason the Docker
# variant checks its client: a package that installed but left nothing on PATH
# is the failure this exists to prevent, and it is far cheaper to catch in the
# build than in somebody's workflow. It is also what keeps the two families'
# package lists honest -- they are not translations of each other, and this is
# what says whether each one is complete.
RUN set -eux; \
    cc --version; \
    make --version; \
    cmake --version; \
    python3 --version; \
    node --version; \
    npm --version; \
    git lfs version; \
    gh --version; \
    shellcheck --version

# The fleet's own packages, last, so that editing the list costs one package
# install rather than the whole toolchain above -- and so that a build with
# EXTRA_PACKAGES set is cheap enough for CI to run one on every variant, which
# is what keeps this build argument from quietly ceasing to work.
COPY --chmod=0755 deploy/runner-dnf.sh /tmp/
COPY --chmod=0755 deploy/runner-apt.sh deploy/runner-extra.sh /tmp/
# Declare this only at its installation step so changing the package list
# reuses the runner download and toolchain layers above.
ARG EXTRA_PACKAGES=""
RUN /tmp/runner-extra.sh "${OS_FAMILY}" ${EXTRA_PACKAGES} && rm /tmp/runner-extra.sh /tmp/runner-apt.sh /tmp/runner-dnf.sh
