## What to decide before code

1. Concept A or Concept B for the hub. A is recommended because it preserves
   simultaneous monitoring and matches the Overview's new grammar.
2. Whether Automatic repairs belongs as a section in the hub or as a separate
   administrator page. This review keeps it in the hub because stopping a policy
   is an operational action, but it is closed by default.
3. Whether the repair page should open setup inline or in a drawer. The mock
   keeps it inline, below the decision, so the failure stays in view.
4. Whether History should open by itself on a quiet fleet. The mock does so
   because, when nothing needs a person, the record is the useful content.
5. Whether the phone page navigation should use More for the last two
   destinations, as the Overview now does.

# Kennel Club layout review

A design review and clickable mock for the Kennel Club pages in both visual
styles. Nothing here ships as code; it was approved on 19 October 2026 and the
changes are recorded in
[decision 0013](../../roadmap/decisions/0013-the-kennel-pages-answer-first-and-fold-the-depth.md).

Open [mockups.html](mockups.html) in a browser. The review bar switches screen,
Classic or Mission Control, light or dark, and turns the numbered callouts on.
It uses illustrative data and sends no requests.

Captures are in [screens](screens) for a quick look without opening the mock.
The shipped Classic captures live in `docs/screenshots/kennel-*.webp`. Mission
Control is captured in [current](current), because the shipped screenshot pass
still writes Kennel Club in Classic only.

Both visual styles were reviewed at 1440 and 375, in light and dark. The
structure is identical between styles, so the proposals apply to both; Mission
Control is taller and is the layout that will break first.

## What the review found

The current pages are careful and well written, but the layout makes the reader
do the ranking. The same information is often repeated in a heading, a panel
description and a card detail.

1. **The Overview answers with seven equal cards.** The one question an
   operator has, "is anything wrong?", is one card among Repositories, Best in
   show, Partly checked, Errors, Warnings and Waived. The seventh and eighth
   cards wrap onto a second row with empty space beside them. The answer
   should be the first thing on the page, not a number to compare.
2. **Every section is open at once.** "By check" lists all checks with equal
   weight, including the ones with nothing open. "What Kennel Club can see"
   occupies a full panel even when every source was read. The page is long
   because nothing is folded, not because the information is large.
3. **The Repositories filter bar stacks.** `Select` is `width: 100%`, so five
   selects become five full-width rows. The table starts below the fold. The
   page already knows the five questions people ask, because the Overview
   counts them, but it does not offer them as quick filters.
4. **The section has three navigation layers and repeats itself.** The global
   sidebar, the Kennel rail, the page title and the breadcrumb all name the
   same place. On the repository page, five tabs then split again into
   sections. The in-page map is missing exactly where the pages are longest.
5. **Findings are full cards by default.** Each finding repeats severity,
   title, summary, "What to change", prompt, evidence, code, Ask Eli and
   Waive. Two findings fill more than a screen. Coverage and waivers are
   pushed below them, and the default tab is fleet activity rather than the
   findings that brought the reader here.
6. **AI Context leads with marketing.** Three benefit columns and two long
   explainers sit above the repositories. A configured card then offers six or
   more buttons. The page's job, managing repositories, starts below the fold.
7. **The rail switch dominates the section.** It is the largest control in the
   rail, it wraps onto two or three lines, and its status sentence competes
   with the navigation. The switch matters, but it is not the page.
8. **Theme parity is structural, not visual.** Classic and Mission Control
   render the same components. Mission Control's larger type makes every long
   panel and every wrapped filter row more expensive vertically, so the
   simplification helps both styles and helps Mission Control most.

## The proposal

Five principles:

- **Answer first.** A verdict band says what needs attention and what is
  clean. Supporting totals are still there, but they are secondary.
- **One map per page.** A sticky in-page anchor row carries counts and keeps
  its current section lit. On a repository, the three tabs are the map and the
  finding areas are the filter chips.
- **Fold depth, not importance.** A check with nothing open, a source that was
  read, and a prompt are all one disclosure away. Nothing is removed.
- **Put controls where the decision is.** Quick filters carry counts. The
  destructive tracking action leaves the primary button row. Each AI Context
  card has one contextual primary action and an overflow menu.
- **Keep the contract.** Status colours, shapes and labels, tokens, URLs,
  permissions and API routes are unchanged. The mock uses the existing
  Classic and Mission Control values.

## Screen notes

### Overview

- A verdict band replaces the seven equal cards: one attention sentence, one
  primary action, then Best in show, Partly checked and Repositories.
- All counts move into one pill disclosure.
- A two-column body puts the action list and checks on the left, and read
  confidence and scope on the right. This uses the width instead of leaving a
  second card row half empty.
- "By check" shows the two checks that are affecting a repository. The ten
  quiet checks fold away.
- Read confidence is an aside with a five-segment bar and a source list. A
  partial read says the counts are a minimum next to the counts.
- A sticky anchor row gives Summary, Attention, Checks and Read confidence.

### Repositories

- Quick filters for All, Needs attention, No open findings, Partly checked and
  Not tracked carry the counts from the Overview.
- Search, Filters and the activity scope sit on one row. The filters move into
  one popover, with removable chips when applied.
- The table keeps Repository, Standing, Open findings and Last read. Visibility
  moves into Columns.
- The scope sentence says how many are shown and makes the hidden count a
  link.
- On a phone the table becomes cards and the selection column waits for a
  deliberate select mode rather than adding a lone tick box to every card.

### Repository

- Three tabs: Findings, Fleet activity and AI Context. Protection and Agent
  guidance become areas inside Findings, with their own filter chips and
  deep-linkable addresses. This is the biggest structural proposal; see
  "Decisions to confirm".
- Tracking is a sentence with a link, not a switch in the primary action row.
  Recheck is the one primary action. Refresh is an icon. Stop tracking moves
  into the overflow menu.
- Findings use a list and detail workbench on desktop. The list is scannable,
  the selected finding gets the room, and prompt, evidence and technical
  details fold away. A single-column accordion is the alternative and the
  phone layout.
- Coverage is a line under the selected finding with details on demand.
- Waived findings remain a disclosure at the foot.

### AI Context

- Repositories come first. The summary band counts repositories in setup,
  ready and needing attention.
- The card shows branch, output, installation and last check in one compact
  row. The action that fits the state is the button; reinstall, amend, remove,
  instructions and badge move into the overflow menu.
- The benefits and setup explanations become one "How AI Context works"
  disclosure below the list. The empty state can still carry the full version.

## Decisions to confirm before code

1. **Findings first on a repository.** Make Findings the default tab when the
   repository has open findings, and Fleet activity the default when it does
   not. This changes decision
   [0008](../../roadmap/decisions/0008-the-repository-page-leads-with-what-the-fleet-knows.md).
2. **Merge Protection and Agent guidance into Findings.** Keep their routes as
   aliases that open Findings with the matching area selected. This changes the
   tab list but keeps every finding, waiver and permission surface.
3. **Keep the section rail.** Decision
   [0010](../../roadmap/decisions/0010-kennel-club-has-a-side-menu-and-the-switch-is-in-it.md)
   is still the right shape. The proposal only makes the switch calmer and
   removes the duplicate breadcrumb, not the rail.
4. **Tracking moves out of the header.** The track switch becomes a state
   sentence with a link and the destructive action moves to overflow. This is
   a workflow change for administrators, not a permission change.
5. **AI Context explainers move below the list.** The text is kept, but it is
   no longer the first thing a returning operator sees.

## Implementation notes

- Use native `details` and `summary` for folding. Keep the disclosure state in
  the URL only where a link should open it, as the current waivers do.
- Give the anchor row `scroll-margin-top` equal to the sticky bar height so a
  focused heading is not obscured.
- The in-page nav is a `nav` with `aria-current` on the active item. The counts
  are text inside the link, not separate badges.
- Keep status colour plus shape plus label. The workbench list uses the same
  severity badge as the detail.
- Touch targets are 44px under a coarse pointer. The mobile table becomes
  cards, and the selection column is not shown until select mode.
- Test both visual styles in both colour modes at 1440 and 375. Mission Control
  is the taller of the two, so it is the one that will break first.
- No new dependency, API route, token or permission is needed.

# Overview design review

19 October 2026. Original concept review, prepared before application changes.
Concept A has since been implemented; see the [implementation captures and
validation record](implemented/README.md).

## Visual concepts

- [A: Calm operations](concept-a-calm-operations.png), the recommended continuous
  page, shown in Mission Control dark, Classic light and a phone layout.
- [B: Focus workspace](concept-b-focus-workspace.png), the view-based alternative,
  with a desktop, phone and previews of the supporting views.

The boards show hierarchy, disclosure and visual direction. View them at their
original size. Actual interface text, type sizes and accessible controls should
follow this review and the existing UI contract rather than the generated
image's small text. In A, the event preview's 'View events' means expanding the
existing feed in place, not introducing another route.

## Recommendation

Use **A, Calm operations** for both Classic and Mission Control. Give both
styles the same information architecture, with their existing palettes and
density. Answer three questions in order: does anything need attention, what
is happening now, and where should I investigate?

**B, Focus workspace** is an alternative for people who frequently investigate
history or hosts. It keeps the live summary visible and puts supporting detail
in separate views. It reduces scrolling further, but makes simultaneous
monitoring harder. The visual style and the layout concept are independent:
either concept can use either style, in light or dark mode.

The generated visual boards are illustrative design sketches. Their sample
numbers, small text and icons are not specifications or validated product
screens. The behaviour and data rules below govern any later implementation.

## Evidence reviewed

- Current `web/src/routes/Overview.svelte` and its overview components, including
  metrics, problem summary, recent failures, repair offers and the host chart.
- `web/AGENTS.md`, `docs/ui-guidelines.md` and the theme token definitions.
- Existing real-product desktop and phone captures in `docs/screenshots` and
  `docs/screenshots/mission-control`, including light and dark examples.
- The previous concepts in `design/theme-review`, to distinguish earlier
  proposals from the current implementation.

This review uses checked-in captures and current source, rather than a new live
browser session. No usability study, runtime accessibility audit or measured
performance improvement is claimed. There is no dedicated UX design skill in
the available skill catalogue; the repository's design guidance and the
available image-generation tool support this review.

## What needs simplifying

| Finding | User cost | Proposed change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Classic leads with the activity matrix and six metric tiles. | History and timings delay current issues and work. | Put attention and four live metrics first in both styles. |
| Mission Control already prioritises issues and collapses timings, but its timing disclosure still precedes current work. | Supporting diagnostics interrupt the main task. | Move timing detail below pools and active jobs. |
| The same page has different section order by style. | Switching appearance changes where information lives. | Keep a stable order; let style change appearance and density. |
| The header repeats Overview and explains several time windows in prose. | A long introduction takes valuable phone space. | Use a short page introduction and local time-window labels. Retain accessible page and shell titles. |
| Scope switches recur in the page and panels. | People must work out whether they control the same data. | One clearly labelled scope control, with specific scope notes where a metric cannot widen. |
| Cards and verbose panel introductions have similar visual weight. | Everything competes for attention. | Compact metric strip, shorter headings and restrained panel borders. |
| Pool ceiling is shown next to a busy-versus-live utilisation bar. | A low busy percentage can appear to contradict an at-limit warning. | Show busy/live separately from the live/max ceiling and explain the queue. |
| Full history and multi-metric host charts share the monitoring page. | Exploration controls lengthen a page intended for glancing. | Keep useful summaries visible and disclose charts on request. |
| There is no page-level orientation or jump assistance. | Returning to a section means searching and scrolling. | Add a small sticky section navigation with current-section indication. |
| The phone captures spend most of the first viewport before pools. | An operator cannot quickly inspect work while away from a desk. | Two-by-two compact metrics, wrapped capacity metadata and fewer introductory lines. |

## A: Calm operations

One continuous page with sticky jump links: **Now, Pools, Jobs, History,
Diagnostics**. Links move within the page; they do not hide other sections.

Reading order:

1. First-run checklist when setup is incomplete. Existing critical problems
   remain visible; do not call an unfinished fleet healthy.
2. Compact attention area: fleet problems, failures needing review and eligible
   Eli offers remain distinct. Show the relevant counts and one action per
   category. Keep the existing maximum of two failure previews, with the full
   list accessible through its existing attention-filtered Jobs view.
3. Four live figures: queued jobs, running jobs, live runners and median queue
   wait with p95. Metrics remain links to the corresponding scoped records.
4. Pools and active jobs in the main desktop column. A short recent-events
   preview occupies a narrower supporting column. Mobile stacks pools, jobs,
   then events. Use ordinary page scrolling for the preview; expanding the
   feed can reveal its existing filters and longer list in place.
5. History, host capacity and startup/registration detail as collapsible
   sections. A closed section still communicates useful context.

Proposed closed summaries:

| Section | Example visible summary | Expanded content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| History | Today: 45 finished, 10 failed | Existing matrix, range, outcome selector and accessible cell interaction. |
| Host capacity | 3 connected hosts; 8 of 10 slots used | Existing host chart, per-host/overlay views, ranges and metric selection. |
| Startup and registration | p50 startup 4.0s; registration 9.0s | Existing p50 and p95 values, their period and runner links. |

History's selected range and the live figures' one-hour trends are independently
labelled. Do not imply one page-wide range changes every section. Summary
values must come from existing authoritative data, with missing or failed data
identified explicitly. Slot capacity, live runners and busy runners are
different quantities and retain different labels.

## B: Focus workspace

Keep attention and the four live figures persistent. Below them, offer
**Work, History, Diagnostics** views. Work contains pools, active jobs and the
short events preview; History contains the matrix; Diagnostics contains host
capacity and timings. This is a view switcher, unlike A's jump navigation.

Benefits: less vertical scanning, more space for analytical controls, and a
clear focus for occasional investigation. Costs: hidden information requires
another action, fewer signals can be read simultaneously, and view-specific
state and keyboard interaction add complexity. Attention counts and loss of
the live connection remain visible regardless of view.

Prefer A for a dashboard left open all day. Choose B if operator feedback shows
that focused investigation matters more than simultaneous visibility. Do not
ship both layouts as another preference without evidence that it is needed.

## Disclosure and navigation rules

- Keep attention and the core live figures visible. Pools and active jobs open
  by default. Collapse supporting detail, rather than every panel.
- Remember explicit expansion choices in this browser, independently of visual
  style. Avoid unexpected scrolling or reordering when data updates.
- Closed sections continue to show live summary state. A newly detected host
  fault appears in the attention area even when its chart is closed.
- Keep categories separate: fleet warnings, unreviewed job failures and Eli
  offers can concern the same underlying event. Never add their counts into a
  fabricated total of unique issues. Marking a failure known is not resolving it.
- Jumping to a collapsed destination opens it and positions its heading below
  the sticky bars. Give sections stable fragments so they can be bookmarked.
- On phones, use **Now, Pools, Jobs, More**; More contains labelled links to
  Events, History and Diagnostics. This menu assists page navigation and does
  not replace the existing bottom app navigation.
- Give jump links visible current-section styling and `aria-current=location`.
  Use native disclosure controls where practical, labelled navigation, visible
  focus, keyboard access and 44px touch targets. Reduced motion applies to
  scrolling and existing animations.
- One page scope control preserves the existing managed/all-runners meaning.
  Queue and Jobs links must match their counts. Host capacity and live runners
  remain this fleet's infrastructure even when external jobs are included;
  a label should make that boundary clear. Changing scope must update a closed
  summary as well as any open list.
- Show a labelled Live, Reconnecting or Disconnected state. Retain timestamps
  or a stale-data message after a connection gap. Do not rely on a green dot.
- Preserve the existing detailed matrix keyboard interaction, read/dismiss
  behaviour, failure distinction, permissions, Eli review flow, saved table
  choices, artwork, vocabulary and reduced-motion preference.

## Visual direction

Classic keeps its compact neutral surfaces; Mission Control keeps its navy or
cool light surfaces and slightly larger type. Both use existing tokens and
status semantics. Blue identifies interaction, cyan running work, amber
pending/warnings and the existing danger colour failures. Decoration does not
carry meaning. Retain original Zoomies branding and Eli artwork; any generated
icon is a placeholder, not a proposed replacement asset.

Use fewer large card enclosures, align section actions consistently and reserve
large numerals for the four live figures. Keep capacity metadata outside narrow
metric cells on phones so it can wrap. Keep long pool names available through
wrapping or an accessible expansion, rather than relying on hover. Keep the
assistant trigger and bottom navigation clear of record actions and safe areas.

## Review targets before implementation

- At 1440 by 900, attention, metrics and useful pool/job rows should be visible
  without opening diagnostics. Check a state with two failure previews as well
  as a quiet fleet.
- At 375 by 900, aim to show the first pool within the initial viewport after
  the compact metric grid, with no cropped capacity text or horizontal overflow.
  This is a target to validate later, not a measured result of these sketches.
- At 200% zoom, allow one-column reflow without lost actions. Check keyboard
  order, focus visibility, sticky offsets, touch controls and reduced motion.
- Verify both concepts' chosen implementation in Classic and Mission Control,
  each in light and dark mode. Do not shrink typography to make a board fit.
- Validate first run, loading, failed fetch, reconnecting/stale data, no work,
  many pools, long names and permissions. Zero and unavailable data differ.
- Usability check: can someone find queued work, identify a pool at its live
  limit, review an unacknowledged failure and reach host diagnostics quickly?

The original concept review included no application changes. The subsequent
implementation follows Concept A and is recorded separately above.

## Implemented behaviour

- Eli defaults to the bottom right of the viewport, retaining saved side choices.
- Both styles share the order: first-run guidance when needed, attention,
  four live metrics, pools, active jobs, recent events and supporting detail.
- One page scope selector controls job figures and links. Infrastructure and
  the activity matrix explicitly retain their fleet scope.
- Sticky page links provide Now, Pools, Jobs, History and Diagnostics. The
  phone has a separately named More overview sections control, with keyboard
  access and Escape dismissal. It leaves the app's More menu independent.
- Jump links open closed destinations, set a bookmarkable fragment and move
  focus below the sticky navigation. Current-section indication follows jumps
  and scrolling, including destinations near the end of the document.
- History, host capacity and startup/registration details start closed, retain
  live summaries and remember explicit expansion choices in this browser.
  Expanding history preserves its range, matrix navigation and day details.
- The recent-events preview shows three entries. Expanding it restores the
  longer feed, category preferences and original controller reason strings.
- Failure attention remains visible with its count and review link. Expanding
  its preview retains inspection, acknowledgement, undo and eligible Eli links.
- Pool rows distinguish busy/live utilisation from the live/maximum ceiling.
  Compact phone metrics keep metadata out of narrow tiles.
- Failed initial fetches retain the retry state. Loading figures do not claim
  zero; interrupted updates are labelled as potentially stale. A history fetch
  error is visible in the closed summary.

# Web UI refresh, signed-in pages implementation plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Produce a mock, in the portal's look, of every signed-in page: an interactive review page with the page today beside the mock, one shared fleet of data, the checker over every combination, and a README.

**Architecture:** Pack 1's method with one concept instead of three. Plain-HTML mocks on the product's own `tokens.css`, served by the dependency-free server, switched by `data-theme` and `data-ui-style`, and judged by the Playwright checker. A small kit of portal-style parts (shell, page header, card, icon tile, pill, stat, stage, table card, steps) is built once and every screen is made of it, so the pages share a look because they share parts. Every screen draws from one fixture fleet held to the REST API's schema, so a count on the Overview agrees with the rows on Runners and no mock shows a column the API cannot supply.

**Tech Stack:** HTML, CSS, vanilla ES modules, Node 22 (`node:http`, `node:test`), `@playwright/test` from `web/node_modules`. No new dependency.

**Spec:** `design/webui-refresh-review/SPEC.md`, "Direction chosen after pack 1". Read it, then `web/src/lib/public/` and `docs/brand.md` ("Using the system in the product") for the look as it is implemented.

## Global Constraints

* No change under `web/src`, `internal/`, `api/` or `cmd/`. No new dependency.
* Tokens only in the mocks: no raw colour, and no raw value that has a token. A new token may appear only in `signed-in/kit-tokens.css`, and the README lists each against the `docs/ui-guidelines.md` section it would change.
* Mocks need no API: they send no request and use `fixture.js`, whose every field is one the REST API returns, held to `api/openapi.yaml` by a test.
* Identity stays: logo and backdrop choices, Eli, paw artwork, from `web/public/brand`; never redraw them.
* Status colours keep their fixed mapping; a state is never carried by colour alone (a word or a shape is always there); status colours are not reused for decoration.
* Contrast 4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for control edges; widths 1440, 375, and 320 for reflow; Classic's known control edge stays in `KNOWN`.
* A table stays a table and scrolls inside its own card, never the page (`docs/ui-guidelines.md`, "Tables use the space they need").
* Prose: British spelling, no em dash, no spaced double hyphen. Commit messages are imperative sentences in plain prose and end with these two lines:
  `Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>` and `Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01GkdhFBr16YDz8GRKZd9MHf`.
* Work on branch `claude/jolly-maxwell-d96vdo`; push after every task; the pull request is eyupio/zoomies#1207. The owner's portal screenshots are reference only and are never committed.

## Review Focus

1. A 300-character repository, workflow or job name and a 120-character unbroken runner label in a table card truncate or wrap with the full text reachable, and never widen the page at 320px.
2. Every table on a phone scrolls inside its card or becomes cards, with every row action reachable by keyboard and at 44px or more.
3. Every list page draws four states, not one: loading, empty, an error with a retry, and rows shown stale after a failed refresh.
4. The sidebar's entries at 375px: a bottom bar with the four primary ones and a menu with the rest, which opens, holds focus, closes on Escape and returns focus to its opener.
5. A status pill keeps its meaning in forced-colours mode and in greyscale: the word is there and the shapes differ.
6. A stage (the dark panel) never carries a status colour that is only legible on the theme it was drawn in.

# Web UI refresh review: design specification

21 October 2026. This is the specification for a concept review of the whole
controller web UI. It describes what will be produced and how it will be
checked. It does not change the application, and nothing in it has been built
yet.

## Intent

The owner asked for the whole web UI to be refactored or improved, starting
with every page that can be seen without signing in and then working across the
signed-in pages, and asked to be shown variations and concepts rather than a
single answer.

What the owner chose:

| Decision | Choice |
| --- | --- |
| Deliverable | Concept pack first. No product code changes until a direction is chosen. |
| What to improve | All four: clarity and flow, visual look and polish, accessibility and phone fit, and code structure. |
| Pacing | Public pages first, then roll on through the signed-in areas using the recommended direction, reviewed as a batch. |
| Boldness | Two evolutions plus one bold concept. |

Assumptions, open to correction: every concept must fit the token system and
work in both visual styles (Mission Control and Classic) in light and dark, and
every concept must include a phone layout at 375px.

## Constraints that come from the repository

* Tokens: no raw colour in a component and no raw value that already has a
  token (`web/AGENTS.md`). Concepts link `web/src/lib/styles/tokens.css`
  instead of copying its values, so they cannot drift from it.
* Status colours are a fixed mapping and are not reused for anything else.
* Identity stays: the Zoomies logo and its backdrop choices, Eli, the paw and
  dog artwork, the Off, Cute and Standard vocabulary, and reduced motion.
* No new libraries. The mockups are plain HTML, CSS and a little script.
* Nothing is shown that the REST API cannot supply. The public status page in
  particular may use only what `GET /api/v1/status` returns.
* Prose follows the repository voice: British spelling, no em dashes, no spaced
  double hyphen, comments that say why.

## What is produced

```text
design/webui-refresh-review/
  SPEC.md                    this document
  PLAN-public.md             the implementation plan for pack 1
  tools/                     the loopback review server, the checker, the capture scripts and their tests
  public/                    pack 1: pages reachable without an account
    README.md                findings, concepts, recommendation, evidence, not claimed
    findings.md              the working notes behind the README's findings, with the measured tables
    mockups.html             the interactive review page, with its review.css, review.js and review-state.js
    screens/                 one module per screen, and the registry the page reads
    components.css, ui.js    the primitives every concept shares, so A, B and C do not each rebuild them
    icons.js                 the Lucide glyphs the concepts draw, generated by tools/make-icons.mjs
    concept-{a,b,c}.css      the styling of each concept
    concept-c-tokens.css     the only place a proposed new token may appear
    concept-c-pairs.json     the contrast pairs those tokens must pass
    current-*.png            the real UI today, from the built binary
    current-measurements.json  the numbers the findings cite, written beside those photographs
    concept-*.png            each concept in Mission Control dark at 1440px and 375px, and the recommended one in Classic light
    concept-measurements.json  where each concept puts things, with the review bar hidden, written by tools/measure.mjs
    viewport-review.json     overflow, contrast and console checks, as data, for every combination
    *.test.mjs               the tests for the page, each screen and the README
  shell-and-monitoring/      pack 2
  fleet-management/          pack 3
  insight-and-repairs/       pack 4
  settings-and-setup/        pack 5
```

The mockup page offers four independent controls: the screen, the concept
(Current, A, B or C), the visual style, and the colour mode. It sends no API
requests and uses illustrative data, as the earlier reviews do.

### The three concepts

* **A, evolution.** Keeps the current page structure and fixes hierarchy,
  wording and spacing. The least risky to ship.
* **B, evolution.** A different layout idea inside the same tokens and brand.
* **C, bold.** A deliberately larger departure. Any token it needs is defined in
  `concept-c-tokens.css` and listed in the README as a proposed change to
  `docs/ui-guidelines.md`, so the cost of choosing C is visible.

Each page ends with one recommendation and the reason for it.

## Pack 1: the public pages

| Screen | Source today | States the pack must show |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sign in | `web/src/routes/Login.svelte` | password only; single sign-on plus password; single sign-on only; a wrong-credentials failure; rate limited; controller unreachable; two-step verify; two-step enrolment and recovery codes; authentication switched off |
| First account | `web/src/routes/Bootstrap.svelte` | empty; field errors; caps lock; weak password; closed because an account now exists |
| Connect an app | `web/src/routes/McpConsent.svelte` | loading; normal request; request with the loopback warning; refused; nothing to approve; expired |
| Fleet status | `web/src/status/StatusPage.svelte` | healthy; slowed; blocked; stale after a failed refresh; sign-in required; not published |
| Not found | `web/src/routes/NotFound.svelte` | the one state |

### Findings from reading the source

These come from reading the code, not from rendering it, and each is confirmed
or dropped in a browser before it appears in the README.

1. **Three brand treatments on three screens.** Sign in uses the lockup on a
   black stage, the first-account form uses a 72px mark, and consent uses a
   28px full logo.
2. **One banner, written three times.** The failure banner is hand-written in
   `Login.svelte`, `Bootstrap.svelte` and `McpConsent.svelte` with different
   radii and icon offsets. The component list has no shared callout. This is
   the clearest code-structure candidate.
3. **The hardest field comes first.** The first-account form opens with the
   setup token, which has to be found in a log. The per-install commands sit
   behind a help control, and the introduction is three sentences long.
4. **The widest audience has the least brand.** The public status page carries
   no logo, and only the Classic style.
5. **Sign in carries four states in one 983-line file.** Layout, banner, form
   and two-step logic are mixed, which makes any visual change expensive.
6. **A question, not a finding: the loopback warning's tone.** The consent
   warning uses the danger treatment for a case that is common and legitimate
   when the client is a local coding agent. Whether that is alarm fatigue is for
   the concepts to explore. Status colours are not to be reused, so any
   alternative must stay inside the fixed mapping.

## Verification

The Playwright MCP that the web design skill prefers is not installed in this
environment, so its automatic verification is skipped. Verification is done with
what the repository already has:

* Serve the pack over loopback HTTP (the earlier review found file URLs
  unreliable) and drive the pre-installed Chromium with the repository's own
  `@playwright/test`.
* For each concept, screen, style and mode, at 1440px and 375px: no horizontal
  overflow, no console errors, keyboard order and visible focus, and contrast
  computed from the token values (4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for control edges).
* Capture "current" screens from the real built controller. That needs
  `npm ci` in `web/`. If the install fails, fall back to the captures already in
  `docs/screenshots` and say so in the README.
* Run `go test ./internal/docs` so the pack obeys the voice and placement rules.

Not claimed, and stated as such in each README: no usability study, no
screen-reader session, no measured performance change, and no end-to-end test
of the real sign-in, bootstrap or consent flows. Counts and names in a mockup
are illustrative.

## Rolling on

After pack 1, the signed-in areas follow in four packs, each with the same
method and the recommended pack-1 direction as its baseline:

| Pack | Pages |
| --- | --- |
| Shell and monitoring | the app shell, Overview, Queue, Jobs, Runners, Workflows |
| Fleet management | Pools, Hosts, Providers, Machines |
| Insight and repairs | Kennel Club, Eli repairs, AI context, Usage, Comparisons |
| Settings and setup | Settings, Audit, Installations, Migrate, the wizards |

Overview, Eli repairs and Kennel Club already have reviews in `design/`. Their
packs build on those reviews and say what has changed since, rather than
starting again.

## Direction chosen after pack 1 (21 October 2026)

The owner did not like the three concepts per page and pointed at
the console's look as the one to follow. That look is now implemented on the
pages before sign in (the pull request that carries this folder), and it is the
approach for the signed-in pages. What changes in this specification:

* **One concept per page, not three.** The console's look is the concept. Each
  signed-in page gets a mock in it, beside a capture of the page today, so the
  review page's concept control offers Current and Console.
* **One pack for every signed-in page**, in `signed-in/`, not four. There is
  nothing left to choose between, so there is nothing to review in batches. The
  pages are the ones in the table under "Rolling on", and the Overview, Eli
  repairs and Kennel Club mocks say what changed since their own reviews.
* **What the look is**, taken from the console's pages and the implemented public
  frame: a rounded Zoomies Black stage with the dog where a page has one thing to
  say; large, calm headings with a small eyebrow above; rounded cards on a quiet
  ground with a tinted tile for the icon; status as a pill with a dot, never
  colour alone; mono for what is technical; outlined numerals for steps; a
  sidebar that names where you are. Spacious where a page is a summary, dense
  where it is a grid: a table stays a table and scrolls inside its own card.
* **Where a mock departs from the console**, it says why in the README, because
  an operator's grid has to hold a hundred rows and the console's pages hold six.
* The constraints, the checks and the "Not claimed" list above are unchanged.

## Out of scope

* Any change under `web/src`, `internal/`, `api/` or `cmd/`.
* New dependencies.
* A change to the Zoomies logo, Eli or the paw artwork.
* Choosing the direction. The README recommends; the owner decides.

## Success criteria

* Pack 1 opens over HTTP, switches screen, concept, style and mode, and shows
  every state in the table above.
* No horizontal overflow at 375px or 1440px, and no console errors, in any
  combination.
* Every concept's text and control contrast meets the stated ratios, except
  where the product's own Classic tokens do not: the Classic control edge is about
  1.62:1 against the surface in both modes, under the 3:1 minimum, and no concept
  built from tokens can change that. The checker records it as a known issue with
  its reason and a floor, each README repeats it, and raising the edge is
  recommended as a token change independent of any concept.
* Each page has a recommendation, and every claim in the README is backed by a
  capture or a check recorded in `viewport-review.json`.
* `go test ./internal/docs` passes.

## Risks

* The scope is large. Splitting it into packs is what keeps each one
  reviewable, and the order above puts the least-seen pages last.
* A mockup is not the product. Choosing a concept starts a separate
  implementation task, and each README says which Svelte files it would touch.
* `npm ci` may be blocked by the network proxy. The fallback above keeps the
  "current" evidence honest, at lower fidelity.

# Web UI refresh review, pack 1: the pages you can see without an account

21 October 2026. Design review only. No application source, API, test or
documentation page was changed: this folder, its tools and the plan and
specification beside it are the whole branch. Choosing a concept starts a
separate implementation task, and each recommendation below says which Svelte
files that task would touch.

The owner asked for the whole controller web UI to be refactored or improved,
with variations and concepts rather than one answer. This is the first of five
packs. It covers the five pages reachable without signing in: Sign in, First
account, Connect an app, Fleet status and Not found. The four signed-in packs
follow, each using the direction recommended here as its baseline
([SPEC.md](../SPEC.md#rolling-on)).

## What the review found

The specification listed six observations from reading the source. Each was
checked in a browser before it was kept; this is what survived.

1. **Three brand treatments on three screens. Confirmed.** Sign in draws the
   lockup at 352px (295px on a phone) on a black stage, First account draws the
   72px mark, and Connect an app draws the 121 by 28 full logo.
2. **One banner, written three times. Confirmed.** The failure banner is
   hand-written in `Login.svelte`, `Bootstrap.svelte` and `McpConsent.svelte`.
   Measured on real failure states, the radius is 4px on one and 8px on the
   others, and the icon sits 1px, 3px and 2px from the top. There is no shared
   callout in `web/src/lib/components`.
3. **The hardest field comes first. Confirmed, with a correction.** The setup
   token is the first input, 425px down at 1440x900 and 511px down on a phone,
   and only the Docker Compose command is visible as a hint. The form's own
   source comment says an earlier lockup pushed the Create button below the fold
   of a 1440x900 screen. That is fixed: the button ends at 851px. On a phone it
   ends at 1017px, 205px below the fold, and no concept claims otherwise at 1440.
4. **The widest audience has the least brand. Confirmed.** The status page has no
   logo and no image, carries no visual style, and so is always Classic.
5. **Sign in carries four states in one 983-line file. Confirmed**, as code
   structure: a visitor cannot see it, and it is what makes any visual change to
   the page expensive.
6. **The loopback warning's tone. Still open.** With the warning showing, the
   Allow button ends at 905px on a 900px screen, 5px below the fold. Whether the
   danger treatment causes alarm fatigue for a common, legitimate local client is
   a judgement the pack has no evidence on. The concepts answer it three ways, and
   it is the owner's call.

The captures added four more, each a number:

* On a phone the Sign in button ends at 839px of 812px, because the black stage
  is 295px tall.
* On a phone Allow ends at 963px of 812px.
* A blocked fleet's twelve reasons make the status page 1724px tall at 1440 and
  2080px at 375, about two and a half screens, in which the two reasons that
  block and the ten that only slow are one undivided stack.
* "Go to the overview" appears twice on the Not found page, as the shell's brand
  link and as the button, so a concept should not add a third.

## The concepts, and one recommendation for each screen

Every concept uses only tokens that exist today, except C, which needs the new
ones listed [below](#the-tokens-concept-c-would-add). Each works in both styles,
in light and dark, and has a phone layout.

Positions below are pixels from the top of the page with the review bar hidden,
as the product would draw the page and as today's pages were photographed. A page
that needs no scrolling reads as exactly the window tall, and is said to fit. They
are written down by `tools/measure.mjs` in
[concept-measurements.json](concept-measurements.json), and a test holds every
number in a table row to that file, or to
[current-measurements.json](current-measurements.json) for Today's.

* **A, evolution.** Keeps each page's structure and fixes its hierarchy, wording
  and spacing, so it is the least risky to ship. It is a tidy version of what is
  there.
* **B, evolution.** A different layout idea inside the same tokens and brand,
  and the one that gives the pages before sign in a frame they share.
* **C, bold.** A deliberately larger departure: the scene behind the Zoomies
  lockup becomes the page, and the state word or the tagline becomes the largest
  type in the product. It is the most memorable and costs the most.

### Sign in

Today the button ends at 590px on a 1440x900 screen and at 839px on a phone, and
the first input starts at 352px and 601px. Measured from the top of the page, in
Mission Control dark, in the password-only state:

| | First input, 1440 | Sign in button's bottom edge, 1440 | First input, 375 | Sign in button's bottom edge, 375 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Today | 352 | 590 | 601 | 839 (below the fold) |
| A, the split layout | 351 | 585 | 309 | 543 |
| B, the shared card | 356 | 590 | 291 | 525 |
| C, a scene | 286 | 520 | 351 | 585 |

* **A** keeps the brand panel and the form side by side, and gives a phone one

### Connect an app

Somebody else's app sends a signed-in person here mid-task to say yes or no. The
bottom edge of the Allow button, in pixels from the top of the page, in Mission
Control dark, with the fold at 900px on a desktop and 812px on a phone:

| | A request, 1440 | With the loopback warning, 1440 | A request, 375 | With the warning, 375 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Today | 820 | 905 (below the fold) | 963 (below the fold) | not measured |
| A, the same card | 769 | 873 | 949 (below the fold) | 1125 (below the fold) |
| B, role cards | 732 | 818 | pinned to the screen's bottom edge | pinned to the screen's bottom edge |
| C, a diagram | 596 | 677 | 749 | 907 (below the fold) |

* **A** keeps the card, groups the destination and its warning in one summary,
  shortens the warning, and names the app on the primary button. It keeps the
  danger colour for the warning, with fewer words.
* **B** shows the role as two cards that say what each allows, lists what the app
  can never do, and pins the buttons to the bottom of a phone without covering
  anything that has focus. It shows the warning as a neutral note with the laptop
  icon.
* **C** draws Zoomies at one end and the app at the other, with the address it
  sends you back to as the checked destination. It labels that address as this
  computer and uses no alarm colour.

All three put Allow inside the fold on a desktop, with and without the warning,
and a test holds that. On a phone, with a plain request, B and C keep it in reach;
with the warning showing, only B does, because C's Allow ends at 907px and A's at
1125px. A's first version put Allow at 995px with the warning on a desktop, worse
than today, and the fix is described in [findings.md](findings.md#what-the-connect-an-app-concepts-change-measured).

**Recommendation: B.** Two role cards make the decision the person came to take
the biggest thing on the page, and the pinned buttons keep Allow in reach on a
phone however long the request is, which is the only way to keep it there once the
warning shows. C gets there for a plain request by being the shortest page, and the
review page's `stress` state shows a 300-character app name to test the rest. Take
B's structure with A's shortened warning in
the danger colour. That combination is not drawn in the pack and so the checker
has not seen it, though both halves use tokens it has. The tone is a judgement
and the owner's decision: nothing here shows that a red warning causes alarm
fatigue, and a consent screen that stops looking like a warning for the one
redirect that reaches this computer is a risk of its own.

### Fleet status

A developer whose job has not started wants to know whether the fleet or their
workflow is at fault, usually on a phone. The page may use only what
`GET /api/v1/status` returns: a state, when it began, two counts as bands, two
waits, and the reasons with the server's sentence for each. No concept draws a
number the API does not send. Measured on a blocked fleet with twelve reasons, in
Classic dark, because that is the only style today's page has:

| | Page, 1440 | Page, 375 | Both blocking causes end, 1440 | Both blocking causes end, 375 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Today | 1724 | 2080 | not measured | not measured |
| A, banner, tiles, grouped | 900 (fits one screen) | 912 | 752 | 776 |
| B, one sentence | 900 (fits one screen) | 812 (fits one screen) | behind a disclosure | behind a disclosure |
| C, a board | 1440 | 2090 | 324 | 734 |

* **A** adds a brand header, a larger state banner and the four facts as tiles
  that stay two across on a phone, and groups the reasons by how serious they
  are, folding the ten that only slow.
* **B** says one plain sentence first, written for the person waiting, and puts
  everything else behind a disclosure. It is the shortest, and its price is that
  the cause is one tap away.
* **C** holds the state and the queue in view on one side while the reasons
  scroll on the other, with the state word at the largest size there is. It helps
  on a desktop and not on a phone, where its page is as long as today's.

In all three the state survives forced colours: the word is on the page, and a
triangle, a dashed ring and a hollow ring differ with no colour at all.

**Recommendation: A.** It cuts the page from 1724px to one screen at 1440 and from
2080px to 912px at 375, puts both blocking causes on the first screen, and keeps
every other reason one tap away, which matters on a page whose reader has nobody
to ask. B is the right trade for
a reader who only wants to know whether to wait, and could be offered as a
summary line over A. C is a desktop idea that needs A's folding to help a phone.

Files: `web/src/status/StatusPage.svelte` and `web/src/status/present.ts`, for
the grouping and the tiles. Two decisions sit outside the pack. The page ignores
the visual style today because its content security policy allows no inline
script to apply one, so giving it Mission Control means the server writes the
style into the HTML (`internal/api/handlers_status.go`). And a logo on a page for
people with no account is a product choice this pack only makes visible.

### Not found

A wrong address is most likely somebody else's stale link. All three concepts
share one rule, and it is a rule, not a style: none says what the address was.
A path taken from the URL is text anybody can put in a link on this controller's
domain, which is why this page never repeats what it was asked for.

* **A** keeps the page and adds a way back beside the way forward.
* **B** keeps the page and offers the three places most people want, Overview,
  Pools and Runners, with the product's own sentence for each from
  `web/src/lib/shell/sections.ts`.
* **C** makes the mark large and offers one calm action with nothing else to
  read.

**Recommendation: B.** The visitor does not know where they have landed, and B
gives them three places the phone's bottom bar already teaches them, without
adding a second "Go to the overview". A's "Go back" is worth keeping as a second
action, with one condition: it needs browser history, and a link opened from
another app has none, so the button must not render then. Nothing is measured
here, because the page is one screen in every concept.

## What was checked

[viewport-review.json](viewport-review.json) records 1,044 combinations, 0
findings and 6 known, from `node design/webui-refresh-review/tools/check.mjs`.
Each combination is a screen, a state, a concept, a style, a mode and a width of
320, 375 or 1440, and the checker looks for:

* a page that scrolls sideways, and text clipped by `overflow: clip` rather than
  scrolled;
* a console error or an uncaught exception;
* a control with no accessible name, a page with no `h1` or with two, a page with
  no `main` landmark or with two, a positive `tabindex`, and a control that hides
  its focus ring or draws it on something at opacity 0, as an invisible radio
  stretched over its label does;
* contrast computed from the real token values in the browser, at 4.5:1 for text
  and 3:1 for the edge of a control, on the 18 pairs of tokens the concepts paint
  (and three more for concept C). A test holds those pairs to the text colours
  the CSS draws, so a new one has to arrive in the list.

It reports and never edits a concept to pass. Each rule was shown to fail on a
page built to break it before it was trusted. Every test in the pack passes under
`node --test`, and `go test ./internal/docs` holds the pack to the repository's
voice and placement rules.

### One known issue no concept can fix

Classic's control edge, `--z-border-strong` against `--z-surface`, is 1.62:1 in
both light and dark, under the 3:1 minimum for the edge of a control. Mission
Control's is past 3:1. The six known entries are this one pair, once for each
of the three concepts in Classic light and Classic dark. No concept built from tokens can change it, so the
checker records it with its reason and a floor, and it would fail if it got
worse. **Raising Classic's `--z-border-strong` is recommended as a token change
independent of any concept**, and would fix it on every page in the product, not
only these five.

## Not claimed

* No usability study. Nobody was watched using any of this, and "recommended"
  means argued from measurements and the source, not tested on people.
* No screen reader session. The checker reads the accessibility tree and proves
  names, headings and landmarks exist; it does not say what a person hears.
* No contrast check of anything outside the listed token pairs. A colour set
  another way, such as text over a gradient or a picture, is not judged by the
  checker, and nothing in the concepts is drawn that way except the scene behind
  concept C's panel, whose own pairs are in `concept-c-pairs.json`.
* No measured performance change. Page heights and positions are measured; load
  time, bundle size and render cost are not.
* No end-to-end test of the real sign-in, bootstrap or consent flows. The
  concepts are static pages with illustrative data, and nothing here drives a
  controller.
* Nothing in a mockup is a specification. Counts, names and host names are made
  up, and the copy that is new is proposed, for the owner to accept or reword.
* The Playwright MCP the web design skill prefers is not installed in this
  environment, so its automatic verification was skipped. The repository's own
  `@playwright/test` and the preinstalled Chromium did the work.

# Web UI refresh review, pack 2: the signed-in pages

The owner chose the portal's look for the pages before sign in, and asked for the
signed-in pages "using this design as the approach and concept". This pack is
that: a mock of every signed-in page in the portal's look, each beside a capture
of the page today, built from one small kit of parts and one fleet of data, and
judged by the same checker as [pack 1](../public/README.md). It is a design to
react to. **Nothing under `web/src` has changed**, and none of it is implemented.

The method, the direction and the reasons are in
[SPEC.md](../SPEC.md) ("Direction chosen after pack 1") and the plan that built
this pack is [PLAN-signed-in.md](../PLAN-signed-in.md). What today's pages are
like, measured, is in [findings.md](findings.md).

## How to look at it

```sh
node design/webui-refresh-review/tools/serve.mjs
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8101/signed-in/mockups.html
```

The page has five controls. **Screen** and **State** pick what is drawn;
**Concept** is Current (a capture of the page today) or the portal style;
**Style** and **Mode** are the product's own two styles in light and dark. The
state of a list is one of rows, loading, empty, error with a retry, or stale rows
(the refresh failed and what is shown is from before). Narrow the window under
800px to see the phone's bottom bar and its More sheet.

The data is one frozen fleet in [fixture.js](fixture.js), four pools on four
hosts. Every field in it is one the REST API returns, which
[fixture.test.mjs](fixture.test.mjs) holds against `api/openapi.yaml`, and every
total a page shows is computed from its rows, so the Overview and the page it
links to cannot disagree.

## What the look changed, page by page

The portal's pages say one thing at a time and put the evidence under it. The
mocks do the same: a calm header, one answer in the stage where a page has one,
the data in a card of its own, and the explanation on request and not in front
of the content. A table stays a table and scrolls inside its card, never the
page. Heights are the stage alone, the way the capture frames it, so a page
shorter than the window is as tall as the window. Today's fleet is smaller than
the mock's (the demo has two pools and ten runners, the fixture four pools and
eleven), so the heights compare layouts and not what a real fleet would do.

## What every page shares

* **A shell**: the product's own sidebar, in its four groups and its order, with
  the Overview alone above them; a top bar; and on a phone a bar of the four
  sections an operator watches a fleet with and a More sheet for the rest. The
  sheet is a native popover, so it opens with focus on its Close button, closes
  on Escape, gives focus back and dims the page behind it. A native popover does
  not hold Tab inside it: the product's own menu on a phone (`NavMenu`) does, by
  making the page behind it inert, and the real build keeps that behaviour.
* **A page header**: small capitals, the title, a short blue rule, one sentence.
* **A card, a stat, a stage, a table card, steps and a checklist.**
* **A pill**: a word and a shape (disc, diamond, ring, triangle, square, bar),
  so a state survives greyscale and forced colours. Colour is the third cue.
* **The four states of a list**, drawn by one function, so no page can forget one.

## Where it departs from the portal, and why

* **Density.** The portal's pages are marketing pages with room to breathe. A
  fleet page has to put rows on the first screen, so cards are smaller and the
  stage is shorter.
* **No decoration in status colours.** A pill's colour is only ever a state, and
  the stage carries neutral white and the brand blue only, because the panel does
  not change with the theme.
* **Tables scroll inside their card.** The portal has none.
* **No dog on every page.** The stage carries the mark once, at the top of a page
  that has a stage, and nowhere else.

## Tokens

The kit proposes **no new tokens**: [kit-tokens.css](kit-tokens.css) is empty on
purpose, and everything is drawn from `tokens.css` as it stands. What
[kit.css](kit.css) writes by hand is a handful of one-off layout measures, which
`web/AGENTS.md` allows and which are listed here so none is hidden.

| Length | Where it is used |
| --- | --- |
| `80rem` | the widest a page's content runs |
| `40rem` | the longest line of a page's subtitle |
| `32rem` | the longest line of a stage's sentence |
| `36rem` | the longest line of an empty state's explanation |
| `14rem` | the widest a truncated table cell grows before it clips, and the narrowest a stat is allowed |
| `20rem` | the narrowest a card in a two-up row is allowed |
| `10rem` | the narrowest a stat is allowed on a phone, and the widest the mark in a stage grows |
| `6rem` | the narrowest the mark in a stage shrinks to |
| `12rem` | the narrowest a list row's main text is allowed |
| `3.5rem` | the width of an outlined numeral |
| `5.5rem` | the mark's size in a stage on a phone |
| `1.4s` | the pulse of a loading placeholder, still for anyone who asks for less motion |
| `0.5` | the dimmest a loading placeholder pulses to |
| `100vh` | the tallest the sidebar grows before it scrolls inside itself |
| `80vh` | the tallest the phone's More sheet grows before it scrolls |

## What was checked

[viewport-review.json](viewport-review.json) is what `node
design/webui-refresh-review/tools/check.mjs --pack signed-in` wrote: 1,392
combinations of screen, state, style, mode and width (320, 375 and 1440), with
0 findings and 4 known, on the 18 pairs of tokens the public pack
checks and 12 the kit adds (the stage's words and accent on Zoomies Black, the
card surface, each pill's word on its tint, a filter's edge). What it looks for is
the same as in pack 1: a page that scrolls sideways or cuts a sentence off, a
control with no name, a focus ring that has gone, a colour pair under 4.5:1 for
text or 3:1 for an edge, a landmark that is not one.

The checker learned two things on the way, each with a test that failed first: a
table inside a region that scrolls is not "cut off", and a region that hides its
spill still is.

Tests hold the rest: the fixture against the API's schema and its totals against
its rows, the Overview's numbers against the fleet, every list page in all five
states and at 320, a 300-character name and a 120-character label held to a line
with all of the text in the title and shown whole while the row has keyboard focus, every row action, filter, page action and search at 44px on a phone, the More
sheet opening and closing and returning focus, the pill shapes being six
different shapes, and a wrong field being marked and described.

### One known issue no mock can fix

Classic's control edge, `--z-border-strong`, is about 1.62:1 against the page
surface and the raised card surface in light, and 1.48:1 on the card in dark,
under the 3:1 minimum for the edge of a control. Mission Control's is past 3:1.
It is the same token as in pack 1 and one change to it clears every instance.
The checker reports it as known every time, so a green run is never silent about
it.

## Not claimed

* **A usability study.** Nobody has used these pages to do anything.
* **A screen reader pass.** The checker looks for a name, a landmark and a focus
  ring; it does not read a page aloud.
* **Performance.** The mocks are plain HTML; what a built page weighs and how it
  paints is not measured. The status page's budget is untouched, since nothing
  here is built into the product.
* **End-to-end behaviour.** The mocks send no request. A retry, a refresh and a
  save go nowhere.
* **A real fleet's data.** The fixture is illustrative and small, so the heights
  compare layouts and not what a fleet of two hundred runners would do. The
  Comparisons figures are a design, not API output.

## What happens next

Nothing here is implemented. Each page is a separate task, in the order the owner
chooses, and starts from its mock. The kit is the first of them: the shell, the
page header, the card, the pill and the four states of a list are what every page
needs, and building them once in `web/src/lib` is what lets a page after that be
a small change.

# Findings from the signed-in pages today

21 October 2026. Working notes for the signed-in README. Every number here is in
[current-measurements.json](current-measurements.json), written by
`tools/capture-signed-in.mjs` against the real controller: the seeded demo fleet,
authentication off on loopback, Mission Control dark, at 1440x900 and 375x812. A
picture is the whole page, capped at 2400px, and the height is recorded beside it.
Nothing was stubbed. The demo fleet is small (two pools, three hosts, ten runners),
so a real fleet's pages are taller than these.

* **Nothing scrolls sideways at 375.** The grids scroll inside their own region, as
  the guidelines ask, so the cost on a phone is height and not width.
* **Five pages are more than three screens tall on a phone**: Usage (6,587px),
  Kennel Club (7,709px), a pool (5,247px), a runner (4,796px) and Hosts (3,515px).
  These are the pages whose structure the look has most to say about.
* **Most list pages open the same way** (Pools, Queue, Jobs, Runners, Hosts and
  Providers; Workflows is the exception): a title, a sentence, four to six small
  stat tiles, a paragraph that explains them, filters, and then the grid. On
  Runners that is six tiles, a provisioning strip, a lifecycle diagram, two
  paragraphs and a disclosure before the first row at 1,000px down, and the grid
  then truncates names ("zoomies-2vcpu-4gb...") because its twelve columns share
  1,160px. The first row is below the fold of a 900px screen.
* **Grids are wide.** Pools has 14 columns, Jobs 12, Runners and Workflows 11,
  Queue 9; at 1440 the columns that name things (name, pool, host) are the ones
  that lose room.
* **The sidebar already does what the portal's does**: groups, one entry filled,
  a footer. What differs is everything inside the page.
* **Each page repeats the same pieces by hand**: stat tiles, a filter row, a
  status cell, a page header. That is the structural finding behind the look: a
  kit of a few parts, used everywhere, is what lets them agree.

## What the look would change, page by page

The portal's pages say one thing at a time and put the evidence under it. The
mocks do the same: a calm header, one summary where a page has one, the data in a
card of its own, and the explanation on request rather than in front of the
content. A table stays a table.

# Zoomies on a single VM, behind Cloudflare.
#
#   1. cp .env.example .env  and fill in the three values it asks for:
#        ZOOMIES_EXTERNAL_URL    the https address GitHub and you reach this at
#        ZOOMIES_ENCRYPTION_KEY  openssl rand -base64 32
#        DOCKER_GID              stat -c '%g' /var/run/docker.sock
#   2. mkdir -p data && sudo chown 65532:65532 data
#      sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/zoomies/shared && sudo chown 65532:65532 /var/lib/zoomies/shared
#   3. docker compose up -d
#   4. docker compose logs zoomies | grep 'setup token'
#   5. open ZOOMIES_EXTERNAL_URL, paste that token, and create the first admin
#
# Step 4 is the gate on step 5. This origin is reachable the moment the
# container starts, and an empty database is not proof of ownership: the setup
# token, which only somebody who can read this container's log has, is. It
# changes on every restart and stops being printed once an account exists.
#
# Steps 4 and 5 are for a person. Where nobody is watching -- this file driven
# by a Terraform module or a configuration-management run -- set the
# ZOOMIES_BOOTSTRAP_* lines and the secrets block below instead: the first
# account is created from a file at startup, /readyz reports
# bootstrap_required false once it exists, and nothing has to be read out of
# the log. docs/configuration.md has the details.
#
# Compose refuses to start with any of the three missing, on purpose: each one
# left to a default produces a container that is healthy and useless. A wrong
# external URL sends GitHub's webhooks and its App-creation redirect to the
# wrong site; a missing key means nothing secret can be stored; and a wrong
# DOCKER_GID leaves the agent unable to open the socket, so every pool queues
# for ever. The Hosts page diagnoses that last one and names the line to
# change, but it is quicker not to have to.
#
# Step 2 is not optional, and the chown needs root: handing a directory to
# another uid is not something the docker group lets you do. The database
# lives in ./data next to this file, bind
# mounted into the container, and a bind mount keeps the host directory's
# ownership -- unlike a named volume, it does not inherit anything from the
# image. The container runs as uid 65532, so a ./data owned by anyone else (and
# Docker creates a missing one as root) gives you:
#
#   store: connecting to /var/lib/zoomies/zoomies.db: unable to open database
#   file (14)
#
# Cloudflare terminates TLS and proxies to this origin over plain HTTP on port
# 80, so the container serves HTTP and Zoomies is told its external URL is
# https. That is what makes the session cookie Secure, the webhook URL correct,
# and the UI's links right.
#
# The controller runs an embedded agent, so this is one container plus the
# runners it creates.

name: zoomies

services:
  zoomies:
    image: ghcr.io/eyupio/zoomies:latest
    # Or build locally:
    # build:
    #   context: .
    #   dockerfile: deploy/Dockerfile
    #   target: controller
    restart: unless-stopped
    # Finish admitted runner creation before replacing the service.
    stop_grace_period: 20m
    # The embedded agent registers this host under the container's hostname.
    # Without one that is the container's random twelve-hex-digit ID, which
    # then follows the host into every scheduler reason and problem message.
    hostname: zoomies
    command: ["controller"]
    # Compose already reads .env to interpolate the ${...} below; this passes it
    # into the container as well, so any of the ZOOMIES_* settings in
    # docs/configuration.md can be set by putting it in .env, with no matching
    # line needed here. The explicit environment: entries below still win.
    #
    # required: false keeps a deployment that supplies its own environment --
    # systemd, a secrets manager, CI -- from failing on a missing .env. It needs
    # Compose v2.24 or newer; on older versions use `env_file: .env`.
    env_file:
      - path: .env
        required: false
    environment:
      # How GitHub and your browser reach this controller. Webhooks are
      # delivered to $ZOOMIES_EXTERNAL_URL/webhooks/github, the GitHub App
      # created from the Installations page redirects back to it, and the
      # https here is what makes Zoomies mark its session cookie Secure.
      ZOOMIES_EXTERNAL_URL: ${ZOOMIES_EXTERNAL_URL:?set this in .env to the https address this controller is reached at}

      # 32 bytes, base64. Generate with: openssl rand -base64 32
      # Back it up: without it the stored GitHub App key cannot be decrypted.
      ZOOMIES_ENCRYPTION_KEY: ${ZOOMIES_ENCRYPTION_KEY:?set this in .env}

      # Inside the container we bind to all interfaces; the published port
      # below is what actually controls exposure. TLS is off here because
      # Cloudflare terminates it -- Zoomies will say so at startup, and that
      # warning is expected in this deployment.
      ZOOMIES_BIND: "0.0.0.0:8080"
      ZOOMIES_TLS_MODE: "off"

      # Without this every audit row and every login rate-limit decision sees
      # Cloudflare's address instead of the real client's, so the whole
      # internet is throttled as one caller and the audit log is useless.
      # Refresh from https://www.cloudflare.com/ips/ when Cloudflare publishes
      # a change.
      ZOOMIES_TRUSTED_PROXIES: ${ZOOMIES_TRUSTED_PROXIES}

      ZOOMIES_DB_PATH: /var/lib/zoomies/zoomies.db
      ZOOMIES_AGENT_EMBEDDED: "true"
      ZOOMIES_AGENT_BACKEND: docker
      ZOOMIES_DOCKER_HOST: unix:///var/run/docker.sock
      # Empty on purpose: the agent works its own capacity out from the
      # machine it measures, which is the only figure here that has seen it. A
      # constant would pin every deployment of this file to the same number of
      # slots however large the host is -- and the capacity is no longer only
      # a slot count: a pool that leaves its runners' size to the host is
      # given the machine divided by it. Set this to override.
      ZOOMIES_AGENT_CAPACITY: ${ZOOMIES_AGENT_CAPACITY}
      # The network runner containers are attached to: the one declared at the
      # bottom of this file. Without this line the agent leaves them on the
      # daemon's default bridge, whatever the comment down there promises.
      ZOOMIES_AGENT_NETWORK: zoomies
      ZOOMIES_WORK_DIR: /var/lib/zoomies/work
      ZOOMIES_LOG_FORMAT: json

      # The gid group_add below is given, echoed into the container so that
      # when it is wrong the Hosts page can say "the container holds 999 and
      # the socket is owned by 987; change DOCKER_GID in .env" rather than
      # leaving you to work out which file the number came from.
      DOCKER_GID: ${DOCKER_GID:?set this in .env to the gid that owns /var/run/docker.sock, which stat -c %g /var/run/docker.sock prints}

      # The unattended first account. Unset, the setup token above is the way
      # in. Set the username and exactly one of the two files; each is read
      # once, on a database with no accounts, and ignored with a warning ever
      # after. The token file holds a token you generated
      # (openssl rand -hex 32) that becomes a platform API token; the password
      # file holds a password for a person's account instead.
      # ZOOMIES_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN: platform
      # ZOOMIES_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN_FILE: /run/secrets/zoomies_bootstrap_token
      # ZOOMIES_BOOTSTRAP_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/zoomies_bootstrap_password
    # The file behind it, if you set one. The long syntax matters: compose
    # mounts a secret 0444 by default, and Zoomies refuses a credential file
    # that group or other can read. The uid is the one the image runs as.
    # secrets:
    #   - source: zoomies_bootstrap_token
    #     uid: "65532"
    #     mode: 0400
    ports:
      # Cloudflare connects here over HTTP. Nothing but Cloudflare should be
      # able to: put the origin behind a firewall that allows only Cloudflare's
      # ranges, or use a Cloudflare Tunnel and publish no port at all.
      - "80:8080"
    volumes:
      # The database, in ./data beside this file -- so backing Zoomies up is
      # copying a directory, and inspecting it does not need `docker volume
      # inspect`. See step 2 above: this directory must be owned by 65532.
      # (Runner containers keep their scratch space in their own filesystem;
      # nothing of theirs lands here.)
      - type: bind
        source: ./data
        target: /var/lib/zoomies
        bind:
          # Compose would otherwise helpfully create a missing ./data -- as
          # root, since the daemon is root -- and hand you error 14 at startup.
          # Failing with "bind source path does not exist" is far easier to act
          # on than a SQLite error code.
          create_host_path: false
      # The shared folder: runners' caches, one folder per purpose, and where
      # later releases add folders of their own -- which is why it has to be
      # owned by 65532 (step 2), and why Zoomies creates what it needs inside
      # it as it starts. It is mounted at the path it has on the host, because
      # the host's Docker daemon binds its subfolders into runner containers,
      # and a path that meant something else inside this container would point
      # a runner at a folder the daemon cannot see.
      - type: bind
        source: /var/lib/zoomies/shared
        target: /var/lib/zoomies/shared
        bind:
          create_host_path: false
      # The embedded agent needs the Docker socket to create runner containers.
      # This is Zoomies' own access to Docker -- it is NOT the same thing as
      # pool.docker_mode=host-socket, which would hand the socket to your jobs.
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
    # The image runs as uid 65532; that user must be able to use the socket,
    # which means joining the group that owns it. That group is read from the
    # socket, not assumed to be called docker: it is 987 on one distribution,
    # 999 or 998 on another, and something else again for a rootless daemon.
    # A container is given its groups when it is created, so after changing
    # DOCKER_GID run `docker compose up -d` again and compose recreates it.
    group_add:
      - ${DOCKER_GID}
    networks: [zoomies]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "/usr/local/bin/zoomies", "healthcheck", "--url", "http://127.0.0.1:8080"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s

# The secret the commented bootstrap lines above name, kept out of .env and out
# of `docker inspect`.
# secrets:
#   zoomies_bootstrap_token:
#     file: ./bootstrap-token

networks:
  # Runner containers are attached to this network by the embedded agent, which
  # keeps them off the host network and off the default bridge.
  zoomies:
    name: zoomies
