-- deletes its work directory as the link fails and the runner's output is the
-- runner's own diagnostics, so by the time the job is reported failed nothing
-- else says the folder was 96% full a sample earlier. Empty is "never
-- measured": a job from before this migration, a runner with no folder in
-- memory, an agent too old to measure, or a host whose /proc does not show the
-- container.
ALTER TABLE jobs ADD COLUMN scratch_peaks TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '';

-- A hypervisor reuses its ids. Proxmox is asked for the lowest free VMID in the
-- range an operator allowed, so once a machine's VM has been destroyed and the
-- provider has confirmed it gone, the next machine is given the same id.
--
-- The unique index on a machine's resource counted every row that ever named
-- one, history included. The first deleted machine therefore kept its VMID for
-- ever, every later allocation picked that id again, and the write that records
-- it before anything is built failed with a constraint error: the provider could
-- build no second machine, and the failures stood it down.
--
-- deleted_at is when the provider confirmed the resource gone, and is already how
-- idx_machines_owned decides that a row still owns something. The unique index
-- now agrees with it. While a resource exists at most one row may name it; once
-- it is confirmed gone the row stays, as the record of what was rented and what
-- it cost, and stops claiming the id.
DROP INDEX idx_machines_resource;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_machines_resource ON machines(provider_id, resource_zone, resource_id)
    WHERE resource_id <> '' AND deleted_at IS NULL;

-- A person can hide a repair from Eli's Recent repairs without deleting it.
--
-- The row is also the ledger behind the daily budget, the deduplication of
-- webhook deliveries and the guard that stops Eli repairing its own repair
-- commit. Deleting it would reset the spend cap and re-open a repair loop, so
-- clearing only records when the history stopped showing it.
--
-- Three places touch this column and nothing else may: the history's where
-- clause reads it, ClearEliRepairs writes it, and EnqueueEliRepair writes it
-- when a person asks again for a cleared repair. A budget, deduplication or
-- loop-guard query that looked at it would start to forget cleared rows.
--
-- NULL means shown, which is what every existing row keeps on upgrade.
ALTER TABLE eli_repairs ADD COLUMN cleared_at INTEGER;

-- The certificate a machine trusts for the controller, apart from the one the
-- controller trusts for the provider.
--
-- providers.ca_pem did both jobs. Every machine was handed it as the only
-- authority it would accept from this controller, so a cluster's own authority
-- became the one thing a machine could verify the controller against, and a
-- controller on a public certificate was refused by every machine it rented.
-- The column below holds the machines' half on its own. Empty means a machine
-- uses its own trust store.
--
-- A provider that already has a certificate is given it here as well. That is
-- what its machines were being told before this migration, and a deployment
-- whose controller is signed by the same private authority as its hypervisor
-- depends on it. Nothing changes for such a provider until somebody edits the
-- field, which the form now explains.
ALTER TABLE providers ADD COLUMN machine_ca_pem TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '';
UPDATE providers SET machine_ca_pem = ca_pem WHERE ca_pem <> '';

-- How many machines a provider keeps ready whether or not anything is waiting.
--
-- Until now a provider owned exactly as many machines as the queue needed and
-- gave each one up when it had been idle for the provider's idle timeout, so
-- the first job after a quiet spell always waited for a clone. A minimum keeps
-- that many machines rented through the quiet, which is paid for in return for
-- a job starting at once. Zero, the default, is what every provider did before.
ALTER TABLE providers ADD COLUMN min_machines INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

-- The size a provider's machines turned out to be, when its row names none.
--
-- A provider whose machine size is left empty builds whatever its template is,
-- and the fit check behind renting judged that machine as one that had measured
-- nothing, which fits every pool by slots alone. A fleet bought 2 vCPU, 3.9 GB
-- machines for a docker-in-docker pool whose runner needs 6.7 GB, and then sat
-- at the provider's ceiling with two machines that could never run a job.
--
-- The columns below are observations, written by the controller: the template's
-- own size when a connection check reads it, and what a machine it built
-- measured itself as once its agent joined. seen_at is when the evidence was
-- true, so that an older machine never overrules a check made after the
-- template changed. They are kept rather than worked out from the machines
-- that exist, because the machines that prove a shape too small are the ones
-- released for it, and a fleet that forgot the reason would buy them again.
ALTER TABLE providers ADD COLUMN seen_cpus INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;
ALTER TABLE providers ADD COLUMN seen_memory_mb INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;
ALTER TABLE providers ADD COLUMN seen_from TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '';
ALTER TABLE providers ADD COLUMN seen_at INTEGER;

-- Evidence survives job retention, but remains an installation's bounded history.
CREATE TABLE comparison_evidence (
    sequence INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    id TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES installations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    repository TEXT NOT NULL,
    initiating_user TEXT NOT NULL,
    version TEXT NOT NULL,
    sha256 TEXT NOT NULL,
    payload BLOB NOT NULL CHECK(length(payload) > 0 AND length(payload) <= 2097152),
    created_at INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX comparison_evidence_scope ON comparison_evidence(installation_id, repository, id);

-- A bounded non-secret observation survives runner pruning for historical joins.
-- Installation removal still removes its observations. Current pool/host state
-- cannot reconstruct an issued task or an agent's past report.
CREATE TABLE runner_creation_observations (
    sequence INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    runner_id TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES installations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    sha256 TEXT NOT NULL,
    payload BLOB NOT NULL CHECK(length(payload) <= 4096),
    received_at INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_runner_creation_observations_scope ON runner_creation_observations(installation_id, runner_id, received_at);

-- No cascading foreign key: retirement and cutover obligations must survive a
-- host re-enrolling, and a deleted record must not make recovery look complete.
CREATE TABLE host_recovery (
    host_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    retired_at INTEGER,
    completed_at INTEGER,
    retired_by TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''
);

-- Private source-bearing previews have their own bounded, installation-scoped history.
CREATE TABLE optimisation_previews (
    sequence INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    id TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES installations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    repository TEXT NOT NULL,
    initiating_user TEXT NOT NULL,
    version TEXT NOT NULL,
    sha256 TEXT NOT NULL,
    payload BLOB NOT NULL CHECK(length(payload) > 0 AND length(payload) <= 262144),
    created_at INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX optimisation_preview_scope ON optimisation_previews(installation_id, repository, id);

-- What the update helper reported about the engine's run: the copy it took
-- before it changed anything, and whether it put the previous release back.
-- Both are for the page, so an operator can restore from the copy and can tell
-- a failure that was undone from one left in place. Empty and zero are an
-- attempt from before this, or one whose result carried neither.
ALTER TABLE update_attempts ADD COLUMN backup TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '';
ALTER TABLE update_attempts ADD COLUMN rolled_back INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

-- A machine an operator asked for to prove a provider works, rather than one
-- demand asked for. It is built, enrolled and released by the same loop as any
-- other, and counts against max_machines; the flag only says that it is a trial,
-- so it is not kept warm, is released once it reports ready, and is not mistaken
-- for supply by the planner.
ALTER TABLE machines ADD COLUMN is_test INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

-- A person has seen this failure and does not need it in front of them again.
-- This is the triage record the Jobs page's attention view stops asking about:
-- a failure with acknowledged_at NULL, no later attempt and a recent queue
-- time is one nobody has dealt with. The name is kept beside the time so a
-- shared fleet can say who looked; both are empty on a failure nobody has
-- triaged yet, which is the ordinary state.
--
-- It is a column on the job rather than a table of its own because there is
-- exactly one per job and it dies with the job's retention. Unlike
-- problem_dismissals it is not per account: an acknowledgement here is the
-- fleet's, so whoever looks first stops the failure being news to everybody.
ALTER TABLE jobs ADD COLUMN acknowledged_at INTEGER;
ALTER TABLE jobs ADD COLUMN acknowledged_by TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '';

-- GitHub can close a PR or settle checks without changing the retained job.
-- Keep that observation separate from a person's acknowledgement and the
-- historical conclusion. New failures after the observation remain visible.
CREATE TABLE job_attention_runs (
    repo TEXT NOT NULL,
    run_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    reason TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    checked_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    attempted_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (repo, run_id)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_jobs_attention_branch ON jobs(repo, head_branch, workflow, job_name, queued_at);

-- The event that started a job's workflow run (push, pull_request, schedule...).
-- workflow_job deliveries do not carry it, so it is filled in from the run when
-- the controller reads one. Eli repairs a pull request's branch and nothing
-- else, so a failure of any other kind of run must not be offered to it.
ALTER TABLE jobs ADD COLUMN run_event TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '';

-- Whether a host keeps its capacity and reserve at what Zoomies recommends for
-- its machine and the fleet's pools, and when the controller last moved them.
-- Its own table, so the central host row and every query that reads it stay as
-- they are: a host with no row follows the fleet's default.
CREATE TABLE host_auto_adjust (
    host_id     TEXT    PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES hosts(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    mode        TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    adjusted_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

-- The disk a provider's machines turned out to have, beside their size.
--
-- Migration 0103 taught a provider the processors and memory its machines
-- turn out to have, because a machine of unknown size fits every pool. It left
-- the disk out, so a pool that needed room to clone and build was still handed
-- a machine whose disk nobody had measured. A template that is a cloud image
-- boots with a few gigabytes, and three jobs on fresh clones died on one
-- before anything said it was too small for them.
--
-- The column is an observation like the others: the template's boot disk when
-- a connection check reads it, and what a machine it built measured itself as
-- once its agent joined, written under the same seen_at and forgotten under the
-- same edits. Zero means not measured, which fits every pool by disk, as
-- before.
ALTER TABLE providers ADD COLUMN seen_disk_mb INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

-- What an agent found when the update helper on a host was not reading requests,
-- as the controller wrote it down: a small JSON document of numbers and fixed
-- words (which stall, how long the request had waited, the units' states, what
-- root repaired). Empty on an attempt that was not stalled. It rides the attempt
-- because the problem it raises has to survive a restart, and a sentence in
-- the error column cannot be told from any other failure's.
ALTER TABLE update_attempts ADD COLUMN stuck TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '';

-- The image a pool's docker-in-docker sidecar runs, for a pool that needs a
-- different one from the host's: a Docker version of its own, or the mirrors a
-- single registry cache needs. Empty means the host's own choice
-- (agent.dind_image, and docker:27-dind where that is empty), which is what
-- every pool already meant, so an upgrade changes no sidecar.
ALTER TABLE pools ADD COLUMN dind_image TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '';

-- The identity provider's own session that a browser session here was created
-- from (the sid claim of its ID token), so that a back-channel logout for one
-- of that person's sessions at the provider ends the sessions it started and
-- not the ones the same person holds from another browser. Empty for a session
-- made by a password and for one made before this column existed, which a
-- logout that names a session therefore leaves alone.
ALTER TABLE sessions ADD COLUMN oidc_sid TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '';
CREATE INDEX idx_sessions_oidc_sid ON sessions(user_id, oidc_sid) WHERE oidc_sid <> '';

-- An approval is a separate, attributed act from keeping a preview. It binds
-- one exact retained preview at the head and source digest the operator was
-- shown, and expires with that preview: deleting or pruning the preview
-- cascades here, and reads require the preview to still be within its lifetime.
CREATE TABLE optimisation_preview_approvals (
    preview_id     TEXT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES optimisation_previews(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    repository     TEXT NOT NULL,
    approved_by    TEXT NOT NULL,
    head_sha       TEXT NOT NULL,
    source_sha256  TEXT NOT NULL,
    preview_sha256 TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at     INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX optimisation_preview_approval_scope
    ON optimisation_preview_approvals(installation_id, repository, preview_id);

-- A publication is the draft pull request opened for one approved retained
-- preview. It is separate from the preview and its approval, cascades with the
-- preview, and records exactly what was written where. Nothing here is a merge.
CREATE TABLE optimisation_publications (
    preview_id      TEXT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES optimisation_previews(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    repository      TEXT NOT NULL,
    published_by    TEXT NOT NULL,
    branch          TEXT NOT NULL,
    base_branch     TEXT NOT NULL,
    base_sha        TEXT NOT NULL,
    head_sha        TEXT NOT NULL,
    source_sha256   TEXT NOT NULL,
    preview_sha256  TEXT NOT NULL,
    pull_number     INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(pull_number > 0),
    pull_url        TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at      INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX optimisation_publication_scope
    ON optimisation_publications(installation_id, repository, preview_id);

-- One retained comparison may be linked to a published optimisation as its
-- verification evidence. It is a separate record and never rewrites the
-- comparison or the publication; the preview expires with both.
CREATE TABLE optimisation_publication_verifications (
    preview_id      TEXT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES optimisation_publications(preview_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    comparison_id   TEXT NOT NULL,
    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    repository      TEXT NOT NULL,
    linked_by       TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at      INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX optimisation_publication_verification_scope
    ON optimisation_publication_verifications(installation_id, repository, preview_id);

-- Private source-bearing cache previews have their own bounded,
-- installation-scoped history. The lockfile content is not retained, only its
-- path, mode and SHA-256, so a large lockfile stays out of the database.
CREATE TABLE optimisation_cache_previews (
    sequence INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    id TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES installations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    repository TEXT NOT NULL,
    initiating_user TEXT NOT NULL,
    version TEXT NOT NULL,
    sha256 TEXT NOT NULL,
    payload BLOB NOT NULL CHECK(length(payload) > 0 AND length(payload) <= 262144),
    created_at INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX optimisation_cache_preview_scope ON optimisation_cache_previews(installation_id, repository, id);

-- An approval of a kept setup cache preview is a separate, attributed act.
-- It binds the preview's head, workflow digest, lockfile digest and preview
-- hash, expires with the preview through the cascade, and publishes nothing.
CREATE TABLE optimisation_cache_preview_approvals (
    preview_id      TEXT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES optimisation_cache_previews(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    repository      TEXT NOT NULL,
    approved_by     TEXT NOT NULL,
    head_sha        TEXT NOT NULL,
    source_sha256   TEXT NOT NULL,
    preview_sha256  TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at      INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX optimisation_cache_preview_approval_scope
    ON optimisation_cache_preview_approvals(installation_id, repository, preview_id);

-- A publication is the one draft pull request opened for an approved setup
-- cache preview. It cascades with the preview, names the branch and base it
-- used, and records exactly what was written where. Nothing here is a merge.
CREATE TABLE optimisation_cache_publications (
    preview_id      TEXT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES optimisation_cache_previews(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    repository      TEXT NOT NULL,
    published_by    TEXT NOT NULL,
    branch          TEXT NOT NULL,
    base_branch     TEXT NOT NULL,
    base_sha        TEXT NOT NULL,
    head_sha        TEXT NOT NULL,
    source_sha256   TEXT NOT NULL,
    preview_sha256  TEXT NOT NULL,
    pull_number     INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(pull_number > 0),
    pull_url        TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at      INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX optimisation_cache_publication_scope
    ON optimisation_cache_publications(installation_id, repository, preview_id);

-- I/O wait beside the CPU figure it explains. cpu_percent counts time spent
-- waiting on disk as busy, so a host stalled on its disk reads as a host hard
-- at work; the gap between the two is the bottleneck an operator is looking
-- for. Nullable for the same reason as every other measurement here: an agent
-- too old to report it is a gap in the chart, not a quiet disk.
ALTER TABLE host_samples ADD COLUMN io_wait_percent REAL;

-- One retained bounded readiness preview: the exact workflow source, the
-- operator's condition, the wait samples and the computed edit. It is private,
-- bounded and separate from the checkout and cache histories.
CREATE TABLE optimisation_readiness_previews (
    sequence        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    id              TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES installations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    repository      TEXT NOT NULL,
    initiating_user TEXT NOT NULL,
    version         TEXT NOT NULL,
    sha256          TEXT NOT NULL,
    payload         BLOB NOT NULL,
    created_at      INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX optimisation_readiness_preview_scope
    ON optimisation_readiness_previews(installation_id, repository, id);
CREATE INDEX optimisation_readiness_preview_created
    ON optimisation_readiness_previews(created_at);

-- An approval of a kept bounded readiness preview is a separate, attributed act.
-- It binds the preview's head, workflow digest and preview hash, expires with the
-- preview through the cascade, and publishes nothing.
CREATE TABLE optimisation_readiness_preview_approvals (
    preview_id      TEXT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES optimisation_readiness_previews(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    repository      TEXT NOT NULL,
    approved_by     TEXT NOT NULL,
    head_sha        TEXT NOT NULL,
    source_sha256   TEXT NOT NULL,
    preview_sha256  TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at      INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX optimisation_readiness_preview_approval_scope
    ON optimisation_readiness_preview_approvals(installation_id, repository, preview_id);

-- A publication is the one draft pull request opened for an approved bounded
-- readiness preview. It cascades with the preview, names the branch and base it
-- used, and records exactly what was written where. Nothing here is a merge.
CREATE TABLE optimisation_readiness_publications (
    preview_id      TEXT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES optimisation_readiness_previews(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    repository      TEXT NOT NULL,
    published_by    TEXT NOT NULL,
    branch          TEXT NOT NULL,
    base_branch     TEXT NOT NULL,
    base_sha        TEXT NOT NULL,
    head_sha        TEXT NOT NULL,
    source_sha256   TEXT NOT NULL,
    preview_sha256  TEXT NOT NULL,
    pull_number     INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(pull_number > 0),
    pull_url        TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at      INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX optimisation_readiness_publication_scope
    ON optimisation_readiness_publications(installation_id, repository, preview_id);

-- One retained Playwright sharding preview: the exact workflow source, the
-- timing samples and the computed edit. It is private, bounded and separate
-- from the checkout, cache and readiness histories.
CREATE TABLE optimisation_sharding_previews (
    sequence        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    id              TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES installations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,

CREATE INDEX optimisation_sharding_preview_scope

CREATE INDEX optimisation_sharding_preview_created
    ON optimisation_sharding_previews(created_at);

-- An approval of a kept bounded sharding preview is a separate, attributed act.
-- It binds the preview's head, workflow digest and preview hash, expires with the
-- preview through the cascade, and publishes nothing.
CREATE TABLE optimisation_sharding_preview_approvals (

    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    repository      TEXT NOT NULL,
    approved_by     TEXT NOT NULL,
    head_sha        TEXT NOT NULL,
    source_sha256   TEXT NOT NULL,
    preview_sha256  TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at      INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX optimisation_sharding_preview_approval_scope
    ON optimisation_sharding_preview_approvals(installation_id, repository, preview_id);

-- A publication is the one draft pull request opened for an approved bounded
-- sharding preview. It cascades with the preview, names the branch and base it
-- used, and records exactly what was written where. Nothing here is a merge.
CREATE TABLE optimisation_sharding_publications (
    preview_id      TEXT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES optimisation_sharding_previews(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    installation_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    repository      TEXT NOT NULL,
    published_by    TEXT NOT NULL,

// The prefixes shared by pairs of files that already shipped. They sort by what
// follows the underscore, which happened to be the right order; nothing after
// them may rely on that again.
var grandfatheredPrefixes = map[string]bool{"0005": true, "0006": true, "0102": true}

func TestMigrationNamesAreFixedAndNewPrefixesAreUnique(t *testing.T) {
	entries, err := fs.ReadDir(migrationFS, "migrations")
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("reading the embedded migrations: %v", err)
	}
	var names []string
	for _, e := range entries {
		if !e.IsDir() && strings.HasSuffix(e.Name(), ".sql") {
			names = append(names, e.Name())
		}
	}
	slices.Sort(names)

	if !slices.Equal(names, shippedMigrations) {
		t.Fatalf("the migration directory does not match the shipped list:\n got  %v\n want %v\n"+
			"a shipped name must never change, and a new migration is added to both", names, shippedMigrations)
	}

	seen := map[string]string{}
	counts := map[string]int{}
	for _, name := range names {
		prefix, _, ok := strings.Cut(name, "_")
		if !ok || len(prefix) != 4 || strings.Trim(prefix, "0123456789") != "" {
			t.Fatalf("%s does not start with a four-digit prefix and an underscore", name)
		}
		counts[prefix]++
		if other, dup := seen[prefix]; dup && (!grandfatheredPrefixes[prefix] || counts[prefix] > 2) {
			t.Fatalf("%s and %s share the prefix %s; take the next unused number", other, name, prefix)
		}
		seen[prefix] = name
	}
}

# The zoomies.sh site.
#
# It publishes the docs that already live in docs/ rather than a second copy of
# them, so the website cannot drift from the repository. install.sh and
# install.ps1 are copied to the site root by the deploy workflow, again from the
# ones in the repository root, so `curl -fsSL https://zoomies.sh/install.sh | sh`
# and the file a contributor edits are the same file.

site_name: Zoomies
site_url: https://zoomies.sh/
site_description: >-
  Free, open-source self-hosted GitHub Actions runners with ephemeral jobs, a
  live web UI, autoscaling across your own hosts and a path off static runners.
site_author: Zoomies contributors
copyright: Zoomies is AGPL-3.0 licensed.

repo_url: https://github.com/eyupio/zoomies
repo_name: eyupio/zoomies

docs_dir: docs
site_dir: site

theme:
  name: material
  # Sharing and structured metadata that Material does not emit by itself.
  # overrides/main.html extends the theme rather than replacing anything. It is
  # outside docs/ so the template is not also published as a page.
  custom_dir: overrides
  language: en
  favicon: brand/favicon.ico
  # The header renders at favicon scale, where v2.1 reserves the paw/swish.
  # overrides/partials/logo.html draws this one on the dark scheme and the
  # black one on the light scheme, since the header sits on the page's ground.
  logo: brand/paw-swish-white.png
  icon:
    repo: fontawesome/brands/github
  # No `font:` key: the faces are self-hosted rather than fetched from Google
  # Fonts. overrides/main.html replaces the theme's font block, and
  # docs/stylesheets/ carries the @font-face rules and the woff2 files beside
  # it. A third-party font stylesheet is render-blocking, and when the host is
  # slow or unreachable the tab spins with nothing to show.
  features:
    - navigation.instant
    - navigation.instant.progress
    - navigation.tracking
    - navigation.sections
    - navigation.top
    - navigation.footer
    - toc.follow
    - search.suggest
    - search.highlight
    - search.share
    - content.code.copy
    - content.code.annotate
  palette:
    # The brand is a near-black identity, so dark is the default and light is
    # the alternative rather than the other way round.
    - media: "(prefers-color-scheme: dark)"
      scheme: slate
      primary: custom
      accent: custom
      toggle:
        icon: material/weather-sunny
        name: Switch to light
    - media: "(prefers-color-scheme: light)"
      scheme: default
      primary: custom
      accent: custom
      toggle:
        icon: material/weather-night
        name: Switch to dark

extra_css:
  - stylesheets/zoomies.css
  - stylesheets/animated-logo.css

extra_javascript:
  - javascripts/animated-logo.js

markdown_extensions:
  - abbr
  - admonition
  - attr_list
  - def_list
  - footnotes
  - md_in_html
  - tables
  - toc:
      permalink: true
      permalink_title: Link to this section
  - pymdownx.details
  # Material's icon sets, as `:material-webhook:` shortcodes. The home page's
  # feature cards and comparison table use them; they render as inline SVG that
  # inherits the text colour, so there is no icon image to theme or to go stale.
  - pymdownx.emoji:
      emoji_index: !!python/name:material.extensions.emoji.twemoji
      emoji_generator: !!python/name:material.extensions.emoji.to_svg
  - pymdownx.highlight:
      anchor_linenums: true
      line_spans: __span
      pygments_lang_class: true
  - pymdownx.inlinehilite
  - pymdownx.snippets
  # Diagrams are Mermaid, rendered in the browser and themed by Material to
  # follow whichever palette the reader is in. A diagram is a fenced block in
  # the same file as the prose it explains, so GitHub renders it too and there
  # is no exported image to go stale.
  - pymdownx.superfences:
      custom_fences:
        - name: mermaid
          class: mermaid
          format: !!python/name:pymdownx.superfences.fence_code_format
  - pymdownx.tabbed:
      alternate_style: true
  - pymdownx.tasklist:
      custom_checkbox: true

plugins:
  # The built-in search index, told where a Zoomies identifier stops being one
  # word: the default separator does not split on a dot or a hyphen, so
  # `scheduler.scale_up_delay` and `zoomies-linux-x64` were each a single term
  # nobody would type in full.
  - search:
      separator: '[\s\-,:!=\[\]()"/]+|(?!\b)(?=[A-Z][a-z])|\.(?!\d)|&[lg]t;'

# Build-time SEO metadata: a real last-edited date per page for the sitemap and
# the sharing tags, and llms.txt generated from the navigation. It is a hook
# rather than a plugin so the docs build keeps to its pinned dependencies.
hooks:
  - hooks/seo.py
  # The header's latest release, stars and forks, resolved once per build and
  # rendered by overrides/partials/source.html. Material would otherwise fetch
  # them in the browser and cache them in the tab for as long as it lives.
  - hooks/source.py
  # Lazy, sized images: the colour scheme a reader is not using is never
  # downloaded, and a page does not reflow as its screenshots arrive.
  - hooks/images.py

  brand/BRANDING_GUIDE.md

# docs/agents/ is guidance for coding agents working in the repository, not a
# page for the people reading the site.
exclude_docs: |
  agents/

# A link in the docs that points nowhere is a broken promise, so a broken one
# fails the build rather than shipping.
strict: true
validation:
  links:
    absolute_links: ignore
    unrecognized_links: warn
    # A heading that gets reworded silently breaks every deep link into it, and
    # a link that lands at the top of a long page looks like it worked.
    anchors: warn

# Zoomies built by Nixpacks, for the platforms that use it -- Coolify, Dokploy,
# Railway, Zeabur, Easypanel -- where you point the platform at this repository
# and it builds and runs the controller for you.
#
# It is the same two-stage build as deploy/Dockerfile: the Svelte UI first,
# because internal/api embeds internal/api/webdist and //go:embed fails on a
# directory that is not there yet, then one static Go binary. Nixpacks' own Go
# and Node providers would each find half of that and neither would wait for
# the other, so every phase is spelled out here.
#
# What this produces is a **controller**, not a fleet. A PaaS gives you no
# Docker socket, so the embedded agent is off and there is nothing on this host
# that could start a runner: join agents from machines that do have a container
# runtime (Hosts -> Add a host). See docs/paas.md.
#
# Verify a change to this file with `make image-nixpacks`.

providers = []

[variables]
# Nixpkgs ships whatever Go it ships, and go.mod asks for a newer one than most
# channels carry. GOTOOLCHAIN=auto lets the Go in the image fetch the toolchain
# go.mod names rather than failing the build on a version skew we cannot pin
# from here.
GOTOOLCHAIN = "auto"
# Pure-Go SQLite, so the binary is static and needs nothing from the runtime
# image.
CGO_ENABLED = "0"
NPM_CONFIG_FUND = "false"
NPM_CONFIG_AUDIT = "false"

# The database, the runners' work area and -- unless you supply
# ZOOMIES_ENCRYPTION_KEY yourself -- the generated encryption key all live
# under these. Mount the platform's persistent volume at /data, or point both
# at wherever it did mount one. Get this wrong and every deploy comes up with
# an empty database and a new key, which cannot decrypt the GitHub App private
# key the old one sealed.
ZOOMIES_STATE_DIR = "/data"
ZOOMIES_CONFIG_DIR = "/data"

# The platform terminates TLS and proxies to this container in the clear.
# Zoomies says so at startup; in this deployment that warning is expected. Set
# ZOOMIES_EXTERNAL_URL to the https address the platform gives you -- it is
# what the session cookie's Secure flag, the webhook URL and every link in the
# UI are built from -- and ZOOMIES_TRUSTED_PROXIES to the proxy in front, or
# the audit log records the proxy's address for every action and the login rate
# limiter throttles every caller as one.
ZOOMIES_TLS_MODE = "off"

# No Docker socket here, so a runner started on this host would fail rather
# than queue. Agents on hosts that do have one connect outbound to this
# controller.
ZOOMIES_AGENT_EMBEDDED = "false"

ZOOMIES_LOG_FORMAT = "json"

[phases.setup]
# git is here for the version stamp below, not for the build.
nixPkgs = ["go", "nodejs_22", "git", "cacert"]

[phases.install]
dependsOn = ["setup"]
cmds = [
  "npm --prefix web ci",
  "go mod download",
]

[phases.build]
dependsOn = ["install"]
cmds = [

## Why this matters

The agent's heartbeat method dereferences the transport's response three
times *before* the `resp == nil` guard that was written to protect those very
dereferences, so the guard is dead code. Both transports in the tree today
always return a non-nil response, but nothing documents or enforces that
contract, and the heartbeat loop's goroutine is not recovered anywhere: one
future transport change that returns `(nil, nil)` panics the whole agent
process, which ends host reporting for every running job on that host. Moving
the guard costs one line and a test pins the contract.

## Current state

- `internal/agent/daemon.go` (2610 lines) is the agent's whole lifecycle.
  `heartbeat` is at lines 1015-1073. It calls the transport at line 1026:

```go
	// internal/agent/daemon.go:1026-1072 (excerpt)
	resp, err := a.tr.Heartbeat(hctx, HeartbeatRequest{
		// ... fields elided; the request is large and does not matter here
	})
	if err != nil {
		a.expireBoosts(ctx)
		return err
	}
	if update != nil && !resp.UpdateHeld {          // line 1050: first use
		a.markUpdateDelivered(delivery)
	}
	a.mu.Lock()
	a.missedBeats = 0
	a.mu.Unlock()
	// The beat carried every runner the agent tracks, so the controller now
	// knows how each finished one ended, and its workload may go.
	a.mutationsPaused.Store(resp.MutationsPaused)   // line 1058: second use
	a.markReported(runners)

	if !a.ready.Swap(true) {
		// ... notify.send READY=1, log line
	}
	a.notify.send(fmt.Sprintf("STATUS=%d runner(s), ...", ...))  // line 1068

	if resp == nil {                                // line 1070: the guard, after every use
		return nil
	}
	a.warnSkew(resp.ControllerVersion)
```

The three uses (1050, 1058) sit before the guard (1070). Note that

## Status

- **Priority**: P1

- **Risk**: LOW
- **Depends on**: none
- **Category**: security (data minimisation in error responses)
- **Planned at**: commit `a0f21dba`, 2026-10-19

## Why this matters

`POST /api/v1/runners/bulk` puts the raw `err.Error()` of each failed drain or
delete straight into its JSON response, while the same error on the
single-runner routes goes through `fail`/`internal`, which maps the known
sentinels to human sentences and sends everything else to the log with only a
request ID in the response. The store's own convention (see
`internal/store/AGENTS.md`, "Sentinel errors") is that unknown errors carry
driver internals; on a transient database fault the bulk route is the one
place that text reaches a client. The fix reuses the mapping `fail` already
states, so both paths answer alike.


### Step 1: Add a pure mapping for one row's error

In `internal/api/handlers_runners.go`, add a helper next to the bulk handler

pure is what makes Step 3's test trivial):

```go
// bulkRunnerMessage is one row's error as the single routes would answer it:
// the store's own sentences for the errors an operator can act on, and a
// short line that carries no cause for everything else. The bulk loop was
// the one route that answered with err.Error() itself, which on a database
// fault is the driver's own text: the sentence the single routes give is at
// internal/api/errors.go, and this is that funnel, per row.
func bulkRunnerMessage(err error) (message string, known bool) {
	switch {
	case errors.Is(err, store.ErrNotFound),
		errors.Is(err, store.ErrConflict),
		errors.Is(err, store.ErrInvalidTransition),
		errors.Is(err, controller.ErrStreamUnknown):
		return err.Error(), true
	case errors.Is(err, controller.ErrConfirmationRequired):
		// The same sentence fail appends, so both routes teach the same
		// way out of a 409 that is asking for consent.
		return err.Error() + ". Send it again with confirm=true to accept that, " +
			"or wait for the job to finish and drain it then.", true
	default:
		return "", false
	}
}
```

Adjust the sentinel list only if the live `fail` (errors.go:328-347) maps
different ones; it is the source of truth, this helper mirrors it.

## Why this matters

A process-backend fleet's runner logs are bounded on the host disk by exactly
two pieces of code: `boundLog` in `internal/backend/process_logs.go` (a
copy-truncate that archives the tail and empties the live file) and
`nativeLogLoop` in `internal/agent/native_logs.go` (the per-minute loop that
calls every backend implementing `logMaintainer`). Neither is referenced by
any test in the tree, so a regression in either, corrupting or deleting
diagnostic logs, or silently stopping the bounding, stays green in CI. The
repo's own standard (root `AGENTS.md`, "Testing": roughly one test file for
every source file) exists to catch exactly this. This plan adds the missing
tests and touches no production code.

```go
	// internal/backend/process_logs.go:15-39 (excerpt)
	func (b *ProcessBackend) PruneLogs(ctx context.Context, limit int64) error {
		entries, err := os.ReadDir(filepath.Join(b.root, runnersDirName))
		if errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist) {
			return nil
		}
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		for _, e := range entries {
			if ctx.Err() != nil {
				return ctx.Err()
			}
			if !e.IsDir() {
				continue
			}
			dir := filepath.Join(b.root, runnersDirName, e.Name())
			if _, err := readMeta(dir); err != nil {
				continue
			}
			if err := boundLog(filepath.Join(dir, runnerLogFile), limit); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist) {
				return err
			}
		}
		return nil
	}
```

```go
	// internal/backend/process_logs.go:40-79 (excerpt)
	func boundLog(path string, limit int64) error {
		if limit <= 0 {
			return nil
		}
		info, err := os.Lstat(path)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if !info.Mode().IsRegular() || info.Size() <= limit {
			return nil
		}
		f, err := os.OpenFile(path, os.O_RDWR, 0)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		defer f.Close()
		opened, err := f.Stat()
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if !os.SameFile(info, opened) {
			return nil
		}
		archive, err := os.CreateTemp(filepath.Dir(path), "log-archive-*")
		// ... io.CopyN(archive, io.NewSectionReader(f, info.Size()-limit, limit), limit),
		//     archive.Close(), os.Rename(archive.Name(), path+".previous"), f.Truncate(0)
	}
```

So after a prune of an oversized log: the live file is 0 bytes, `path +
".previous"` holds exactly the last `limit` bytes, and the inherited
descriptor stays valid (that is the point of copy-truncate; the file's own

## Why this matters

`GET /api/v1/runners/{id}` is among the most-opened views in the UI, and
today it answers by re-reading the fleet to render one row: `RunnerRenderer`
lists every pool and every host (the host listing runs a GROUP BY over every
live runner to fill counts), then the handler reads the host again (re-running
that GROUP BY for one host's counts), then the pool and a whole `PoolRenderer`
before it. The repo already has the cheaper pattern: `jobViewIn`
(`internal/controller/views.go:742-753`) renders a job from rows the caller
already holds. This plan gives the runner detail the same shape, without
changing the response the API promises.

```go
	// internal/api/handlers_runners.go:74-106 (excerpt)
	func (s *Server) handleGetRunner(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		run, err := s.ctrl.Store().GetRunner(r.Context(), chiURLParam(r, "id"))
		if err != nil {
			s.fail(w, r, "reading the runner", err)
			return
		}
		view, err := s.ctrl.RunnerRenderer(r.Context(), []*store.Runner{run})   // lists every pool and host
		if err != nil {
			s.internal(w, r, "reading the runner", err)
			return
		}
		detail := runnerDetailResponse{
			RunnerView: view.View(run).For(isVisitor(r.Context())),
			Timeline:   runnerTimeline(run, s.ctrl.Now()),
		}

		if host, herr := s.ctrl.Store().GetHost(r.Context(), run.HostID); herr == nil {   // second host read + counts GROUP BY
			h := s.ctrl.HostView(host).For(isPlatform(r))
			detail.Host = &h
			detail.LogsAvailable = host.Healthy(s.ctrl.Now()) && run.State != store.RunnerRemoved
		}
		if pool, perr := s.ctrl.Store().GetPool(r.Context(), run.PoolID); perr == nil {   // second pool read
			if pv, verr := s.ctrl.PoolRenderer(r.Context()); verr == nil {                 // its own aggregates
				p := poolFor(r, pv.View(pool))
				detail.Pool = &p
			}
		}
		writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, detail)
	}
```

### Step 2: Add `Controller.RunnerViewIn`, the `jobViewIn` shape for runners

In `internal/controller/views.go`, next to the renderer:

```go
// RunnerViewIn renders one runner for a caller that already holds its host
// and pool rows, the way jobViewIn names a job from pools in hand: a detail
// route reads its host and pool anyway, and listing every pool and host to
// name one runner is the fleet read a single drawer never needed. The busy
// runner's job is fetched here, and a job row that has gone since the runner
// was read is tolerated the way RunnerRenderer tolerates it: the runner is
// rendered without it.
func (c *Controller) RunnerViewIn(ctx context.Context, run *store.Runner, host *store.Host, pool *store.Pool) (RunnerView, error) {
	var job *store.Job
	if run.CurrentJobID != "" {
		j, err := c.st.GetJob(ctx, run.CurrentJobID)
		if err != nil && !errors.Is(err, store.ErrNotFound) {
			return RunnerView{}, fmt.Errorf("reading the job a runner is executing: %w", err)
		}
		job = j
	}
	return runnerView(run, pool, host, job), nil
}
```

## Why this matters

Four edges of the log relay mislead an operator, each silently:

1. A viewer joining an existing follow stream gets no tail at all: its `Tail`
   request is ignored, so a second tab (or a reconnect) shows an empty pane
   until the runner prints more.
2. A log download that exceeds the relay's byte budget is truncated with no
   mark: the agent's own buffer says what it dropped
   (`internal/agent/logbuffer.go:93-101`), the controller's relay drops bytes
   silently (`internal/controller/logs.go:269-280`), so a 20 MB CI log can
   arrive as a seamlessly gapped file with a 200 status.
3. A download that gets no first chunk within 10 s returns 200 with an empty
   attachment, because the headers are written before the wait, and the wait
   can be shorter than task delivery (an agent in poll backoff waits up to
   30 s, `internal/agent/daemon.go`'s `maxPollBackoff`).
4. A viewer attaching in the instant between "the last viewer left" and "the
   stream is torn down" joins a stream that is closed under it moments later.

### Step 1: Close the teardown race by deciding "last viewer" under one lock

Reorder `unsubscribe` so the last-viewer decision and the map removals happen
under `lr.mu` together, before `s.close()` can race a join:

```go
func (lr *logRelay) unsubscribe(s *logStream, subID int) {
	// Decide "last viewer" and empty the maps under one hold of lr.mu, or a
	// viewer arriving between the two sees a stream in byRunner that is
	// being torn down, joins it, and has its channel closed moments later.
	// Lock order is lr.mu then s.mu everywhere now (subscribe already takes
	// them in that order), so this cannot deadlock with add/close.
	lr.mu.Lock()
	last := s.remove(subID)
	if last {
		if lr.streams[s.id] == s {
			delete(lr.streams, s.id)
		}
		if lr.byRunner[s.runnerID] == s.id {
			delete(lr.byRunner, s.runnerID)
		}
	}
	lr.mu.Unlock()
	if !last {
		return
	}
	// ... the TaskCancelLogs enqueue and s.close() stay as they are
}
```

`remove` (which takes `s.mu`) is now called while `lr.mu` is held; confirm
by reading `add`, `close`, `send` and `isClosed` (logs.go:328-392) that none
of them takes `lr.mu` (they do not; they are per-stream), and that
`subscribe` takes `lr.mu` then `s.mu` via `s.add()` (it does, logs.go:132-155).
`AcceptLogStream`'s own cleanup (logs.go:255-264) takes `lr.mu` then calls
`s.close()`; the same order, still safe.

## Steps

### Step 1: Write the keyed concurrency budget

Create `internal/api/mcp_budget.go`, package `api`:

```go
// inProcessBudget bounds how many route answers one caller may be holding
// at once. Every tool call buffers a whole answer (mcpResponseLimit is 32
// MiB), and the agent routes answer a caller that tries this with 429
// before reading a byte; the MCP and assistant paths funneled through
// inProcessAPI were the two entry points with no such ceiling, and they run
// on the process that owns the SQLite writer. A keyed semaphore rather than
// auth.RateLimiter, which bounds how often a key may call, not how many
// calls it may hold.
type inProcessBudget struct {
	mu        sync.Mutex
	held      map[string]int
	totalHeld int
}

const (
	// inProcessPerCaller is the ceiling per identity. Two concurrent large
	// log reads (one live, one download) are a plausible legitimate pair;
	// a third held answer from the same caller is a loop, not a reader.
	inProcessPerCaller = 2
	// inProcessTotal is the fleet-wide ceiling, so many callers together
	// still pin a bounded slice of this process's memory.
	inProcessTotal = 16
)

// take spends one slot for key and reports how long to wait when the
// ceiling refuses. key is the caller's identity string; the empty string is
// every call without an identity, which cannot happen on a real path but
// must not bypass the budget.
func (b *inProcessBudget) take(key string) (ok bool, retryAfter time.Duration)
// give returns one slot for key. It is safe to call without a matching take
// (a give for a key holding nothing is a no-op), because release runs on
// every exit path of do, including the ones a panic-free rewrite of do
// might add later.
func (b *inProcessBudget) give(key string)
```

Implement the two methods (mutex, map counts, total count; `retryAfter` is a
fixed short constant, for example 2 s, since the refusal is about calls in
flight, not a window; keep it simple and say why in the comment). Sweep the
map the way `auth.RateLimiter.sweep` does only if entries can leak: they
cannot, every `take` that returns true is paired with a `give` by `do`'s
defer, so no sweeping is needed; if you decide otherwise, document why.

**Verify**: `gofmt -l internal/api/` clean; `go vet ./internal/api/` clean;
the type compiles (`go build ./internal/api/`).

```go
			message: "this caller already has tool answers being read; wait for one to finish and ask again"}

```

## Why this matters

Every frame the event stream sends calls `s.resolveIdentity(r)` for each
narrowed frame kind, and each resolution is a SQLite session read, per
frame, per connected tab. The stream already knows the cheaper shape and
uses it for `reader` (the kind-checking identity): it resolves at open and
once per heartbeat, with a comment saying exactly why ("a busy fleet sends
many frames a second, and each resolution of a session is a database read",
`internal/api/sse.go:237-241`). This plan moves the *narrowing* identity to
the same tick. The cost: a role demotion reaches the narrowed fields up to
one heartbeat (20 s) late, which is the same staleness the stream already
accepts for `reader` and for `endIfRevoked` (the revoked check runs on the
same tick); the security posture (fail closed when resolution fails, drop
frames the caller may not see) is unchanged.

# improve.md: the advisor's handoff

Written 2026-10-19 against commit `a0f21dba` (the drift check every plan

## What this repository is

Zoomies: a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner fleet controller. One Go binary
(controller, agent, gateway, installer, CLI by subcommand), Svelte 5 UI
embedded with `go:embed`, SQLite (`modernc`, pure Go, one writer) in
`internal/store`, no Kubernetes, no database server. Build and verify:

```
make build-nogui   # once in a fresh checkout: writes the UI placeholder
                   # internal/api embeds; plain go build/vet/test fail without it
make test          # go test -race -count=1 ./...
make lint          # go vet, gofmt, staticcheck when present, UI lint (npm)
```

Conventions the plans assume throughout (each plan restates what it needs):
British spelling in prose; no em dash characters and no spaced double
hyphen used as a dash (tests in `internal/docs` fail the build on both);
comments explain why, not what; test names are sentences about behaviour;
commit messages are imperative sentences in plain prose, sentence case, no
prefix; package boundaries are load-bearing and held by tests (see the root
`AGENTS.md`, which is the contributor's map too).

Four parallel read-only sweeps (correctness, security, performance and
test coverage, tech debt and dependencies and docs), every candidate finding
then verified by the advisor against the cited code before it reached the
findings table. The repo's own intent documents were read first
(`AGENTS.md` and the scoped ones, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `ROADMAP.md` and
`roadmap/`, `docs/architecture.md`, `docs/dependencies.md`), so that
documented tradeoffs were treated as settled, not re-reported.

# Which Claude model drives which stage

The roadmap is implemented by Claude Code sessions, and the model behind a
session is a choice with a cost and a failure mode of its own. This page says
which model and which effort setting to use for each kind of work in the
programme, and why. It is guidance to be measured against, not a rule to be
obeyed: every entry in [progress.md](progress.md) records the model and effort
that produced it, so the choice can be revisited on evidence rather than on
price per token.

The rule underneath all of it: **choose by what the stage risks, not by what a
token costs.** The measure is cost per merged, green pull request whose
behaviour survived review, and a cheap session that leaves a wrong invariant
behind, with tests that enshrine it, is the most expensive session in the
programme.

## The models

Prices are Anthropic's first-party API rates per million tokens, as cached on
24 June 2026 by the reference this page was written from. Check the Models API
before a large run; the point of the table is the ratios, which move less than
the numbers.

| Model | ID | Input | Output | Context | What it is for here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Fable 5.1 | `claude-fable-5-1` | $10 | $50 | 1M | Design, invariants, verification, review. The most capable widely released model; thinking is always on and controlled by effort. |
| Claude Opus 5 | `claude-opus-5` | $5 | $25 | 1M | The bulk of implementation on a settled design. The recommended default for agentic coding. |
| Claude Sonnet 5 | `claude-sonnet-5` | $2 | $10 | 1M | Bounded, checkable slices with a specification in hand. |
| Claude Haiku 4.5 | `claude-haiku-4-5` | $1 | $5 | 200K | Sub-agent reading with a checkable output. Not for code changes in this repository. |

Three properties of Claude Fable 5.1 matter operationally. Its turns are
longer: a single request on a hard task can run many minutes while it gathers
context, builds and verifies, which is what you want for ZF-102 and not what
you want for a documentation row. It carries safety classifiers that can end
a request with a refusal, which matters for the hostile-input tests in ZF-104
(see below). And it is only available to organisations on 30-day data
retention, so a workspace on zero data retention cannot run it at all.

## The tiers

### Claude Fable 5.1: where a wrong answer is expensive

Use it where the deliverable is an invariant, a boundary, or a judgement about
whether something is proven, and where the design space is still open. Its
measured gains over the tier below are on exactly this work: long-horizon
autonomous runs, first-shot implementations of well-specified systems, code
review and debugging, and searching a repository's history for how something
came to be.

| Work | Why this tier |
| --- | --- |
| ZF-001 and ZF-002, the reconciliation and the measurement contract | The rest of the programme is only as sound as the classification of what exists. This document was produced by a Claude Fable 5.1 session orchestrating fresh-context verifier sub-agents, and that shape is the recommendation for every later gate review too. |
| ZF-101, one eligibility policy across ingest, scheduler and explanations | A missed call site is a cross-target allocation. The work is reading every path a job takes, not writing much code. |
| ZF-102, convergent reconciliation and fencing | Concurrency and restart semantics; the failure mode is a race that a test written by the same session will not think to exercise. Run at `xhigh`. |
| ZF-103, the reservation model | The design decision (what is reserved, when it is released, how an old pool migrates) is the whole package; the code that follows is Opus-tier work. |
| ZF-104, the access and secret matrix | Building the matrix from the router and proving each row negative is review work. If a session writing hostile-input or escape-sequence tests hits a safeguard refusal, move that slice to Claude Opus 5 rather than rephrasing around it. |
| ZF-302, the design of each drill and the reading of its result | Deciding what a drill proves, and whether a green result is honest, is judgement. |
| Every decision record in [decisions/](decisions/) and every gate review | A gate is a claim about evidence. Give it the model that is best at finding what is missing. |
| Review of every pull request in the programme, whichever model wrote it | Its precision and recall on real bugs is the reason to pay for it here. A second, fresh-context session reviewing is worth more than the writing session reviewing itself. |

Effort: start at `high`, which is the default. Use `xhigh` for ZF-101,
ZF-102 and ZF-103 design, where the reasoning is the deliverable. Do not run a
long document or a whole-file rewrite at `xhigh` or `max`: the model drafts
it in its thinking and again in its reply, which doubles the tokens for no
gain. Give it the whole task specification up front, tell it where the memory
surface is (the progress record and the decisions directory), and require it
to audit every progress claim against a tool result before reporting.

### Claude Opus 5: implementation on a settled design

The recommended starting point for agentic coding. On a coding benchmark it
matched Claude Fable 5 within noise at about 60% of the cost, and it completes
tasks rather than leaving stubs. Use it once the invariant is written down and
the work is to make the code and its tests match it.

| Work | Effort |
| --- | --- |
| ZF-103's host reporting and the operator's view of it | `high`; the reservation decision and the scheduler's fit predicate are Fable tier, as ZF-103's session line in the plan says |
| ZF-105, cleanup, retention and bounded retry | `xhigh`: retry and cleanup interact with the reconciliation invariants from ZF-102 |
| ZF-201, the first-job journey in Svelte and its Playwright coverage | `high` |
| ZF-202, diagnostics and the support bundle | `high` |
| ZF-203, the backup and restore commands and recovery mode | `high`; the fenced-recovery design itself is a decision record (Fable tier) |
| ZF-204, compatibility policy, upgrade and rollback tooling | `high` |
| ZF-205, telemetry, retention bounds, pagination, the load fixture | `xhigh` for the reconnect and resync path, `high` for the rest |
| ZF-301, extending the end-to-end harness | `high` |
| ZF-302, implementing the drills a Fable session designed | `high` |

On long-horizon coding this model gave up about two points of pass rate at
`medium` for half the cost, and about eight points at `low` for a quarter of
it. That is a real trade, so `medium` is for a slice whose tests are the
checker, not for one whose correctness is judged by reading. Fast mode is an
option for an interactive loop with an operator watching; it changes speed, not
the model.

### Claude Sonnet 5: bounded and checkable

Use it where the specification is complete, the output is mechanically
checkable, and the surrounding code already shows the pattern.

* Rows in `docs/problem-codes.md`, `docs/configuration.md` and `docs/cli.md`
  for a code, key or command another session added, with the `internal/docs`
  tests as the checker.
* The OpenAPI document and the two generated clients for an endpoint whose
  shape is already decided; CI diffs them.
* Table-driven tests for a listed set of scenarios, sized like their neighbours.
* Playwright specifications for a journey that is written down step by step.
* A migration that adds a column, with the next unused prefix.
* Lint, format and generated-file fix-ups on a red pull request.
* Bookkeeping in the progress record.

Effort: `high`, and `xhigh` for anything that has to reason about more than
one file. It respects effort strictly at the low end and will under-think a
moderately complex task at `low`, so do not use `low` on this repository for
anything beyond a lookup. Its tokenizer uses about 30% more tokens than the
Opus tier for the same text, so compare cost per task, not per token.

### Claude Haiku 4.5: reading, never writing

Not for code changes here. As a sub-agent it is right for bulk reading with a
checkable output: summarising a CI log, listing the files that match a
criterion, extracting evidence links for the progress record. It answered
knowledge questions at about a tenth of Claude Opus 5's cost per question and
about two-thirds of its accuracy, which is the shape of a task where the
orchestrator checks the answer, not one where the answer is the deliverable.
It has a 200K context and the older `budget_tokens` thinking control rather
than an effort setting.

## Effort before model

Effort is the first lever to reach for; the model tier is the last. Two
patterns from Anthropic's measurements apply directly:

* **Re-run failures at higher effort.** Where a slice has a failure signal (the
  Go tests, `svelte-check`, Playwright), run it at a lower effort and re-run the
  failures at the default. In the coding runs measured, running everything at
  `low` and re-running failures at the default passed about 93% of tasks for
  about half the cost of running everything at the default, which passed about
  92%. Starting at `medium` passed about 94%. Use this for the saving on Sonnet
  and Opus slices, and price in the doubled wall clock on the failures.
* **Sweep effort on the current model before dropping a tier.** Lower effort
  on Claude Fable 5.1 often exceeds the top effort of the previous generation,
  and at `low` it is frequently competitive with the tiers below on cost per
  task while performing better. So the alternative posture to the tiers above
  is one model with effort as the only lever. It is simpler to run and to
  reason about; it costs more on the mechanical slices; and it removes the
  question of which session wrote what. That choice is recorded as a decision
  for the owner in [ROADMAP.md](../ROADMAP.md).

## Orchestration

The review that produced this roadmap ran as a Claude Fable 5.1 orchestrator
with one sub-agent per work package mapping it to the code, one adversarial
verifier per mapping trying to refute it, and a final critic asking what the
whole set had missed. That shape is right for every gate review and for the
larger reviews in ZF-104 and ZF-302: fresh-context verifiers outperform a
session critiquing its own work, and independent packages are exactly the bulk
an orchestrator is for.

It is the wrong shape for one dependent chain. A package that is one sequence
of edits, each depending on the last, is cheaper and better in a single
session at lower effort than as a plan, a handoff and a merge. Reading-heavy
fan-out (many files to read, one judgement to make) can go to Claude Sonnet 5
sub-agents; the judgement stays with the orchestrator.

## What to write in the progress record

For every package entry: the model, the effort, whether the work ran as one
session or an orchestration, and the number of review rounds before merge.
Once a phase is complete, that column answers the only question that matters
about this page, which is whether the tiering paid for itself.

## Outcome and scope

## Architecture: style and colour mode are independent

Do not turn `ThemeChoice` into `light | dark | system | mission-control`. That creates an undefined “Mission Control follows what?” mode and breaks the current first-paint contract.

Proposed independent types:

```ts
export type UIStyle = 'classic' | 'mission-control';
export type ThemeChoice = 'light' | 'dark' | 'system'; // unchanged
```

| Concern | Storage / DOM contract | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Colour mode | Existing `zoomies.theme`; existing `data-theme` | Preserve existing validation, system listener and cycling |
| Visual style | New `zoomies.ui-style`; `data-ui-style="mission-control"` | Missing, unknown or legacy value means Classic; Classic removes attribute |
| Style state | New `web/src/lib/state/ui-style.svelte.ts` | One validated reactive source, shared by Appearance and NavMenu |
| Logo treatment | Existing preference and logo attributes | Never reset it on a style change |
| Status vocabulary | Existing Off/Cute/Standard preference | Never derive it from style |
| Phone grid layout | Existing explicit grid/global choices | Preserve them; new-style fallback only when unset |
| Navigation collapse | Existing browser preference | Keep default breakpoint logic and stored choice |
| Column widths/order | Existing local/account preference | Never remount/reset the grid for a style change |

Add a pure resolver, preferably in `state/ui-style.ts`, so bootstrap, tests and the runes module can agree on valid values. Keep the inline bootstrap small; if importing the resolver before paint is unsuitable, cover both resolver and inline allowlist with one parity test. Do not create a blocking script request just to select a style.

### Persistence and first paint

1. In `web/index.html`, alongside the existing theme bootstrap, read only the validated new style key in the same guarded storage path. Set `data-ui-style` before first paint. A failure to access storage leaves Classic; no toast is needed.
2. Initialise the runes state from the same allowlist without repainting the page incorrectly. `set(style)` updates state, DOM and browser storage; blocked storage means the choice lasts for the current page.
3. Keep the selected `ThemeChoice` intact. Mission Control + System resolves with the existing `matchMedia` listener; it does not silently force dark mode. A system change must update the palette without changing the selected style or reloading the app.
4. Update browser `theme-color` for the resolved style/mode. Existing `pinBrowserChrome` only selects media tags. Extend its palette mapping or token-derived synchronisation; cover first paint and subsequent system changes. Preserve ordinary CSS `color-scheme` for native form controls and scrollbars.
5. Switching style is an in-place root attribute change. Do not key App, route components or grids by style. Preserve focus, route, scroll position, form drafts, table selection and assistant conversation.
6. The preference stays in this browser, including sign-in, consistent with current appearance settings. Do not add a server preference or fleet setting for it. Explain this in the selector description.
7. Existing browsers remain Classic, including when `zoomies.theme='dark'`. Unknown style values and cleared storage remain Classic. Remove only the new key when resetting style, not `zoomies.prefs` or `zoomies.theme`.

## Token contract

Keep existing token names where their meaning fits. Add style-scoped overrides in `tokens.css` after the existing palette definitions, with matching explicit-mode and system-mode selectors. Avoid copying whole themes or overriding brand/status constants accidentally.

Recommended neutral and interaction palette:

| Semantic token | Mission Control dark | Mission Control light | Intent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--z-bg` | `#090e18` | `#f4f7fb` | Page background |
| `--z-surface` | `#111b2b` | `#ffffff` | Panels |
| `--z-surface-sunken` | `#0c1421` | `#eaf0f7` | Code and bounded detail |
| `--z-border` | `#2b3a50` | `#b9c8da` | Quiet grouping; not the only control edge |
| `--z-text` | `#eef4fc` | `#122235` | Primary reading |
| `--z-text-muted` | `#afbed2` | `#455d76` | Metadata and help |
| `--z-accent` | `#65d9f2` | `#00657a` | Interactive accent |
| `--z-accent-contrast` | `#07131d` | `#ffffff` | Filled button text |

Derive `surface-raised`, hover, strong border, accent hover/active/subtle/border, selection, focus, chart grid, scrim and terminal mappings as part of the same token package. Do not ship only the eight entries above: they are the design direction. Existing token inventory and contrast tests are the authority for all required variants.

The mock uses a minimal palette and illustrative series colours. Its green, amber, red and purple are not the production status specification. Production must preserve each existing semantic state's hue family and icon mapping, adjusting luminance only as required to meet contrast in the new surfaces. The public guidelines reserve Fast Cyan for moving work; document the new style's cool cyan interactive accent explicitly and keep running-work cues distinguishable through state labels and glyphs. If this proves confusing in side-by-side review, keep Runner Blue for interaction and use cyan only for moving work. That is a palette refinement, not an architectural change.

Contrast acceptance: normal text ≥4.5:1, large text and meaningful non-text controls ≥3:1; target ≥7:1 for long secondary explanations. Quiet panel borders need not pretend to be control boundaries. Focus, inputs, selected radios/tabs and resize handles require stronger edges. Test complete combinations, including accent text on subtle backgrounds, status text in badges, disabled explanation text, tooltip surfaces and error banners. Maintain non-colour icons, labels and patterns.

## Responsive layout and screen specifications

Use the existing breakpoints: phone ≤768px, narrow desktop 769–1180px, full desktop ≥1181px. Do not introduce “almost phone” variants that disagree with `viewport.svelte.ts`. Test 375px specifically; current suite Pixel 7 coverage is not a substitute for that width.

### Overview

- First-run checklist retains priority when the fleet has not yet run its own job.
- Operational order: problems summary, current queue/running/live/queue-wait group, pools and active jobs, recent events, historical activity, detailed performance/capacity. Show no warning banner when no actionable problems exist.
- Keep all six current metrics. Startup and registration are available in an expandable Performance block or secondary row; the concept's four tiles are the primary hierarchy, not a data removal instruction.
- At 1440×900, show title, issues, primary metrics and at least one pool or active-job row without scrolling. At 375×900, show the main issue action and primary status before historical charts. The review toolbar is excluded from these production targets.
- Use two columns for short phone metrics if they remain readable; use one when zoom/text scaling requires it. Long subtitles must wrap without clipping.
- Pool bar keeps busy/live, floor, ceiling and current verdict. Events have a bounded list height only on desktop; avoid nested vertical scrolling on phones.
- History chart remains current `FleetActivity`/ActivityMatrix. Move its position; do not rewrite its sampling, legend, failure classification or click-to-filter behaviour.

### Pools and pool detail

- Cards can form three columns on wide desktop only if the actual content fits, two on narrow desktop, one on phone.
- Prominent identity, enabled state, GitHub installation and routing labels; then allocation and floor/ceiling; then busy/live and verdict. Keep automated routing explanations available without filling the page with unrelated banners.
- Primary Create pool stays permission-aware. Detail leads to existing edit/pause/delete operations with existing confirmations. Do not turn every metric into a badge.
- Preserve current import/export, sizing advice and actual host compatibility. Long names wrap or reveal full value via current tooltip behaviour.

### Runners, Workflows, Jobs and Queue

- Use current DataGrid, shared status maps and workflow/job filters. Restyle primitives once.
- Phone Jobs: status, search, Filters(active count), then records. Supplementary metrics/outcomes are initially collapsed, with clear labels and no lost data. Preserve selected filter values when collapsing.
- Rows/Cards remains visible above records. Fresh Mission Control fallback can be Cards; explicit saved choices always win. Do not mistake a stored global default for an explicit choice when migrating preferences. Add an explicit-set marker if necessary rather than changing every existing browser.
- A card begins with identity, repository, state and timing; Inspect remains a labelled action. All other columns are accessible in labelled detail, including wide-priority columns.
- Workflow cards show run/repository identity and expand to jobs. Preserve cancel permission and confirmation. Queue shows why demand is waiting and what Run now actually changes; “priority” must not imply bypassing capacity or labels.
- Empty source list, no filter matches, stale cached data, fetch failure and loading are separate states. No-results Clear filters changes only filters, not style or saved columns.

### Usage, Hosts and Providers

- Usage preserves range, grouping, scoped data, export, axes/units and estimate/provenance text. Style changes cannot turn estimated costs into measured savings.
- Hosts: identity, connection/OS state and current capacity are primary. Preserve CPU/memory/slots as separate units. Reboot pending has an explicit safe next step; no implicit restart on click.
- Providers: show spending limit, machine lifecycle and inventory. Keep backend/provider-specific config in existing wizards. Theme cards do not conceal errors or pending enrolment.
- Capacity and utilisation fills use semantic series tokens and existing legends. Keep chart accessibility and touch inspection.

### Repairs, Kennel Club, Migrate, Audit and Settings

- Repairs distinguishes offered diagnosis, investigation, review and verified outcome. Existing permission/sandbox rules remain. Purple decoration must not look like a critical alert.
- Kennel Club: repository list and findings become a single-column progression on phones. Keep tracked/partially checked/off/failure states distinct; “no findings” is not equivalent to “not checked”.
- Migrate: retain exact diff review before opening a PR. Desktop before/after can remain side-by-side; phone prefers explicit Before/After tabs or stacked blocks with local code scrolling. Never auto-apply YAML from a visual mock.
- Audit: keep timestamp, actor, role, action, target and details. On phone cards, start with action/target then actor/time; details expand. Do not discard IP or machine-readable event identity.
- Settings: restyle all existing panels and forms. Appearance gets the new style cards, existing colour-mode selection, logo treatment, navigation, vocabulary and phone-table controls. Other settings remain unchanged in purpose and permissions.

### Drawers, assistant and overlays

- Reuse shared Drawer and current EliWidget. Problems remains grouped worst first, with reason and next step. Keep snooze, dismissal and restoration semantics.
- Desktop assistant starts closed, stays movable/resizable and uses current viewport constraints. Do not copy the reference's full-height permanent clipped rail.
- Phone sheet uses current visual-viewport sizing when the keyboard opens, inert background, focus containment, Escape/close, return focus and safe-area spacing. Use existing sheet helper; do not invent another modal stack.
- Do not turn the current nonmodal desktop assistant into a blocking modal just because the mock's placeholder uses a dialog. The mock's focus handling demonstrates an overlay, not the production assistant contract.
- When a modal and assistant could compete, retain existing application arbitration or explicitly test topmost focus and close order. No focusable content behind a modal.

## Appearance interaction contract

1. On Appearance, show a labelled radiogroup of two preview cards: Classic and Mission Control. Prefer a real radio input and label or an existing accessible selection primitive over ad hoc clickable divs.
2. Each card has style name, small static preview, concise description and a checked marker that is not colour-only. Entire card is a target; arrow keys and Space work according to the chosen control's semantics.
3. Selection applies immediately. Keep focus on the selected control; announce “Mission Control selected for this browser” once in a polite region. No confirmation modal, trial gate or reload.
4. Colour mode remains System/Light/Dark below the cards. System description says which palette is currently resolved.
5. Provide “Reset visual style to Classic”. This resets only style. Do not label it Reset appearance if it leaves other preferences unchanged.
6. A phone reaches Appearance through the existing More menu. A quick style control is optional; if added, read the same state and allowlist, with clear names and no contradictory toggle cycle.
7. Sign-in/bootstrap and public status page need an explicit decision: apply the visual style to the controller's ordinary sign-in/bootstrap document; do not extend the separate `/status` build's bootstrap automatically. Either add compatible status style support within its <30KB budget or leave that separate document Classic and document the boundary in the setting. The first release recommendation is the latter, because the status page is a separate public document, not part of the operator UI.

## Verification requirements

Do not claim success because the happy-path screenshot looks good. Test what switching actually risks.

### Focused automated checks

- Resolver: absent/valid/unknown style, blocked storage fallback, correct Classic reset.
- First paint: persisted style + explicit light/dark, persisted style + System, opposite system palette. Assert initial root attributes before app hydration; check no incorrect first-frame palette in captures.
- System mode: dispatch media change, retain style and mode choice, update palette/native chrome.
- Preference integrity: style switching leaves logo, vocabulary, navigation collapse, per-grid view/columns, route and draft intact; do not remount an editor or reset an open conversation.
- Mobile fallback: explicit per-grid > explicit global > Mission Control fresh default > Classic default. Legacy saved choices remain unchanged. Existing rows can still be selected on a phone and restore across reload.
- Appearance: keyboard selection, visible focus, clear selected state, reset only style; two independent browser contexts do not accidentally share account/fleet style.
- Contrast: extend existing `web/unit/text-contrast.test.ts` rather than testing CSS variable strings without evaluating colours. Account for style selectors when extracting values.
- Layout: no document overflow at 1440, 1180, 1179, 768, 375 and 360px; local grid/code scrolling is intentional. Test 200% zoom and enlarged text separately.
- Jobs: with deterministic fixture data, a job identity and Inspect are visible within the first phone screen after primary controls. Filter expansion/collapse never loses selected filters.
- Overview: concise critical issue precedes history; first-run checklist remains first when applicable; all six timing/live metrics remain available.
- Drawer and assistant: keyboard focus, return focus, phone keyboard, nested close order, resize bounds and reduced motion. Use existing helper tests and fixture providers; no paid AI calls are needed.

Run first-run, connect and diagnostics fixtures for onboarding/blocked-state work. The full Go race suite is appropriate if P8 changes backend contracts; do not run it as substitute evidence for a CSS-only patch.

Budgets remain shell <200KB gzipped, ordinary route <80KB except existing documented allowances, and separate status document <30KB. The current baseline build passed its configured budgets. Preview thumbnails should be compact static HTML/CSS or tiny inline SVG, not large image bundles on every page. Keep style code in the shell small.

## Release and rollback

Ship Classic as default. Mission Control is an explicit opt-in browser choice. Stage style state/tokens/selector before layout changes so a regression is easy to isolate. There is no fleet migration and no new backend setting.

Rollback is returning to Classic via Appearance or clearing only `zoomies.ui-style`. A release rollback whose older bootstrap does not recognise the key must safely render Classic. Avoid hard-coding new style assumptions into route markup, so removing a root attribute reverses the appearance without editing data.

Before completion, attach the final four style/mode captures for representative screens and current first-run, empty, failure and phone-keyboard evidence. Update the existing screenshot generation tooling where appropriate; do not retouch real UI captures. Keep the concept files labelled as concepts even after implementation.

## Exact instruction to the next coding agent

Implement P0–P4 first as an additive, opt-in visual style. Follow the repository's token and status contracts; reuse existing components and keep Classic behaviour. Preserve all appearance, table and route state while switching. Complete the specified tests and capture both styles in both modes at 1440 and 375px. Then implement P5–P7 as a separate reviewable layout package using the same criteria. Leave P8 as a separate scoped feature unless explicitly assigned. Use the mockups for hierarchy and material; use current source and this plan for routes, permissions, data semantics and real interactions. Do not ship dummy controls, invented counts, fake dispatch actions or abbreviated mock navigation.
