# Let an operator see what automatic repairs are doing, and stop them

Agreed in conversation on 18 October 2026, written against checkout `607c68a`.
The owner's words were: "Don't forget auto repairs if enabled. User needs
visibility and controls." The repair pages in
[2026-10-18-eli-repair-workspace.md](2026-10-18-eli-repair-workspace.md) are built
and merged (#1156), and that document never mentions automatic repairs. This one
closes the gap, and all of it is built, in the pull request that carries this
document. The implementation plan is
[2026-10-18-eli-automatic-repairs-plan.md](2026-10-18-eli-automatic-repairs-plan.md),
which says where the build departed from it.

## What was asked

A repository set to **Automatic** has Eli repair its failed pull request checks
with nobody asking: no button, no offer, a commit on the pull request's branch and
tokens spent on the installation's provider. Whoever switched that on should be
able to see that it is on, where, what it has done and what it may still spend,
and to stop it. Where nothing is automatic, the pages should say nothing about it.

## What the code does today

| Fact | Where | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An Automatic policy admits a failed `workflow_job` delivery, queues a repair keyed `automatic:<repo>:<head>` and the worker pushes one commit | `enqueueRepairWebhook`, `runEliRepair` in `internal/controller/eli_repairs.go` | An operator who switched it on has no page that says it is on, where, or who pays |
| The hub counts only repositories that ask first | `web/src/lib/repairs/SetupBar.svelte`, `hub.ts` | A repository on Automatic is counted nowhere on the hub |
| A repository's allowance (1 to 50 attempts in 24 hours) is shared by requests and automatic repairs, cleared repairs included. When it is spent an automatic repair is not queued, and the only trace is the log line "Eli repair budget reached" | `EnqueueEliRepair`, `enqueueRepairWebhook` | Failures stay unrepaired and nothing in the product says why |
| If the installation provider is deleted or disabled, each queued automatic repair fails when the worker reaches it | `runEliRepair` | Nothing says in advance that Automatic can no longer work |
| Automatic repairs have no owner, so only administrators can read them | `GetEliRepair`, the history scope | Visibility belongs to administrators, and so does the control (`PUT /assistant/repairs/policy` is an administrator route) |
| The only way to stop Automatic is to save the repository's whole policy again in setup, and that save is refused while the policy's provider is missing or disabled | `handleSetEliPolicy` | Stopping is the moment a person is least able to fill in a form |
| The attempt page says "Started automatically" and nothing about why, which policy, or how to stop it | `web/src/lib/repairs/attempt.ts` | |
| The repair page offers **Fix with Eli** on a failure the repository would have repaired itself, without saying so | `DecisionCard.svelte` | A person can spend an attempt repeating one Eli already made, or wait for one that will never start |
| An automatic repair starts only from GitHub's report of the failed job. Nothing reconciles it afterwards, as the five-minute look-back does for offers | `reconcileEliOpportunities` | A failure from before Automatic was switched on, or one whose webhook never arrived, is never repaired on its own |

## Design

### Four rules

1. **A repository that is not automatic adds nothing.** No panel, no empty state,
   no hint, on any page, for anyone. The owner's "if enabled".
2. **Stopping is one deliberate step and always works. Starting is a decision made
   in setup.** The hub stops automation and never turns it on.
3. **Every page that can start or follow a repair says whether the repository is
   automatic**, so nobody repeats an attempt Eli already made or waits for one it
   will not start.
4. **Administrators see and stop. Everyone else sees one sentence.** Automatic
   repairs have no owner and an ordinary user cannot read them, so the pages do not
   claim what an ordinary user cannot check.

| Who | Sees |
| --- | --- |
| Administrator | The panel on the hub, the card on an automatic repair, the full note on the repair page, the stop controls |
| Anyone else who can use Eli repairs | On the repair page of an automatic repository: one sentence saying so. Nothing else |

### The hub: Automatic repairs

A panel on `/repairs` for administrators when at least one enabled policy is
Automatic. Between **In progress** and **History**, so the page still opens on
what needs the person.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  setup["Setup line: Ready to repair, Automatic on 2 repositories"] --> needs["Needs you"]
  needs --> progress["In progress"]
  progress --> auto["Automatic repairs (2)"]
  auto --> history["History"]
```

Title **Automatic repairs**, description "Eli repairs failed pull request checks
on these repositories without asking. It pushes one commit and never merges."
The header action is **Stop all** when there are two or more, and **Setup**. One
row per repository, repositories with a problem first and then by name:

* the repository name, and under it who pays ("Paid by Team provider, model-name")
  and whether workflow file edits are allowed;
* **health**: "Ready", or the problem in a sentence with the way to fix it
  ("The provider is disabled. Choose another in setup." linking to
  `/repairs/setup?repo=`). The problem is that the installation provider is
  missing (deleting a provider leaves its policies with none), disabled, or not
  an installation provider at all. A removed GitHub installation cannot appear:
  its policies are deleted with it;
* **allowance**: "3 of 5 attempts used in the last 24 hours" with a bar. Requests
  and automatic repairs share it, and the row says so in its tooltip. When it is
  spent: "All 5 attempts used. Automatic repairs here wait until 14:05." (the
  moment the oldest attempt leaves the window), in the warning tone;
* **last**: the outcome badge of the most recent automatic repair that is still in
  the history, its pull request and how long ago, linking to its page, or "None
  yet"; and "1 running now" when one is queued, working or checking;
* **Stop automatic repairs**, which opens the dialog below.

On a phone each row stacks: name and health, allowance, last, button. The panel
reads on the hub's ten-second timer with the rest of the page, and a failed read
keeps the last answer and says so in one line.

### Stopping

One dialog, used for a repository and for all of them. It names what will stop,
then asks what should happen instead:

* **Ask me first** (chosen): "When checks fail, Eli offers a repair under Needs you
  and waits for you."
* **Turn repairs off**: "Eli neither offers nor starts a repair here, and nobody
  can request one, until it is turned on again in setup."

and says what happens to work in flight: "A repair that has not pushed yet stops
without changing the branch. One that has pushed carries on watching its checks."
The button is **Stop automatic repairs**. Afterwards a toast says what the
repository does now, and the panel drops it.

Turning repairs off clears only the policy's enable switch. The mode, provider,
allowance and workflow setting stay, so switching it back on in setup resumes
Automatic as it was. Choosing Ask me first keeps them too. Neither needs the
provider to be working, which is the point: it is the route for the day the
provider is the problem.

The stop never turns anything on. There is no **Resume** on the hub.

### The attempt page

For an automatic repair:

* the facts gain **Started by** "Automatic repairs, by the repository's policy";
* an administrator gets a card, **Automatic repairs on acme/widgets**, saying
  where the policy stands now: still automatic (allowance used, who pays,
  **Stop automatic repairs**), or no longer ("This repository asks first now",
  "Repairs are off for this repository", "Automatic repairs are no longer set for
  this repository"), with the link to its policy in setup. If the status cannot be
  read the card says so and the rest of the page is unaffected.

### The repair page

Readiness says which mode the repository is in (`policy_mode`). When it is
automatic, a note sits above the decision:

* **Administrator, Eli has already tried this failure on its own**: "Eli already
  tried this on its own: [outcome]. [View the attempt]. It does not try the same
  commit twice by itself, so starting again here is the retry." The match is the
  pull request and the commit the page is about;
* **Administrator, nothing started**: "No automatic repair has started for this
  failure. Eli starts from GitHub's report of a failed job, so a failure from
  before Automatic was switched on, or one whose report did not arrive, is not
  picked up. A spent allowance also holds it back. You can start one yourself
  below." When the allowance check is the blocked one, the note says that is the
  reason;
* **Anyone else**: "This repository repairs failed checks automatically. An
  administrator can see what Eli has done."

A repair that is running opens its own page, as before, so the note never has to
describe one.

### The setup line

Gains "Automatic on 2 repositories" next to "Ask me first on 1 repository", for
administrators, when the number is above zero. It is the count of enabled
policies set to Automatic.

## Data and API

All additive. No migration: both new reads are queries over `eli_repairs` and
`eli_repair_policies`.

### `GET /assistant/repairs/automatic`

Administrator (`assistant.read`). One entry per enabled Automatic policy:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `repo`, `installation_id`, `provider_id` | The policy |
| `provider_name`, `model` | The installation provider, empty when it is gone |
| `problem` | Present only when automatic repairs here cannot run, in a sentence |
| `allow_workflows`, `daily_limit` | The policy |
| `used` | Attempts on this repository in the last 24 hours, by anyone, cleared ones included: the number `EnqueueEliRepair` compares to the limit |
| `next_free_at` | When the oldest attempt in the window leaves it. Present when `used` is above zero |
| `running` | Automatic repairs queued, working or checking |
| `last` | `{id, state, pull_number, updated_at}` of the newest automatic repair not cleared from the history |

### `POST /assistant/repairs/automatic/stop`

Administrator (`assistant.write`). Body `{repos: [..1 to 50..], then: "ask_first" | "off"}`.
Answers 200 with `{results: [{repo, changed, error?}]}`:

* a repository that is Automatic and enabled is changed (`then` `ask_first` sets
  Automatic off and Ask me first on; `off` clears the enable switch) and
  `changed` is true;
* a repository that is not automatic any more is `changed: false` with no error,
  so a second press, or a second administrator, is not an error;
* a repository with no policy is `changed: false` with an `error` saying so.

An empty list, more than fifty, or any other `then` is 422. One audit row
`assistant.repair_automatic_stop` is written per repository changed, with the
actor and `then`. The route validates nothing about the provider, because it only
relaxes a policy.

### Readiness says the mode

`policy_mode` on the readiness answer: `automatic`, `ask_first` or `manual`, absent
until readiness has reached the policy check.

## Security and privacy

* Both new routes are administrator routes. A viewer or operator is refused by the
  role gate, as for every other administrator route, and the route-authorisation
  table covers them.
* The overview holds provider names, model names and counts. It holds no key, no
  log text, no pull request title.
* The stop route can only relax a policy. It cannot enable a repository, change a
  provider or raise a limit.
* The ordinary user's sentence on the repair page comes from `policy_mode`, which
  readiness already computes for them, and tells them nothing about attempts they
  cannot read.

## Tests

* Store: usage counts the window and no more, cleared rows included, per
  repository; activity counts running automatic repairs only and returns the
  newest non-cleared automatic repair per repository.
* Controller: the overview lists enabled Automatic policies only; reports a
  missing, disabled and personal provider as problems and a working one as none;
  `next_free_at` is the oldest attempt plus 24 hours;
  stop changes `ask_first` and `off` as specified, keeps provider, limit and mode,
  succeeds with the provider gone, is idempotent, and reports an unknown
  repository; a queued automatic repair of a stopped repository is blocked when
  the worker reaches it (existing behaviour, pinned); readiness names the mode.
* API: role table rows for both routes; the shape of the overview; the stop
  route's 422s, per-repository results and audit rows; a viewer is refused.
* UI unit: the allowance, last-repair and problem wording, the ordering, the
  setup count, the dialog copy, the note's three states.
* Playwright: the hub panel (absent when nothing is automatic and for an ordinary
  user, present with rows otherwise, a full allowance, a problem, stop one, stop
  all, a refused stop), the setup line, the attempt card, the repair page note in
  its three states; the accessibility and phone audits cover the panel and the
  dialog; the gallery shows every state.

## Delivery

One pull request after the merged one. Docs: `docs/eli.md` (a section on watching
and stopping automatic repairs), `docs/ui.md` (the tour), `docs/api-surface.md`,
the OpenAPI definition and its two generated copies, and one hub screenshot with
the panel in it.

## Out of scope

* A **Resume** button, a pause that remembers, or a schedule. Starting automation
  stays a decision in setup.
* Stopping one repair. Turning the repository off already stops a repair before it
  pushes.
* Overview, Recent failures learning that Eli is repairing a failure. The repair
  page already follows a running repair.
* Changing the allowance, provider or workflow setting from the hub.
* Notifications when a limit is reached.

## Decisions taken, and how to reverse them

| Decision | To reverse |
| --- | --- |
| Stopping is a route of its own and not the policy save, so it works when the provider is the problem, writes its own audit row and is one call for many repositories | The hub sends `PUT /assistant/repairs/policy` for each repository |
| Turn off clears only `enabled`, so setup's switch resumes it | Clear the mode too |
| No Resume on the hub | Add a button that sends the policy save |
| No undo on the stop's toast | A toast action that sends the policy save with the old values |
| The panel sits between In progress and History | Move the element |
| The panel is for administrators because automatic repairs have no owner | Give automatic repairs an owner, which is a migration |

## Risks

* The hub makes one more read every ten seconds for an administrator. It is three
  small queries over a table that holds a repair per failure, and an administrator
  with nothing automatic gets an empty list.
* The allowance shown is the repository's, shared with requests, so a person's own
  limit of ten a day is not in it. The repair page's readiness already shows that.
* A stop that races a repair already publishing cannot take the commit back. The
  dialog says so ("One that has pushed carries on watching its checks").
* A pull request opened from a failure that Zoomies learnt only by polling is
  never repaired automatically. The note says so; making Automatic reconcile as
  Ask me first does is a larger change and not part of this one.

# Give every Eli repair a page that says what it is fixing

Agreed in conversation on 18 October 2026, written against checkout `6efa071`.
The design was reviewed as a mockup (hub, repair page, attempt page, and the
phone versions of two of them) before this was written, and approved with one
choice made by the owner: the failing job's error output is shown **on demand,
redacted, and never stored**. All of it is built, in the pull request that carries
this document. The implementation plan is
[2026-10-18-eli-repair-workspace-plan.md](2026-10-18-eli-repair-workspace-plan.md),
which says where the build departed from it.

## What was asked

From Overview, Recent failures, **Fix with Eli** lands on a page that does not
say what the request is. The owner wants to see which repository, which pull
request, which job and which step, with links to GitHub and the failure's
details, and wants the whole experience brought to a professional standard, on a
phone as much as on a desktop. A separate repair page, apart from the setup
material, was suggested as one way to get there.

## What the code does today

| Fact | Where | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fix with Eli passes only `repo` and `run` | `web/src/lib/overview/RecentFailures.svelte`, `web/src/lib/jobs/JobWhy.svelte` | The page cannot say which job was opened, though Zoomies holds the workflow, job, failed step, branch, commit and run link for that run |
| The arrival state prints "Fix the failure in repo, run N", then readiness | `web/src/lib/repairs/RepairJourney.svelte` | A person decides whether to spend an attempt with no view of the failure |
| Readiness fetches the PR's title, author, branch and link, and returns only the number and head | `internal/controller/eli_experience.go`, `github.RepairPull` | The facts the server already has are thrown away |
| Readiness returns before it looks the pull request up when the identity or write-access check fails | same | The blocked state, the one a person most needs explained, has the least context |
| A repair started from the page or an offer records no run and no job, and no repair records a PR title, branch or failing job | `requestPinnedEliRepair`, `store.EliRepair` | History rows and a single repair cannot say what they were about |
| Links are written as `https://github.com/...` | `RepairRow.svelte`, `RepairJourney.svelte` | Wrong on the GitHub Enterprise Server installations the product supports |
| One 600-line component stacks offers, the flow, setup and history, and Settings embeds the same component | `web/src/lib/settings/EliRepairs.svelte`, `AssistantPanel.svelte` | The page is long, the first screen on a phone is mostly chrome, and there is no address for one attempt |
| There is no read of one repair | `internal/api/router.go` | An attempt cannot be linked to or followed by id |

## Design

Four pages, each doing one job, and a repair that can be linked to.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  overview["Overview: Recent failures"] -->|Fix with Eli| new["/repairs/new"]
  why["Job drawer: Why"] -->|Fix with Eli| new
  hub["/repairs"] -->|Review repair| new
  hub -->|Repair a PR| new
  new -->|Fix with Eli| attempt["/repairs/:id"]
  hub --> attempt
  attempt -->|Try another attempt| new
  hub --> setup["/repairs/setup"]
  new -->|Repair setup| setup
```

| Address | Page | Job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/repairs` | Hub | What needs me, what is running, what happened |
| `/repairs/new` | Repair page | One failure: what failed, can Eli act on it, start |
| `/repairs/:id` | Attempt | One repair: live progress, outcome, what to try next |
| `/repairs/setup` | Setup | The GitHub account link, repository policies and verification |

`/repairs/new` and `/repairs/setup` are listed before `/repairs/:id` in the router,
as `/pools/new` is before `/pools/:id`. The navigation entry stays one item,
Eli repairs, lit on all four because they live under one path.

### The repair page, `/repairs/new`

It is addressed by what it is about: `?repo=&run=` (from a failure), `?repo=&pull=`
(a pasted pull request), or `?offer=` (an offer). `?job=` names the Zoomies job
the person opened, so it can be marked "You opened this one". A pasted GitHub
pull request URL is parsed as today and becomes `?repo=&pull=`.

From the top, in one column on a phone and with a decision card beside it from
1180px wide:

1. **The case.** A card with a red rail: when it failed; the title (the pull
   request's title once it is known, otherwise "CI #482 failed on branch");
   links and chips for the repository, the pull request number, the branch, the
   commit (short SHA, a copy button for the full one) and the run; and facts:
   where it ran (pool and runner), which jobs failed with the step each failed
   at, and where the person came from. When the pull request has not been looked
   up the card says so in a dashed chip instead of leaving a gap.
2. **The decision.** One card that states the single next thing. Blocked: what
   to fix and the button for it (check again; manage access on GitHub; repair
   setup). Ready: the payer and model, the attempts left and when they reset,
   whether workflow files may be edited, the branch it will push to, an optional
   note to Eli, and **Fix with Eli**. It says what Eli will not do: merge, or
   force-push. On a phone it follows the case.
3. **What failed.** One disclosure per failed job (the one the person opened
   first and open), each with the job name, a badge saying whether the workflow
   or the fleet is to blame, the failing step and its number, how long it ran, a
   link to the job on GitHub and one to the job in Zoomies, and:
   * the explanation, from the job's `fault_domain` and `fault_fix`. When the
     fleet caused the failure (out of memory, runner lost) the card says a repair
     is unlikely to help and points at re-running, so an attempt is not spent on
     something code cannot fix;
   * **Error output**: the failing job's error lines, read from GitHub when the
     disclosure is opened, redacted, labelled "Read from GitHub a moment ago.
     Nothing here is stored.", with Copy and Fetch again. If the person cannot
     read logs yet (write access not verified) it says why instead;
   * the steps, collapsed once error output is available and open when it is
     not.
4. **Can Eli act on this?** A checklist of every check readiness makes, in the
   order it makes them, each `ok`, `blocked` with its sentence and its own
   action, or **not checked yet** when an earlier blocker stopped the run. When
   everything passes it collapses to one line ("All 9 checks passed") with the
   list one click away.

The page keeps today's behaviours that matter: it checks readiness on arrival and
never calls a model to do so; **Fix with Eli** is the only thing that spends an
attempt; a target that changed (`fixed`, `closed`, `superseded`) replaces the
card with the explanation, the original run link and "Check the current PR"; a
refused start because the head moved re-reads readiness. After a start the
browser moves to `/repairs/:id`.

### The attempt page, `/repairs/:id`

Header: the pull request title (or the case summary when no title was kept), a
status badge, who asked and with which kind of provider, when it started. Actions:
Open PR, Open run, Refresh. Beneath it:

* **Progress** for a running repair: queued, read the failed checks, preparing
  the fix, pushing the commit, watching CI, as a horizontal track on a desktop and
  a vertical one on a phone, with elapsed time and a line saying the person may
  leave. It polls every four seconds while the repair is active and stops at a
  terminal state. The existing `REPAIR_TRACK` and `trackIndex` are kept.
* **Outcome** for a finished repair: a banner in the outcome's tone with the
  repair's own message, then **What to try next**, which is the existing retry
  guidance made specific by failure code (see below), with Try another attempt,
  Open PR and Repair setup.
* **What Eli was asked to fix**: the case, from the snapshot the repair kept
  (below), with Error output on demand again.
* **Technical details**, collapsed except on a finished repair: the model calls
  as a table (input tokens, output tokens, request size, time; "unknown" where the
  provider did not report usage, never zero), source supplied, stage reached,
  failure code, Copy investigation details.
* A side card with the facts of the attempt (id, result, started, finished, took,
  provider, commit pushed) and, once finished, a timeline.

A repair that is not the caller's (or does not exist) answers 404, and the page
says "This repair is not in your history." without saying which.

### The hub, `/repairs`

* A one-line **setup bar**: ready or not, the linked GitHub account, and for an
  administrator how many repositories are on Ask me first; **Manage setup**.
* **Needs you**: offers, each with the PR title and number, repository, branch,
  when it failed, the failing jobs and steps, **Review repair** and **Dismiss**.
* **In progress**: running repairs with the stage and a five-segment indicator.
* **History**: the existing filters, paging and clearing, with richer rows (status
  badge, PR title, repository and number, branch, the failing job and step, the
  fix commit when there is one, who or what triggered it, when and how long) that
  link to the attempt page. Selecting repairs to clear them moves behind a
  **Select** button, so the list reads as a record until somebody wants to edit
  it.
* Actions: Refresh, **Repair a PR** (paste a URL), Setup.

### Setup, `/repairs/setup`

The account card, repository policies and link-an-account forms move out of
`EliRepairs.svelte` into `RepairSetupPanel.svelte` unchanged in behaviour. The
repair page's blockers still open a setup wizard for the failure in hand
(`RepairSetup.svelte`) so a person fixes what is missing and stays on the
failure. Settings, Eli AI Assistant no longer embeds the whole composite; it
shows a short card that links to the hub and to setup.

### Old addresses

`/repairs?repo=&run=` and `/repairs?repo=&pull=` keep working: the hub replaces
the address with `/repairs/new` and the same query, so bookmarks, docs and the
problems drawer's old links land in the right place. The offers banner on the
Overview keeps pointing at `/repairs`.

## Data and API

Every change is additive. No migration: what a repair remembers goes into the
existing `details` JSON, and an old row without it still decodes and renders.

### Readiness says what it found

`GET /assistant/repairs/readiness` keeps `blockers` and gains:

* `pull`: `{number, title, author, branch, base, url, open}`, present once the
  pull request has been looked up, including when it turns out to be closed or
  out of date, because "PR #1131 is closed" reads better with its title. It is
  set only after the access check, so it never reaches someone whose GitHub
  account cannot write to the repository, which is the rule offers already follow.
  `github.RepairPull` gains `Base` (GitHub's `base.ref`) for it.
* `checks`: one entry per check in the order `identity`, `provider`,
  `installation`, `access`, `policy`, `budget`, `pull`, `checks`, `permissions`,
  each `{code, status, message}` with `status` one of `ok`, `blocked`,
  `unchecked`. A check the function returned before reaching is `unchecked`.
  `blockers` is unchanged, so an older client reads the same answer. The labels
  are the UI's, keyed by `code`; an unknown code from a newer server shows its
  code.

### One repair, by id

`GET /assistant/repairs/{id}` returns one `EliRepair`, scoped as the list is:
an administrator reaches every repair, anyone else only their own, and a
caller with no identity reaches nothing. A missing id and one the caller may
not see both answer 404 with the same words. A cleared repair is still readable by
id, since clearing hides a row from the history and does nothing else.
Role: viewer, action `assistant.own`, as the list.

### What a repair remembers

`EliRepairDetails` gains `case`, written when the repair is queued from the page
or an offer (the pull request is in hand) and filled in by the worker for the
other triggers once it has resolved the pull request:

```text
case: {
  pull_title, pull_url, author, branch,
  run_url, workflow, run_number,
  jobs: [ { name, step, url, duration_ms } ]   // at most 10
}
```

The jobs come from Zoomies' own records (`store.JobFilter.RunIDs` when the run is
known, otherwise the repository's failed jobs at the pull request's head), the
step from `Job.FailedStep()`, so the page and the job drawer name the same step.
Every string is clipped, and none is ever rendered as markup. It holds no log
text. `EliRepairDetails` is the one JSON blob the row already writes on every
save, so the snapshot survives the worker's saves without a second write path.

### Starting from a failure

`POST /assistant/repairs` takes an optional `run_id` and stores it on the row, as
the offer's accept does from the offer's own `run_id`. It changes nothing about
evidence: `RepairFailures` still reads one job only when `job_id` is set, and
the UI path never sets it. The point is that a repair can say which run it came
from.

### Error output, on demand

`GET /assistant/repairs/error-output?repo=&job_id=` returns
`{lines: string[], note?: string}` for one job, with `job_id` being GitHub's.

* Personal account only and `assistant.own`, as readiness. The caller's linked
  GitHub account must still have write access to the repository, checked the
  way readiness checks it, so job logs, which can hold anything a workflow
  prints, are read only for someone entitled to them.
* It uses `RepairFailures` with an empty pull request and the job id, which is
  the path the worker already uses for a single job (`ContextJobErrors`: the
  last 8 MiB of the log, `##[error]` lines and the line before, bounded), then
  runs every line through `prrepair.Redact`. No new GitHub client method.
* A log GitHub no longer has is an answer, not an error: `lines` is empty and
  `note` says so.
* Cached in memory for a minute by repository and job, so a person pressing
  Fetch again costs one download, not one each. Never written to the database,
  never logged.

### Links

The UI no longer writes `https://github.com/`. A job's `html_url` is GitHub's own
job address for the host that sent it, so the run, repository and commit
addresses are derived from it (`links.ts`, a pure helper with unit tests), and the
pull request's from `pull.url` or the snapshot. Only `http` and `https` addresses
become links.

## Security and privacy

* The pull request's title and author appear only after the caller's GitHub
  account is verified to write to the repository (readiness) or on a repair the
  caller owns or administers. The repair record now keeps a title, branch and
  author as the offer record already keeps a title. The MCP tools read these rows
  through a field whitelist and so do not see them.
* Error output is never stored, is redacted by the same filter that protects the
  model's input, and is fetched only for a verified writer. Redaction cannot
  recognise every secret, which the documentation already says about model use.
* Everything a workflow controls (job, step, workflow and branch names, error
  lines) and every pull request title is untrusted. It is rendered as text, and
  the hostile-input specs gain a case for these pages.
* The page never starts a repair without the press of the button that says so,
  and readiness never calls a model.

## UI structure

Routes: `web/src/routes/EliRepairs.svelte` (hub, rewritten),
`EliRepairNew.svelte`, `EliRepairAttempt.svelte`, `EliRepairSetup.svelte`.

Components in `web/src/lib/repairs/`: `CaseCard`, `FailedJobs` (with
`ErrorOutput`), `ReadinessChecklist`, `DecisionCard` (blocked and ready),
`ProgressTrack`, `OutcomeBanner`, `RepairStatusBadge`, `RepairRow` (rewritten),
`OfferList`, `SetupBar`, `RepairSetupPanel` (extracted), and `RepairSetup`
(kept). `RepairJourney` and `lib/settings/EliRepairs.svelte` are deleted once
nothing imports them.

Pure TypeScript with unit tests: `case.ts` (the case from readiness, jobs and a
snapshot), `links.ts`, `checks.ts` (codes to labels and actions), `guidance.ts`
(next steps), `workspace.ts` (the page's states, replacing the stage machine in
`journey.ts`), and the repair-state mapping onto the fixed status tones in
`lib/status.ts`, which is where every status in the product comes from:

| State | Tone | Shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| queued | pending | dashed |
| working | busy | filled |
| checking | busy | filled |
| succeeded | idle | filled |
| checks_failed, failed, blocked, interrupted | danger | triangle |
| superseded | neutral | square |
| unverified | pending | hollow |

Tokens only, no new library, no raw colour. Every state the new components can be
in (blocked, ready, changed, running, each outcome, locked and loaded error
output) gets an entry in the component gallery before a route reaches it.

### What to try next

`guidance.ts` maps a failure code, or a terminal state when there is none, to
a headline and at most three steps. The copy as first written; a wording change
in review does not change the mapping:

| Code or state | Say |
| --- | --- |
| `unsupported_fix` | Add a note that points at the file or the test, then try again. Read the error output. The quickest fix may be yours |
| `context_limit` | The failure and the source were too big for one attempt. Name the file or the test so Eli reads less |
| `source_unavailable` | Eli could not read the source. Check the App's Contents permission and that the PR changes fewer than 100 files |
| `provider_unavailable` | The provider failed. Test it in Eli settings, then try again |
| `rate_limited` | The provider is rate limiting you. Wait, or check the quota |
| `provider_credentials` | The provider refused your key. Update it in Eli settings |
| `output_limit` | The model ran out of room. Lower its reasoning effort or choose a model with more output |
| `setup_needed` | Eli's access changed. Check repair setup, then check readiness again |
| `checks_failed` | Eli pushed a commit and the checks still fail. Open the commit; another attempt starts from the new head |
| `interrupted`, `unverified`, `superseded`, `blocked` | One sentence each: what happened and the one thing to check |

## Tests

**Go.** Store: `GetEliRepair` scoping (owner, other user, administrator, no
identity), the `case` round trip, and an old row without it. Controller: readiness
returns `pull` once looked up and not before the access check, returns `checks`
with `unchecked` after an early blocker, and keeps `blockers` as it was; a
UI-started repair records its run and its case; the worker fills a missing case;
error output refuses an unverified caller, redacts, and caches. API: the new
routes in the route and role table in `api_test.go`, a 404 that does not tell
"missing" from "not yours", and the 422s. `make openapi` leaves the tree clean.

**Unit** (`web/unit`, built to the generated types): `case.ts`, `links.ts` (including
an Enterprise Server address and a non-http one), `checks.ts`, `guidance.ts`,
`workspace.ts`, the status mapping.

**Playwright**: a new spec for the repair page (blocked, ready, changed, a fleet
fault, error output, the start moving to the attempt page), one for the attempt
page (running, finished, not found) and updates to `repairs.spec.ts`,
`repair-history.spec.ts` and `repair-setup.spec.ts` for the hub and setup split.
Each runs on a desktop and a phone viewport with the accessibility pass, in both
themes, with no horizontal scroll. The gallery spec covers the new states. The
screenshot script gains the new pages.

**Docs**: `docs/eli.md` (the page tour and the repair flow), `docs/ui.md`,
`docs/api-surface.md` (the new and changed rows), the nav description in
`docs/ui-guidelines.md`, and `roadmap/progress.md`. Prose follows the repository
voice.

## Delivery

One draft pull request, built test first in four stages, each of which leaves
the product working:

1. **Data**: readiness `pull` and `checks`, `GET /assistant/repairs/{id}`,
   `details.case`, `run_id` on start, error output, `make openapi`, the Go tests.
2. **The repair page**: `/repairs/new`, the new components, the entry points from
   Overview and the job drawer, the old address handled.
3. **The attempt page and the hub**: `/repairs/:id`, the status mapping, the
   rewritten hub and history rows.
4. **Setup and docs**: `/repairs/setup`, the Settings card, the deleted
   composites, docs and screenshots.

## Out of scope

* Live repair events on the stream: the pages poll, as the history does.
* Storing error output with a repair. The owner chose on demand.
* A change to what a repair does: limits, payer, evidence, safety rules.
* Notifications outside the product, and MCP tools for the new data.
* One page per pull request holding all its attempts.

## Decisions taken, and how to reverse them

* **Error output on demand and not stored.** Storing it would add a redacted,
  bounded excerpt to `details`, which is the owner's call to revisit.
* **The pull request's title only after access is verified.** Relaxing it means
  setting `pull` before the access check in `EliReadiness`.
* **Clearing behind a Select button.** The bulk logic is unchanged and only its
  entry point moved.
* **Steps collapsed once error output exists.** A default, one attribute.

## Risks

* **GitHub API volume.** Readiness already calls GitHub on every visit. Error
  output is opt-in and cached for a minute.
* **Retention.** Zoomies' job records may be pruned, so a repair keeps its own
  snapshot, and the repair page degrades to "details no longer retained".
* **Size.** The UI change is large. Four stages, a unit-tested core and the
  gallery keep each step reviewable, and the app shell budget is untouched
  because every new page is a lazily loaded route.

# E3 checkout preview: policy and web flow

Date: 19 October 2026. Package: ZF-244. Follows merged #1024.

## Outcome

An operator can read one workflow file for an exact successful push run, review
it, declare that full history is not needed, and keep an immutable preview of the
one-line change, from the web UI, with the same two calls on the REST API. Nothing
is published, approved or run.

## Decisions

* **Policy is two instance settings**, `optimisation.source_reads` and
  `optimisation.workflow_edits`, both off by default and live. `OptimisationPolicy`
  reads the running configuration on every call, so the existing before-read and
  before-save policy rechecks see a withdrawal at once. No request field carries
  policy.
* **Inspection is separate from capture.** A history review has to bind the digest
  and head the operator was shown, so the source must be read before the review
  can exist. Inspection runs the same admitted read as capture (shared flight,
  hourly allowance, half-core reserve, seven requests) and retains nothing.
  Capture reads again and refuses a digest that moved. The cost is two admissions
  from the 20 an hour; the alternative, retaining unreviewed source, was refused.
* **The scope of the declaration is fixed by the server.** A request supplies
  `history_reviewed: true` and the head and digest it saw.
* **Replay never returns the file.** Source is shown once, at inspection. A
  retained preview answers with the one changed line.
* **New actions** `optimisations.read` and `optimisations.write`, operator, with
  `jobs:read` also required, public visitors refused.
* **IDs.** GitHub run and job IDs are decimal strings on the wire and in the form.

## Enablement is part of the flow

The owner asked that nobody be sent to Settings. The switches are turned on at the
point of need, never silently:

* `GET /optimisations/enablement` tells any operator the state and, when they cannot
  change it, why. `PUT` (administrator) sets both settings together through the
  settings planner, so the environment lock, validation and audit row are the Settings
  page's own.
* The Checkout preview page opens with a card that says in plain words what it allows,
  with one press for an administrator and a copyable request for everyone else. A 403
  re-reads the state, so a switch turned off elsewhere is noticed.
* Repair setup offers it as an unticked box for an administrator. It is not on by
  default because repairing a pull request does not need source previews, and the
  handoff keeps each mode's grant separate.
* Eli has no mutation tools and gains none: it can point at the page, not press it.

## Nobody calls an endpoint

The owner's rule: customers and users use the web UI, never URLs. So every route in
this slice has a screen that drives it, and the screens ask for as little as possible.

* **No positions.** A selection is a run, an attempt and a job. A `Locate` read finds
  the job's one previewable checkout step from the source it already reads, within the
  same seven requests, and returns the positions it found. Two candidates or none is an
  explained refusal, never a guess. Capture is sent the positions the reviewer saw.
* **A picker, not a form.** The page lists a repository's recent successful push jobs
  from the existing jobs list; the job drawer has a **Preview a checkout change**
  button on exactly those jobs. Typing IDs survives only as a collapsed fallback.
* **Names, not numbers.** The review step says which step in which job was found.

## Not in this slice

Approval, draft publication, E2 verification of a published change, CLI, MCP and
Eli access. The retained envelope stays private; Eli is not offered these routes.

## Verification

Controller: policy follows live settings; inspection refuses while either switch is
off before any read, retains nothing. API: inspect, capture and replay shapes against
the spec; settings gate with the setting named in the refusal; roles, scopes,
anonymous and visitor refusals before any read; malformed and forged-field bodies;
unconfirmed review spends no read; stale digest is a 409 and is not retained. Web:
unit tests for exact identity parsing; browser tests on desktop and phone for escaped
source, the declaration gating the button, a selection edit dropping the review, a
refusal naming the setting, and a replay with no overflow. No live GitHub, model or
fleet.

# Keeping a host at its recommended size

Date: 19 October 2026.

## Why

A CI job failed with `no space left on device` on a rented Proxmox machine whose
capacity and reserve were not the ones **Adjust** recommends. The dialog already
knows the right numbers; nothing applied them, and nothing counted the disk when
deciding how many runners a machine holds.

## Decisions

* **What is adjusted:** capacity (the number of runners) and the CPU, memory and
  disk reserves. Not the operating system: host tuning stays consent-based and
  never unattended (`internal/hosttune/AGENTS.md`).
* **The disk is a budget as well as a reserve.** Capacity is the smallest of the
  CPU, memory and disk counts, with 10 GiB of working room per runner
  (`scheduler.AutoAdjustRunnerDiskMB`). It is a constant for now; the audit row and
  the page say when it was the binding figure.
* **One source of truth.** The recommendation is a pure function in
  `internal/scheduler/recommend.go`, held to the same cases as
  `web/src/lib/hosts/recommend.ts`. `GET /hosts/{id}/recommendation` serves it, and the
  dialog uses it where the disk is the binding figure.
* **A per-host choice with a fleet default.** `host_auto_adjust` in its own table
  (`on`, `off`, or no row to follow `scheduler.host_auto_adjust`, **on by default** at the owner's request, so a machine nobody sized is covered without anyone finding the switch),
  so the central host row and its queries do not change. Provider-rented hosts are
  hosts, so the fleet default reaches them.
* **Guardrails.** Never un-pause (capacity 0), never touch a cordoned, retired,
  incompatible or silent host, five minutes between moves, and the same
  stranded-pool refusal a person gets. Every move is audited under the system's name.

## Not done

A runtime response to a disk that is filling now (a throttle rung for disk
pressure, or pruning) is a separate piece. The reserve already stops new runners
starting when free disk is at or below it, and this keeps the reserve right.
The 10 GiB allowance is not yet a setting.

# E3 cache preview: supplied-evidence foundation

Date: 23 October 2026. Package: ZF-244. Starts the wider optimisation
catalogue with dependency/build cache, after checkout scope.

## Outcome

A pure calculation turns one complete workflow file and one root lockfile at a
pinned head into a reviewable proposal: add `cache: npm`, `cache: yarn` or
`cache: pnpm` to the one pinned `actions/setup-node` step. It reads nothing,
calls no model, retains nothing and publishes nothing.

## Decisions

* **One supported tool and one step.** Only `actions/setup-node` pinned to a
  commit is supported. Zero or more than one such step is an explained refusal,
  not a guess about which one the lockfile belongs to.
* **The lockfile decides the manager.** A root `package-lock.json` or
  `npm-shrinkwrap.json` means npm, `yarn.lock` means yarn and `pnpm-lock.yaml`
  means pnpm. A nested lockfile, an unknown name, more than one supplied
  lockfile, an oversized or non-UTF-8 one is refused. The lockfile content is
  used only for its digest; the proposal keeps its path and SHA-256.
* **Repeated setup evidence is a declaration.** The caller supplies an evidence
  ID, the same head and source/lockfile digests, and the number of runs and mean
  setup milliseconds (2 to 100 runs). It is not independently attested; the
  collector that binds exact run identities is a later slice.
* **The edit is an insertion, not a reserialisation.** The new key goes directly
  after the step's `with:` line at the indentation of its first key. The exact
  preimage must be unique. Inline/flow mappings, an empty mapping, an existing
  cache key and duplicate preimages are refused. Comments, unrelated bytes and
  line endings are preserved, and the same `prrepair` bounds apply.
* **No saving claim.** Verification is always `inconclusive`. The setup time is
  descriptive, the cache is the action's own and shared with whoever can write
  the repository's cache, and passing CI alone cannot establish improvement.
* **No runtime yet.** There is no GitHub collector, store row, route, CLI, MCP,
  Eli or UI change. Those follow only after this calculation and its refusals
  are stable.

## Not in this slice

Reading the workflow or lockfile from GitHub, selecting a setup step from a
real run, retention, approval, draft publication, E2 verification, CLI/MCP/Eli
and UI. Bounded readiness polling and sharding remain later catalogue items.

## Verification

Tests cover npm, yarn, pnpm and npm-shrinkwrap mapping; insertion position and
byte preservation; CRLF; unpinned, missing, duplicate and unsupported setup
steps; cache already set; inline and empty mappings; nested, oversized,
mismatched and non-UTF-8 lockfiles; policy, head, digest, run-count and setup-time
refusals; and currentness refusal when the source, lockfile or policy changes.
No live GitHub, model or fleet.

Date: 23 October 2026. Package: ZF-244. Follows the cache source binding.

An operator can inspect a cache preview, keep the exact one they reviewed, and
replay it for fourteen days. The retained record is private and immutable: the
workflow source and setup samples are stored, the lockfile is represented by its
path, mode and SHA-256, and a transport returns the insertion block and evidence
summary but never the full workflow or lockfile.

  `optimisation_cache_previews` with the same fourteen-day lifetime, twenty
  installation and one hundred global caps as checkout previews, an `opc_` ID
  prefix, an atomic audit row and cascade on installation deletion. The checkout
  table and envelope are untouched.

  the preview and returns its head, workflow digest, lockfile digest, insertion
  block, package manager, setup samples summary and explanation. Nothing is
  retained. `POST /optimisations/cache/previews` re-reads the source and history
  and requires the same head and both digests; a moved source is a 409.

# E3 checkout preview: reconciled draft publication

Date: 23 October 2026. Package: ZF-244. Follows the attributed approval slice.

## Outcome

An operator can turn an approved checkout preview into one draft pull request.
The server re-reads the run, its branch, the live settings, the source and the
approval, refuses any change, commits the one reviewed line on a new branch and
opens a draft against the branch the push ran on. It never force-pushes and
never merges.

## Decisions

* **A third instance setting.** `optimisation.publish` is off by default and
  live. Publication needs `optimisation.source_reads`,
  `optimisation.workflow_edits` and `optimisation.publish`; the one-press card
  beside the approved preview turns the publish switch on and turns the two
  preview grants on with it. Turning it off leaves the preview grants alone.
* **Its own action.** `optimisations.publish` is separate from
  `optimisations.write`, so a token that may read, keep and approve previews
  need not be able to write to a repository. It is an operator action, as
  retaining and approving are.
* **The branch is the run's branch.** Checkout evidence now records the push's
  head branch. A preview retained before that has none; it stays readable and
  reproducible, and publishing it is refused with a request to preview again.
  Older evidence needs no migration because the field is optional.
* **The base is pinned.** The draft is based on the preview's head commit and
  refuses if the selected branch has moved. The new branch is derived from the
  preview ID, so a retry finds the same branch.
* **Fresh checks before writing.** The controller re-reads the run, job and
  source through the same admitted read as inspection, rechecks the live policy
  before and after, runs `optimisation.CheckCurrent`, and re-reads the approval
  and retained record. A changed head, source, branch, policy, approval or
  expiry is a refusal.
* **The permission trio.** GitHub needs Contents write, Pull requests write and
  Workflows write to change a file under `.github/workflows`. The App is probed
  before any write and a missing permission is a 403 that names it.
* **Reconciliation, not blind replay.** The branch name is deterministic. A
  retry reuses an existing branch only when its commit has the same tree,
  message and base, and reuses an existing pull request only when its title and
  body match and it is open. Anything different is preserved and refused. A
  lost pull-request response is reconciled by listing the branch's pull
  request; if that read fails, the branch is kept for the retry.
* **One publication per preview.** Migration 0120 adds
  `optimisation_publications`, keyed by the preview and cascading from it. It
  records the branch, base, both commits, the exact approval and preview
  digests, the actor, and the pull request number and URL. The store refuses a
  preview that is expired, unapproved or bound differently, and a repeat
  returns the existing record. Publishing is audited as
  `optimisation.preview_published`.
* **No untrusted text in the pull request.** The title, body and commit message
  are built from the preview ID and server-owned wording, not from repository
  content or the changed line. The diff on GitHub shows the exact change.
* **Not a merge.** Zoomies never merges, never force-pushes and runs no job.
  Verification stays `inconclusive`; the draft is for the repository's own
  review and checks.

## Not in this slice

E2 verification of the published change, CLI, MCP and Eli access. The retained
envelope remains private; publication is web-only.

## Verification

Store: binding, approval requirement, idempotency, audit rollback, expiry,
cascade and corruption. Controller: fresh source/branch/policy/approval checks,
one draft, retry reconciliation, permission refusals and no record after a
failed GitHub write. GitHub: pinned base, draft flag, one commit on a new
branch, reconciliation after a lost response, permission hint and conflicting
branch preservation. API: route authorisation, scopes, moved binding, missing
approval, live publish setting, audit and replay shape. Web: approval gates
publication, the publish button sends the approved binding, the draft link and
no-form state render, publishing turns on from the page, and a phone does not
overflow. All against fakes and mocked routes only.

expires with the preview. It publishes nothing.

## Decisions

* **Approval is a row, not a rewrite.** Migration 0119 adds
  `optimisation_preview_approvals`, keyed by the preview and cascading from it.
  The immutable preview envelope and its storage digest are untouched, so replay
  still recomputes exactly what the reviewer kept. A read returns the approval
  beside the preview, never inside the evidence.
* **The binding is checked, not trusted.** The request names the head and source
  digest. The controller replays the retained preview from stored input, refuses
  anything that does not match, then asks the store to record the approval
  against the preview's storage digest. A moved head, a changed source or a
  corrupt record is a refusal.
* **The server names the actor.** The approver comes from the authenticated
  identity, as the reviewer did. The answer carries both `reviewed_by` and
  `approved_by`.
* **One approval per preview.** The first binding wins. Repeating the same
  approval returns the original record and writes no second audit row. A
  different binding is a conflict. The recommended default is kept: the same
  operator who reviewed may approve, with both people recorded. The owner's
  decision on requiring a different approver remains open and would be a later
  setting, not a silent change to this record.
* **Approval is not publication.** It reads no GitHub source, calls no model and
  consults neither optimisation setting: it neither reads source nor edits a
  workflow. It does not re-read the head, so `currentness` stays `not_checked`.
  Publication remains a later slice with its own opt-in and fresh head, policy
  and source checks.
* **Expiry follows the preview.** The store reads an approval only while its
  preview is inside the fourteen-day lifetime. Pruning or eviction of the
  preview cascades to the approval, and the audit row remains.
* **The page is the surface.** The retained preview card shows the commit and
  source digest, offers an approval declaration to an operator, and shows the
  recorded approver and time once approved. A viewer is not offered the form.

## Not in this slice

Opening a draft pull request, E2 verification of a published change, CLI, MCP
and Eli access. Eli still has no mutation tools for previews.

## Verification

Store: binding, scope, idempotency, audit rollback, corruption, expiry and
cascade. Controller: reviewer and approver recorded, moved binding refused,
replay carries the approval, expiry and cross-scope misses. API: route
authorisation and scopes, malformed and moved bindings, one audit row, replay
shape. Web: the declaration gates the button, the request names the preview's
own binding, the approved state replaces the form, and a phone does not overflow.
No live GitHub, model or fleet.

# A pure preview for bounded readiness polling

**Status:** implemented, awaiting pull request.

## Goal

Turn one fixed sleep in a root workflow into a bounded poll of a readiness
condition, as an exact preview with no GitHub read and no guessed command.

## Owner decision

The condition is supplied by the operator, never inferred from a service name, a
port or a nearby command. The original sleep duration becomes the bound, so the
new step cannot wait longer than the old one. The change is limited to one
literal `sleep <seconds>` step on a literal Ubuntu runner; anything else is
refused. The preview is always inconclusive and never claims a saving.

A fixed sleep is evidence only that the job waited. The caller supplies the
repeated wait timings from the fleet's history; the collector that binds exact
job identities is a later slice.

## What changed

* `internal/kennel/workflow/readiness.go` finds the one fixed sleep on an Ubuntu
  job, returns literal job and step names, and replaces the run scalar with one
  bounded shell loop while preserving bytes outside that block and the file's
  line endings.
* It refuses more than one candidate, a non-Ubuntu or expression runner, a
  Windows/macOS label, a comment, a second command, a folded scalar, fractional
  or suffixed sleeps, and values below two seconds or above one hour.
* `internal/optimisation/readiness.go` computes the preview from a supplied
  workflow, head, evidence and operator condition. It quotes the command for
  `sh`, bounds it with the original duration, applies the edit and reports
  inconclusive verification. `CheckReadinessCurrent` recomputes it.
* The generated step is:
  `timeout <N> sh -c 'until <operator command>; do sleep 1; done'`.
  A timeout exits non-zero, so the old wait's failure boundary is preserved.
* No route, migration, setting, web page, CLI, MCP or Eli access is added yet.

## Refusals

* No unique fixed sleep on a literal Ubuntu runner.
* An empty, multiline, NUL-bearing or oversized condition.
* A stale head or source digest, fewer than two wait samples, or disabled source
  or edit policy.
* A workflow outside the root `.github/workflows` directory.

## Verification

* Workflow tests cover plain and block scalars, CRLF, ambiguity, non-Ubuntu
  runners, comments, extra commands, suffixes and short waits.
* Optimisation tests cover the exact edit, shell quoting with apostrophes,
  currentness, and refusals for policy, head, digest, condition, samples and
  source path.
* `make test`, `make lint`, strict docs and whitespace checks run before the pull

## Next

add the web page that asks for the readiness command and shows the exact block.
CLI/MCP/Eli read access, approval and publication follow the cache pattern. Test
sharding remains a separate catalogue item with its own evidence and capacity
refusal.

# Test sharding foundation: the pure preview

**Status:** implemented, awaiting pull request.

## Goal

A pure, supplied-evidence preview that rewrites one Playwright test job into a
shard matrix plus an aggregator that keeps the job's name, mirroring the cache and
readiness foundations. It reads no source, calls no model and has no runtime
surface.

## Owner decision

[Decision 0014](../decisions/0014-test-sharding-is-offered-for-one-native-shard-flag-and-preserves-the-whole-suite.md):
Playwright's native `--shard=INDEX/TOTAL` only; the original job name survives
through an aggregator; refusals are named; verification is inconclusive.

## What changed

* `workflow.FindPlaywrightTest` finds the one step whose run script is exactly
  `npx playwright test`, `pnpm exec playwright test` or `yarn playwright test`
  with only `--reporter`, `--workers`, `--retries`, `--timeout` and a literal
  `--project`. Anything else is a `ShardRefusal` that says why, including an
  argument that already shards, filters or narrows, `|| true`, and a path.
* It refuses a job that has a strategy, services, outputs, a condition,
  `continue-on-error`, a container or its own concurrency group; a non-Ubuntu or
  expression runner; a name that collides with `<id>-shards`; any artifact upload,
  codecov, coveralls or coverage step; an unnamed or conditional test step; and a
  job too large to review as one block.
* `workflow.ShardChange` renames the job to `<id>-shards`, adds
  `fail-fast: false` and a literal `shard: [1..N]` matrix, appends
  `--shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/N`, and adds a job with the original ID and name
  that `needs` the shards, runs `if: ${{ always() }}` and fails unless every shard
  succeeded. Bytes outside the job's block are untouched and line endings are kept.
* `optimisation.PreviewSharding` takes the source, the evidence and the policy.
  `ChooseShardCount` picks the largest count up to eight and the pool's headroom
  that leaves each shard at least 90 seconds of test. It refuses a suite under
  three minutes and a pool that cannot start two runners at once.
* `ShardEvidenceFromSamples` needs 10 to 100 distinct successful runs and uses the
  median of the test step and of everything before it, so a few slow runs do not
  move the count. The evidence ID is order independent.
* The preview discloses runner time before and after (every shard repeats the
  setup), the runners needed at once, and a wall-clock estimate, and says plainly
  that it is an estimate from medians and not a measured saving. Verification is
  always inconclusive.
* The optimisation purity test lists the new workflow helpers it may call.

## Refusals

No supported step; more than one step; a command that shards, filters or
narrows; a job shape above; fewer than ten runs; a suite too short for two
shards; no headroom; stale or foreign evidence; policy off.

## Verification

Table-driven tests for every refusal, the exact rewrite with CRLF and no job
name, a rewritten workflow that still parses and is refused a second time, the
count rule at its boundaries, medians that ignore outliers, and order-independent
evidence.

## Next

Bounded GitHub source binding and inspection: read the one selected push job and
its workflow, take the timings from the fleet's retained history, and read the
pool's headroom.
